# Changelog

Every release, newest first: what was wrong, why it was wrong, and what changed.
Not a list of commit subjects.

**This file is generated** from the changelog page by
`scripts/changelog-md.py`, which runs as part of the release. Edit the page at
`docs/app/docs/changelog/page.tsx`, not this file: an edit here is overwritten
by the next release, and CI fails on one that has not been.

The rendered version, with syntax highlighting and the weekly rollup, is at
**[gritframework.com/docs/changelog](https://gritframework.com/docs/changelog)**.

Also worth knowing:

- **[Releases](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/releases)** on GitHub, with the
  binaries, their checksums and the signing material described in
  [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
- **[What is stable and what is not](https://gritframework.com/docs/stability)**, per subsystem.
- `grit update` brings the CLI to the latest release; `grit upgrade` brings an
  existing project's framework files up to the CLI it is run with.

---


## v3.535.0 - November 14, 2026

### The system hub and the health page

The fourth redesign release. Two pages that existed to answer &ldquo;is anything wrong&rdquo; and made you read eight cards to find out.

#### Health opens with the answer

One card at the top: the sentence, the counts, and a bar in those proportions, so the answer arrives before any of the words do. Under it the components are grouped into{" "} **Running** and **Not configured**. A single grid put Redis, which a deployment may run without on purpose, between two working components with only a word in small type to tell them apart.

Each not-configured card carries what turning it on would take, in a dashed well:{" "} `Set REDIS_URL in .env to turn this on`. &ldquo;Off&rdquo; answers what, and leaves why and how.

States are pills now. They were a tick for healthy, a warning triangle for degraded, and small uppercase text for the other two: three different objects for one dimension, two of them colour-only, which is nothing at all to a reader who cannot separate the green from the red.

The header's status pill is gone. It said the same thing as the pill in the top bar and the same thing as the card below it: one sentence, three times, on one screen.

#### The hub filters across every tab

Typing in the filter searches all five tabs, because the reason somebody uses it is that they do not know which tab the thing is under. The tabs carry counts, the tiles say{" "} **Open**, and their status pills are live: System health reads &ldquo;6 healthy &middot; 2 off&rdquo; and, on a deployment without Redis, Background Jobs and Cron read &ldquo;Off &middot; needs Redis&rdquo;.

#### One health query

The top bar pill, the sidebar badge, the dashboard tile, the hub tiles and the health page read one{" "} `useSystemHealth()`. They were separate fetches with separate copies of the response type, which is five requests per page load and, worse, five answers that can differ: the pill saying all clear while a tile two inches below says two components are off.


## v3.534.0 - November 14, 2026

### The dashboard, and a donut that stopped making things up

The third redesign release. The dashboard's four tiles are the same strip the resource pages use, its quick-access tiles say what is in each resource, and the severity chart is a quarter of the size it was.

#### A chart that invented a number

With no events in the last 24 hours, the severity donut was handed `[{ name: "Info", value: 1 }]`: a made-up data point, so it had something to draw. A quiet day and a day with one sign-in rendered identically, and nothing on the card said which you were looking at.

It now shows an empty state when there is nothing, and the real counts when there is something, with all three severities listed even at nought. A legend that grows a row when the first warning arrives moves everything under it, and &ldquo;Critical 0&rdquo; is an answer somebody wanted.

#### And one that was drawn outside its box

The donut's radii were absolute pixels, 40 and 70, so in any box narrower than 140px it was drawn wider than the box and clipped: a thick C with the right-hand side missing. Percentages now. The padding angle is also dropped when there is a single slice, where the gap between slices became a notch in a closed ring.

#### Tiles that say something

Quick access read &ldquo;Manage blogs&rdquo; under a tile titled Blogs, which is the title again as a verb. It reads &ldquo;4 blogs&rdquo; now, and the System hub tile reads &ldquo;6 healthy &middot; 2 off&rdquo;, from the same health query the top bar and the sidebar badge read. The counts come from the hook the per-resource widgets further down the page already use, with the same parameters, so React Query serves both from one request.

#### One strip frame

The dashboard's tiles and a resource page's stat cells are different things: one is a link, the other fetches a count and can narrow a table. The border, the radius, the hairlines and the fold points are identical, and were about to be written twice, so they are a component.


## v3.533.0 - November 14, 2026

### One strip, one primary button, and the dangerous things behind a menu

The second redesign release. The shared vocabulary the remaining pages are written in, proved on the two list pages that use all of it.

#### Four cards became one strip

Four bordered cards with gaps between them is four of everything: four borders, four backgrounds, each announcing itself as a separate object. The numbers belong together and are read together, so they are one card with hairlines between the cells.

Each cell now says what its number counts. Four bare numbers raise the same question four times, and a strip is only worth its space if a reader can answer it without clicking: Total reads &ldquo;All users matching the filters&rdquo;, This Week reads &ldquo;Added in the last 7 days&rdquo;.

#### One primary button per page

Every resource page had two New buttons: one in the page header, one in the table toolbar four inches away, with the same words, the same colour and the same action. Two primary buttons is not twice the affordance, it is a reader working out whether they do the same thing. The header keeps it. Import, Export and Bulk Create stay in the toolbar, because they are other ways in rather than another copy of the main one.

#### Delete and Erase do not sit next to View

The users table showed View, Edit, Delete and{" "} *Erase (GDPR)* side by side in the same grey, which puts &ldquo;remove this person's data permanently&rdquo; one mis-click from &ldquo;look at them&rdquo;, in a row 44px tall repeated down the page.

View and Edit stay. Everything destructive moves into a{" "} `...` menu, in red, and a divider separates Delete from Erase: Delete is reversible and the row comes back from the trash, and nothing below that line does. The menu closes on Escape and on a click outside, and returns focus where it came from.

#### A boolean is a pill, and can choose its words

Down a column of twenty rows, ticks and crosses read as punctuation: the eye finds the shape before the colour and the two shapes are the same size. A filled pill has a silhouette, so a scan finds the odd one out without reading any of them.

Yes and No stay the default, because they are the only pair that is right for every boolean: a contact's{" "} `starred` column saying Inactive is worse than one saying No. A column that knows better says so with{" "} `booleanLabels`, and the generator fills it in for{" "} `active`, `published` and{" "} `archived`.

#### Seven primitives

Pill, empty state, segmented control, underline tabs, radio card, hub tile and note. Each had three or four hand-rolled versions across the panel, differing in padding, in radius, and in whether a state was a word or just a colour. The empty state requires a title and a description, because &ldquo;No data&rdquo; is the most common sentence in an admin panel and the least useful one.


## v3.532.0 - November 13, 2026

### The admin gets a shell

The first of several releases bringing the admin panel up to a redesign of all seventeen of its pages. This one is the frame the rest sit in: the tokens, the sidebar, a top bar, and a command palette.

#### A top bar, so the page header can be about the page

Every page's header carried the theme toggle, the notification bell and the user menu on the same line as that page's own title and its own primary button. The one control the page existed for was the least prominent thing in the row, and three panel-wide controls were re-rendered on every screen.

Those move to a sticky top bar: breadcrumbs derived from the path, a status pill reading the system's health, refresh, theme and notifications. What is left in the page header is the page: where it sits, what it is called, what it is for, and its actions.

#### Cmd+K instead of a button that covered the last row

The floating quick-access button offered one action from on top of whatever was underneath it, and the page reserved 72px at the bottom to keep it off the last row. It is gone.{" "} `Cmd+K` (or `Ctrl+K`, or the search button in the sidebar) opens a palette over every page and every resource, built from the same registry the sidebar reads, so a resource generated tomorrow is in it without anybody adding it.

#### The sidebar says which deployment you are in

Under the app name, in mono. Two tabs of the same admin look identical, and the fact worth knowing before pressing a destructive button is which database is behind it. Worked out from the API URL rather than a variable somebody has to remember to set, because a label configured separately from the thing it describes is a label that will one day say staging on top of production.

The active nav item changed too: it was a tinted fill in the accent colour, which put the one saturated thing on the screen on the item you are already looking at, and left its label reading like a link to somewhere else. It is a neutral fill with full-strength text and a bar on the sidebar's own edge.

#### Tokens that every theme gets for free

Tinted fills, hairlines, a stronger border, a pressed surface and a recessed input fill. Derived from the colours each theme already declares rather than written out per theme: eight tables of seven values is eight places to forget, and the ninth theme somebody adds would get none of them, which renders as a pill with no fill and reports nothing.

#### And a test for the class of bug this release hit

The sidebar imported the palette from one path while the palette shipped at another. Nothing in Go noticed, because both are strings: the project scaffolded cleanly, the upgrade reported 192 files updated, and then every page answered 500. Every `@/...` an admin template imports is now checked against the files the admin actually ships, in both admin shapes.


## v3.531.1 - November 13, 2026

### The architecture list was drawn twice

On Git Bash, `grit new` showed the architecture picker twice: a stale copy a few lines short and missing `Mobile`, then the live one underneath it, each with its own cursor. Which list the arrow keys were moving through was anyone's guess.

The picker is one form of several groups, and a form is drawn at the height of its tallest group. The architecture list needs nine lines and the theme list twelve. huh learns the terminal's size from a message queued during start-up, which means it arrives after the first frame is already on screen: the form goes up at nine lines and is repainted at twelve. Repainting at a new height means moving the cursor up and erasing, and Git Bash does not reliably erase, so the short frame stayed where it was.

The size is now measured and handed to the form before the first frame, so there is only ever one height to draw and no repaint at a different one to get wrong. The numbers are the same ones huh arrived at on its own: what changed is when they are known, not what they are.

Every picker in `grit new` and `grit setup` goes through the same path now. A test drives the form as the model it is and measures the first frame against the frames after it, with a companion test that fails if the two ever agree for free, so the guard cannot quietly stop testing anything.


## v3.531.0 - November 13, 2026

### grit generate field reaches the test factory

Adding a column updated the model, the handler, the service, the schemas, the type and the admin screen, and left the test factory alone. It was the one generated file the command did not touch.

A new NOT NULL column therefore broke every test that creates a fixture, with a constraint error pointing at the factory rather than at the command that caused it. A nullable one was worse: every fixture quietly got the zero value, so the tests passed while describing a record nobody would ever save.

The factory now carries the same kind of marker the admin definition and the routes file already had, and the value comes from the generator's own `factoryValue`, so a field type added tomorrow produces the same fixture whichever command wrote it.

One case worth naming: the counter. The generator only writes `n := next()` when a field interpolates it, decided from the fields the resource had at generation time, so a column added later can be the first one that needs it. Without the declaration the injected value referenced an undefined `n` and the factory package stopped compiling, which breaks the build of every test in the project.

#### And the drift check stops reporting a file it should not

`generated-file-behind-its-source` was reporting the generated handler test after a field was added. Reading it settles the question: it builds fixtures with `factory.CreateX`, sends empty maps for its update assertions, and names one field in the bulk-edit patch. A new column changes none of that.

Safe to exclude because the failure mode is loud. Rename or remove the field it names and the patch targets a column the API does not have, so the test fails on the next run. The silent wrong answer is what the check is for, and a test cannot produce one.

Together these mean the supported way to add a column finishes with `grit doctor` clean, which it did not before. A check that reports something the framework itself causes on its own happy path is a check people learn to ignore, and it takes the real findings with it.


## v3.530.0 - November 13, 2026

### Two things that floated over the page

The admin has two elements that sit above everything, and both were sitting on top of content.

**The mobile menu toggle covered the page title.** It is fixed at `top-3 left-3` and 36px square, so it occupies the first 48px of the viewport. The page header is `sticky top-0`, which puts the two in exactly the same place as each other at every scroll position, and the toggle has the higher z-index. On every list page, on every phone, the title was underneath it the moment anybody scrolled.

**The quick-access button covered the last thing on the page.** It is fixed at `bottom-6` and 48px tall, so it reserves the final 72px of the viewport, and nothing reserved that space. At 1440 it was the "Last" pagination button; at 375 it was the search field.

Both are a utility each: left padding on the header at small widths, bottom padding on `<main>` at every width. Desktop is unchanged apart from the bottom, where the overlap was real too.

The first attempt at the toggle was top padding on `<main>`, which looked right at rest and did nothing once the page was scrolled: a sticky element pins to the viewport, not to its parent's box. The test records that, so the next person does not try it.


## v3.529.0 - November 13, 2026

### The orphan sweep asks before it deletes, and authorization stops reloading the user

#### Files a record was using, deleted the next day

Reported from production twice, on MinIO and then on R2 (grit#219). Every image a hand-written service had uploaded and kept the key for was gone the day after it was uploaded, with the record still pointing at it.

The cause was an assumption rather than a bug in any line. The daily sweep treated `claimed_at IS NULL` as "nothing uses this", and `claimed_at` is only set by `files.ClaimRefs`, which only sees `*FileRef` and `FileRefs` struct fields, and only when a service remembers to call it. A key kept in a plain string column, in a JSON settings blob, or by any code that had not heard of `ClaimRefs`, was indistinguishable from an abandoned upload. Data loss was the default for code that did not opt in.

The sweep now looks. For each page of candidates it scans the project's own tables for text containing the key, keeps anything it finds, and claims it so the next pass does not pay to look again. One query per text column per pass, not one per candidate, with the substring match in Go: a nightly job can afford that, and the alternative is the version that is cheap and loses files.

It fails safe. A table it cannot read is treated as referencing everything, and says so in the log, because a sweep that cannot see must not delete. An orphan that survives another day costs storage; a file deleted because a query failed costs somebody their data, and they find out from a broken image.

#### Two queries on every authenticated request

Found by the query log that shipped in v3.526.0, on its first run (grit#220). `GET /api/users` cost five queries on a warm cache and two of them were `authz.RoleNamesFor`: the join on `user_roles`, and a second load of the same user row the auth middleware had loaded four lines earlier, for its `role` column alone.

It was the only part of authorization that was not cached. `GrantsFor` has had the answer the whole time, and `GrantsForRole` already showed how to reuse it: cache in the same map under a key prefix, inheriting the generation counter, the cluster watch and the single drop path. Revocation stays immediate across replicas, because exactly one thing still drops the cache.

Measured on a running project, before and after: **five queries per request to three**. What is left is the user load and the two the list itself needs.

#### And the tests now travel with the code

`internal/authz/grants.go` is rewritten by `grit upgrade` and `grants_test.go` only ever reached a new project, so an upgraded one ran today's authorization against the assertions of whatever version it was scaffolded with. The half of the pair that would notice a regression was the stale half.


## v3.528.0 - November 13, 2026

### The admin moves like one thing

The panel had no easing curve. Every transition in it ran on Tailwind's default at Tailwind's duration, which is not wrong, it is just nobody's decision: a hundred components that each took whatever they were given. It had `transition-all` in thirty-seven places. And `prefers-reduced-motion` appeared nowhere in the entire scaffold, so the one accessibility switch that motion has was simply absent.

#### One curve, set once

```css
@theme {
  --default-transition-timing-function: cubic-bezier(0.17, 0.55, 0.55, 1);
  --default-transition-duration: 180ms;
}
```

Every `transition-*` utility in Tailwind v4 reads those two variables, so this reaches every transition already written across the admin without touching a single class string. The sidebar, the table rows, the cards and the dropdowns all move the same way now, and none of their files changed.

#### transition-all, replaced rather than banned

`transition-all` asks the browser to watch every animatable property, so the day a utility adds a width to that element it animates the width too and relayouts the page every frame. Nobody writes that bug; it arrives. All thirty-seven are now `transition-grit`, a named property list with no layout property in it.

One of them was animating `width` for real: the upload progress bar. It moves on `scaleX` now, which the compositor does for free.

#### The button has eight states

It had five. The press is new, at 0.97 over 120ms, which is the only feedback that arrives before the network does. Error and success are new, which are the two always missing.

And the busy state was wrong in the way that matters most: it greyed the button out, which says "you cannot do this" when what happened is "I am doing it". A busy button now keeps its colour, sets `aria-busy`, and takes a `busyLabel` so the word changes from Save to Saving. A spinner says nothing to a screen reader and nothing to anybody who looked away.

It also stops being `disabled` while busy, because that attribute takes it out of the tab order: a keyboard user standing on the button when the request starts loses their place and is told nothing about why.

#### Reduced motion, considered rather than blanket

The usual implementation sets every duration to `0.01ms`, which takes away the colour change on a hover and the fade on a focus ring along with the movement. Those are information, not motion. Here the transition property list is narrowed to the paint properties, so transforms stop and colour feedback survives.

Against the standard at [details that make an app feel premium](https://jb.desishub.com/blog/details-that-make-an-app-feel-premium) . Five tests pin it, including one that fails if a second easing curve appears.


## v3.527.0 - November 13, 2026

### The manifest knows what each generated file came out of

`.grit/manifest.json` has always answered one question: have you edited this file. That is what lets `grit upgrade` replace the files nobody has touched and leave the rest alone.

It could not answer the other one. **Is this file still what the model says?** `grit sync` regenerates the shared types and the Zod schemas, so those stay honest. It does not regenerate the handler's create request, the service's writable column list, or the admin form. Add a column to a model by hand, which is a reasonable thing to do, and all three describe the model as it was: the form has no input for it, the API drops it if something sends it anyway, and the only symptom is that the value does not save.

So each entry now records what it was generated out of, and the hash that source had at the time.

```bash
$ grit doctor

  33 checks over 2 resource(s)

  ⚠ apps/api/internal/models/widget.go has changed since the files generated
    from it: 9 files behind it.
    apps/api/internal/handlers/widget.go, apps/api/internal/services/widget.go,
    apps/admin/resources/widgets/widgets.ts and 6 more
      run grit sync for the shared types and schemas, and grit generate
      resource Widget to bring the handler, service and admin screen back
      in line
      (generated-file-behind-its-source)
```

One finding per model rather than one per file, and it counts separately the ones you have edited, because regenerating those takes your work with them.

Generated from a model is not the same as invalidated by it. A route file lists endpoints, which do not move when a column arrives; the React Query hooks are generic CRUD; the admin page wrappers render a resource by name. Those are not reported. Nor is anything Grit refuses to regenerate, like the policy stub and the `.custom.tsx` overlay: a finding that cannot be cleared is one people learn to ignore, and it takes the ones beside it with it.

#### Two commands have never recorded what they wrote

Found while testing the above, and worth more than the feature. Neither `grit sync` nor `grit generate field` opened a manifest session, so every file either of them rewrote read as hand-edited from then on, and `grit upgrade` stopped maintaining it.

`grit generate field` is the worse of the two. It is the supported way to add a column, and it touches the model, the handler, the service, the schemas, the type and the admin screen: one run quietly opted the entire resource out of framework fixes. Three of its writers used `os.WriteFile` directly and told the manifest nothing. Both commands record now.

Borrowed from Bud, which tracks what each generated file depends on so it can rebuild only what changed. Grit uses the same record to answer a different question: not what to rebuild, but what is quietly out of date.


## v3.526.0 - November 13, 2026

### One place to register a database callback, and a record of what a run queried

The framework installs eight GORM callbacks: field encryption, HTML sanitising, the append-only guard, the field-type checks, the soft-delete touch, the pagination count scope and the sync hooks. Each calls `db.Callback()` from its own Install function, which works because they were all written here and their order was decided once.

A project adding a ninth has none of that. It registers on whichever handle it holds, so the callback is on the main pool and not on the one the test suite opens, or the desktop's local mirror, or the one a worker made: the application then behaves differently from its own tests and nothing says why. It lands in an order nobody declared, and a callback before `crypto:encrypt_map_values` sees plaintext while one after it sees ciphertext. And nothing can tell you what is on the chain, which is the first question when one of them is slow.

#### internal/dbchain

```go
dbchain.MustRegister(dbchain.Link{
    Name:   "myapp:stamp_region",
    Op:     dbchain.Create,
    When:   dbchain.After,
    Anchor: "fieldtypes:create",
    Why:    "fills region from the actor's organization",
    Fn:     stampRegion,
})
```

Registering touches no connection. `dbchain.Apply(db)` does, and `database.Connect` calls it, so a link registered from an `init` is on every handle opened afterwards rather than on whichever one happened to exist.

An anchor that names nothing is refused. GORM takes `After("nope")` without complaint and gives you no ordering at all, which is a callback running in the wrong place and saying nothing about it.

#### And what a run actually queried

Set `GRIT_QUERY_LOG` and the chain writes one JSON line per query: the request that issued it, the matched route, the SQL with its placeholders, the row count, and the line of your application it came from. No code change, and nothing is written when the variable is unset.

```bash
GRIT_QUERY_LOG=.grit/queries.jsonl go test ./...
grit doctor
```

`{`⚠ GET /api/v1/posts runs the same query 23 times in one request, from internal/services/post.go:88 (in 14 requests): SELECT * FROM \`users\` WHERE id = ?`}` `query-repeated-in-one-request` is the 32nd doctor check and the only one that reads something a run produced. It is still offline: the application writes a file and the check reads the file, so nothing talks to a database or a server and it stays usable in CI. Silent when there is no log, and it says so when the log is older than the code, because a report from before a change reads exactly the same as one from after it.

The request id now travels on the request's own context as well as the gin context. Only the first reaches a GORM callback, so without it every recorded query was unattributed and "the same query many times in one request" had no request to be many times inside of.

The registry is Beego's filter chain, which is the thing it has that a pile of direct registrations does not. Timing and live profiling stay with Pulse: this answers a question Pulse cannot, which is what to fail a build on.


## v3.525.0 - November 13, 2026

### A column can say it is a secret

The expression engine that shipped in v3.518.0 carries a list of column names it will never let a filter touch: `password`, `token`, `secret`, `api_key` and a dozen spellings of those. That list is a guess about what people call things, and it is wrong the moment somebody writes `recovery_phrase`.

A filter is a read. `recovery_phrase ~ "aband"` returns the row or it does not, and the value never has to appear in the response for that to recover it one character at a time. The only thing standing between an attacker and a column was whether its name had occurred to me.

#### One declaration

```bash
grit generate resource Wallet label:string phrase:text:sensitive
```

The column is written and never read back, and five things follow from the one word:

- The model gets a `MarshalJSON` that drops the key. Not from a list, not from the body answering the write that set it, not from a webhook payload, not from an audit event. Every one of those marshals the model, so that is the one place that has to be right.
- The rules engine refuses to resolve the name in a filter, a sort or a row rule.
- It is not an admin table column and not a filter.
- It is not in the CSV or XLSX export.
- It is not searchable, so `?search=` cannot confirm it by returning the row either.

The create and update schemas keep it, so a form can still set it. A value you can never write is a comment, not a column. The row type and the entity schema drop it, because those describe a response.

#### And a check for the ones that have not said so

`grit doctor` gained `secret-column-not-declared`: a column whose name ends in `_token`, `_secret`, `_password`, `_api_key`, or that is a recovery phrase or a security answer, and that the API returns. It matches on the end of the name rather than anywhere in it, so `token_count` and `secret_santa` stay quiet, and it skips a column already stored encrypted, which is the fix the PII check recommends.

`:sensitive` is not `:encrypted`. One is about a database dump and still sends the value over the API; the other is about the response and still stores plaintext. They combine.

Borrowed from Pagoda, which marks an Ent field sensitive and lets the generated admin omit it.


## v3.524.1 - November 13, 2026

### Two upgrades that left a project not compiling

Both the same shape, and it is the shape worth naming: **a framework file that an upgrade rewrites, beside a project file that it does not.**

#### A model the framework ships

`internal/services/session.go` is framework code and an upgrade rewrites it. `internal/models` is the project's own, so an upgrade leaves it alone, which is right for every model a project wrote and wrong for the handful the framework ships. When the service learned about `Session.RotatedAt` in v3.464.0, a project upgrading into it got a service referencing a field its model does not declare:

`{`internal/services/session.go:105: replayed.RotatedAt undefined (type models.Session has no field or method RotatedAt)`}` The field is carried across by a repair now, which is the only thing allowed to edit a file in `internal/models`, and only when the service beside it actually uses it.

#### A function without its import

The rate-limit table from v3.520.0 reached an existing `routes.go` through the repair that replaces the auth-limit block. The import it needs lives in the scaffold's own template, which an upgrade does not rewrite for a routes.go the project has edited, so the project stopped compiling with `undefined: ratelimit`. The repair adds the import it names, and says so plainly rather than silently if it cannot.

Both found by the check that upgrades the checked-in example twice and compares, which is the only test in this repository that asks what an *existing* project gets.


## v3.524.0 - November 13, 2026

### A private file in an img tag, and a prune that gives the disk back

#### Short-lived keys for one file

An upload is read through an authenticated route scoped to whoever may see the row. That is right, and it leaves one thing impossible: putting the file in an `<img src>`, an `<embed>`, or a PDF viewer. None of them send an `Authorization` header and none of them ever will.

`{`POST /api/v1/uploads/u_123/token {"data": {"token": "...", "url": "/api/v1/uploads/u_123/file/"}}`}` The key names one upload, is signed, and lasts two minutes. Minting it requires exactly the permission the download does, which is what makes it safe to put in a URL: it can only be obtained by somebody who could already have downloaded the file.

Serving it is its own unauthenticated route with the token in the path, rather than a `?token=` on the existing download. That route is behind required authentication, so relaxing it to let the handler decide would put a private file one mistake away from public on the path that already works. The first attempt did exactly that and the middleware refused before the handler ever saw the token, which is how the design was found.

Signed with the application's own `JWT_SECRET`, so one rotation ends every outstanding file link at the moment it signs out every session. A key for one upload does not work on another, and editing the expiry breaks the signature.

#### Pruning the activity log gives the disk back

Deleting rows does not shrink a database. SQLite puts the pages on a free list and the file stays as large as it was at its peak, which on a deployment whose whole point is a small single file is the opposite of what pruning was for. After a prune that removed more than twenty thousand entries, the space is reclaimed: `VACUUM` on SQLite, `ANALYZE` on Postgres where autovacuum handles the space and the planner needs telling, `OPTIMIZE TABLE` on MySQL. Best effort always: a failure there is a larger file, not a lost log.

#### On an app that updates itself

Grit already has this where it belongs. A `grit new-desktop` app ships an in-app updater that swaps its own binary from GitHub Releases, with a modal and a banner. A server deployment does not get one and should not: containers are immutable and a systemd unit is replaced by a deploy, not by the process rewriting itself while serving traffic.

#### And two checks that had stopped describing their subject

- The sweep asserting the upload handler does not read its MIME allowlist from the environment banned `os.Getenv` anywhere in the file, so it caught an unrelated fallback added later. Narrowed to the three things that were actually wrong.
- Narrowing it to the setting's name then matched the five comments explaining the setting. It guards on `os.Getenv("UPLOAD_ALLOWED_MIME")` now: a check that matches its own prose passes whatever the code does.


## v3.523.0 - November 13, 2026

### The first run, without a password in the repository

A deployment with nobody who can administer it now mints a one-time link and prints it, instead of waiting for somebody to seed a known email with a known password.

`{` Nobody can sign in to this deployment yet. Open this link within 30m0s to create the first administrator: http://localhost:8080/setup/7e474b648b27b9a6...`}` The link opens a form served by the Go binary itself: one page, no build step, no dependency. That is deliberate rather than lazy. A deployment that cannot be administered is exactly the deployment where the frontend has not been built yet, and a form that is forty lines of HTML does not need a framework to render it.

#### What makes the link safe

- Thirty-two random bytes, compared in constant time against a SHA-256 of itself. The server never holds the secret after it has printed it.
- Half an hour, then it is dead. It lives in memory, so a restart mints a new one and a link found in an old log is already useless.
- Spent the moment it creates an administrator, and spent only *after* the row exists: spending first would turn a failed insert into a deployment nobody can get into.
- The route is not mounted at all once the deployment has an administrator, and the handler checks again before creating one, so two people opening the link at the same time cannot both succeed.
- The password is held to the same rules as every other password in the project, including the part about reusing the email address.

The seeder is unchanged: ask for `grit seed` and you still get the demo accounts in development. This is for the deployment nobody has seeded, which is every real one.

Found on the way: the sweep that checks every email field has an `autocomplete` knew only React's spelling, so it reported this plain HTML form as missing an attribute it has. A check that cries wolf is a check people learn to ignore.


## v3.522.0 - November 13, 2026

### POST /api/v1/batch: many writes, one transaction

A client creating an order and its six lines makes seven requests today, and if the fourth fails it has four rows it has to clean up itself, over a connection that may already have gone. The only honest answer is a transaction, and a transaction cannot span seven requests.

`{`POST /api/v1/batch { "requests": [ {"method": "POST", "url": "/api/v1/orders", "body": {"customer_id": "c1"}}, {"method": "POST", "url": "/api/v1/order-lines", "body": {"sku": "A", "qty": 2}}, {"method": "PATCH", "url": "/api/v1/stock/s1", "body": {"on_hand": 8}} ] }`}` Every request is replayed through this application's own router, so a batch can only do what the caller could have done one request at a time: the same routes, the same permissions, the same row rules, the same validation. There is no second code path to keep in step, which is the whole design. One of them answering 400 or above rolls the lot back and says which, because a batch that half happened is the state the caller used a batch to avoid.

#### The part that took the longest

A batch holds a transaction, and on SQLite that is the only connection the process has. Anything inside a replayed request that asks the pool for a second one does not get an error: it waits. The request hangs until the client gives up, the connection stays held, and every later request queues behind it. The server is down and nothing in the log says why.

It took a goroutine dump to find the last one: `authz.RoleNamesFor`, called from the authentication middleware two lines after the user lookup that had already been fixed. Every database read on the way into a request now goes through `dbtx.Use`, which hands back the batch's transaction when there is one.

And a deadline, as a safety net rather than a policy: the same mistake made again is a clear error in thirty seconds, naming the batch and saying a request inside it is waiting for a connection the batch itself is holding. A bug report rather than a mystery.

#### Also

- A batch cannot contain a batch, and a sub-request cannot set its own `Authorization` or `Cookie`: otherwise a batch authenticated as one person carries a request authenticated as another.
- A sub-request URL must be a path on this API, checked before anything runs. Without it a batch is a request forger: the server would follow an absolute URL, with the caller's cookies, from inside the network.
- Fifty requests per batch, and its own rate rule of three a second, which was already in the table from v3.520.0.
- An existing project joins batches through a repair, so an upgraded resource does not keep writing outside the transaction.


## v3.521.0 - November 13, 2026

### Row rules: which rows, as a condition on the query

Roles answer whether somebody may use an endpoint. This answers the question after it, and it is where the bugs live, because it has to be asked again at every place a row can be read or written and one of them is always missed.

`{`// internal/rowrules/rules.go Register("Order", Rules{ List: \`@request.auth.id != "" && user_id = @request.auth.id\`, View: \`user_id = @request.auth.id\`, Create: \`@request.auth.id != ""\`, Update: \`user_id = @request.auth.id && status = "draft"\`, Delete: \`user_id = @request.auth.id && status = "draft"\`, })`}` The language is the one `?filter=` uses, so a rule can cross a relation, quantify over many related rows, or talk about the request. Every generated service applies its own rules at four sites: the list, the single read, and the load that an update and a delete both go through.

#### Three layers, not three alternatives

`{`internal/authz may this kind of person use this endpoint at all internal/rowrules which rows may they see, as a condition on the query internal/policies is this particular loaded record an exception`}` The middle one is new and it is the only one that can filter a list. A Go callback over a loaded record cannot: by the time it runs the page has already been chosen, so the caller gets somebody else's rows minus the ones the callback refused, which is a shorter page rather than a correct one. It is called `rowrules` and not `policy` because this project already has `policies`, and two packages a letter apart is a trap for every future reader.

#### The decisions inside it

- Applied to the query, so a record you may not touch is **not found** rather than refused. A 403 on a row you may not read confirms the row exists.
- An empty rule adds nothing, which is the default. A project that has not written a rule has not decided nobody may read anything. `Denied` says the other thing out loud.
- An admin, and the application acting on its own behalf in a job, are not subject to them. A nightly invoice run reads every invoice.
- A create rule is evaluated before the row exists, so naming a column there is reported with a message saying why, rather than quietly ignored.
- A rule that does not parse **refuses the query** rather than running it unfiltered, and every rule is parsed at start-up so a typo is a line in the log before the first request.

Nothing is injected into your rules file. `grit generate resource` leaves it alone: it is yours, it has a worked example at the top, and a generator that writes into it would be a generator that has to be able to take it out again.


## v3.520.0 - November 13, 2026

### One rate-limit table for the whole API

A limit written at a route is a limit somebody has to remember, and nothing in a handler says &ldquo;this one needed one and has none&rdquo;. Review 2.8 found five auth routes without one. The set of routes keeps growing; the set somebody remembered to limit does not.

Every request now produces a list of labels, most specific first, and the first rule that matches wins:

`{`POST /api/v1/orders -> "POST /api/v1/orders" the route and the method -> "/api/v1/orders" the route, any method -> "*:create" the class of action -> "/api/v1/" a prefix -> "/api/" a shorter prefix`}` So one rule covers every create, and a route nobody thought about is still bounded by the prefix at the end. Specificity decides rather than position in the file, so writing the catch-all first does not silently give everything the loosest limit you have. A rule set to zero is off and the match stops there, rather than falling through to a broader rule and quietly reinstating a limit somebody removed.

`*:auth` is matched on the path rather than a list of routes, so a new passkey endpoint under `/auth/` is covered the day it is written.

#### And one thing it deliberately does not do

The credential rule carries no audience. The middleware runs before each route's own authentication, so all it can know is whether a request *carries* credentials, not whether they are real: split that rule and a credential-stuffing client sends one junk bearer token and buys the signed-in budget. There is a test that fails if anybody adds the split back.

Callers see `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` on every response, and a refusal carries `Retry-After`, because a client told only &ldquo;no&rdquo; retries immediately.

The counters are in process and per instance, which makes this a floor rather than a ceiling: it needs no Redis and it cannot fail open. Sentinel still bounds the total across replicas, and where both apply the stricter refuses first.

Found while writing it: `/organization-invitations/preview` was listed in the auth paths as `/invitations/preview`, with a leading slash the real path does not have, so the route the entry was added for matched nothing.


## v3.519.0 - November 13, 2026

### Asking for less, and asking for more

`?fields=` and `?expand=`, on every generated list endpoint, beside the `?filter=` that landed in v3.518.0.

`{`GET /api/v1/orders?fields=id,total,customer.name GET /api/v1/orders?expand=customer,lines.product`}` A list screen showing four columns does not need forty, and a phone on a slow connection pays for every one it throws away. The projection is applied to the marshalled document rather than to the `SELECT`, because a partial select leaves the struct's other fields at their zero values and they serialise anyway: the client asks for two columns and receives forty, thirty-eight of them untrue. A field that was not asked for is **absent**, which is the only honest way to send less. Dotted paths walk into an expanded relation, and two paths into the same object merge.

`?expand=` is the other half. Without it a list of orders carries `customer_id` and the client makes one request per row to turn it into a name, which is the N+1 problem moved onto the network where nobody can see it. Each name is resolved against the model's own schema and translated into the association GORM knows, so the client writes `line_items.product` the way the JSON spells it and `Preload` gets `LineItems.Product`. An unknown relation is a 422 naming the ones that exist rather than an error from inside the ORM. At most six per request, three levels deep.

#### And a filter can now cross a relation

`supplier.country = "UG"` was refused on every generated resource, because the whitelist a filter is held to is derived from the `Filterable` map, and that map holds columns: a relation is not one. A derived whitelist now includes the model's relations, since a relation is already readable through `?expand=` and filtering across one discloses nothing that asking for it would not. A whitelist written out by hand in `FilterFields` is left exactly as written, because somebody decided that list on purpose.

Verified over HTTP against a generated `Part` belonging to a `Supplier`: projection, expansion, both together, and a filter across the relation.


## v3.518.0 - November 13, 2026

### A query language on every list endpoint

Until now a list endpoint answered the questions somebody thought of when they generated it: page, search, sort, a date range, and equality on whichever columns made it into the `Filterable` map. Anything else was a new query parameter, a new branch in the handler, and a release.

Every generated list endpoint now takes `?filter=`, an expression over the model's own fields:

`{`GET /api/v1/machines?filter=status = "active" && hours > 100 GET /api/v1/orders?filter=total >= 500 && created_at >= @monthStart GET /api/v1/posts?filter=author.country = "UG" || tags.label ?= "urgent" GET /api/v1/invoices?filter=paid_at = null && due_at Relation paths walk as deep as six hops and compile to correlated subqueries, so a filter over a has-many does not multiply the rows the way a join would. `comments.approved = true` asks whether every comment is approved; `?=` asks whether any is. `@request.auth.id`, `@request.query.x` and `@request.headers.x_id` are what the server knows about the caller, and `@monthStart` and its fourteen relatives resolve in Go so a rule means the same thing on every database.

#### What makes it safe is the schema, not the parser

Every identifier is resolved against the model's GORM schema, which is the only description of the table anybody maintains, so there is no second list to keep in step. A name the model does not declare is refused with the names it does:

`{`unknown field "nonsense" at position 0 (this endpoint accepts: created_at, hours, id, name, serial, status)`}` That is a **422, not a 500**: the caller's sentence is wrong, not the server. Every value is a bound parameter, so a filter with a quotation mark in it is a string with a quotation mark in it. Columns that look like credentials are never filterable whatever the model calls them, because `password ~ "$2a$10$ab"` reads a hash one character at a time and a whitelist that forgot to exclude it would not stop that.

#### Which fields, without anything new to remember

The union of what the endpoint already admits it can be searched, sorted and filtered on. An endpoint willing to sort by a column has already decided the column is public, so a generated resource gets this from the `Filterable` map the generator writes anyway. `Config.FilterFields` says it explicitly, which is what you want on anything served without authentication.

#### And a cheaper page

`?skip_total=1` drops the `COUNT` from an offset page. The page is a `LIMIT` over an index; the total is a scan of everything that matched, and on a large filtered table it is most of the request. `meta.has_more` answers the only question a next button has.

The engine is `internal/rules` in your project: a tokeniser, a parser and a compiler, with eleven tests that run the generated SQL against a real database rather than comparing it to a string. It is the same engine that will evaluate a declared access rule.

The allocation budget in `internal/handlers/perf_test.go` caught the first version of this at 54 allocations per list request against a budget of 50: it was building the request context on every request, filter or no filter. It is built when there is an expression to evaluate, which is what the budget is for.


## v3.517.1 - November 13, 2026

### grit doctor could not be run on a single project

It looked for the Go module in `apps/api` or at the project root. A `--single` project keeps it in `api/`, with the frontend owning the root, so every run ended on the first line:

`no Go API at my-app: run grit doctor inside a Grit project` Thirty checks, none of which ran. The command whose whole job is finding problems was the one that could not be started, on an entire architecture.

This is the seventh place the same question was answered by hand. v3.516.0 found six of them in the generator and made one resolver the only implementation; doctor has its own because it is deliberately file-only and offline, and it was missed. It now probes the directory rather than reading `grit.json`, so a project scaffolded before the module moved into `api/` still reads correctly.


## v3.517.0 - November 13, 2026

### An admin panel that is the whole app

Plenty of what people build with Grit has no public side at all: a back office, an operations console, an internal tool whose every user signs in. Until now the nearest shape was `--single`, which gave you a landing page, a navbar, a footer and a blog you did not want, with the panel tucked away under `/admin`.

`grit new my-app --api --admin` builds that app directly. The panel is served at `/`, so `/` opens the dashboard and the sign-in page is at `/login`. There is no public site, no site chrome, and no blog example to delete afterwards. Everything else `--single` gives you is unchanged: one Go binary with the SPA embedded in it, and no Node.js in production.

#### What it took, which is the interesting part

Two transforms repoint the admin's code as it is written into a host app, and both of them prefix its links: the panel says `href="/dashboard"`, and inside a `--single` project that screen is at `/admin/dashboard`. Guarding one and not the other left the auth shells pointing at an `/admin` that this shape does not serve, because the first transform had already rewritten the file before the second could decline.

The same question, asked a third time, was where the panel's route files are. The guard matched `/src/routes/admin/`, which at the root matches nothing, so forty route shims kept their `@/pages/...` imports: forty files importing a directory the SPA does not have.

And the blog comes out by running the removal `grit remove resource Blog` runs, rather than by a second list of blog paths inside the scaffolder. Thirty-eight writers put a blog file somewhere, and the blog is also injections: the sync registry, the nav menu, the seeder call, the authz catalog, the WAF exclusion. Removal did not know this layout either, so it deleted the resource definition and left the route files importing it, which is a build error rather than a stale screen.

#### Also

- `grit remove resource` now takes the resource's route folder with it when nothing is left in it. An empty `resources/blogs/` still reads as &ldquo;the blog is sort of here&rdquo;, which is the thing a removal exists to settle.
- `--admin` with `--next` is refused rather than half-built: the flag embeds the Vite admin into one binary, and a Next frontend runs as its own process.

Reported as [#89](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/89) .


## v3.516.0 - November 13, 2026

### Six commands that each worked out where the Go code lives, and four got it wrong

A `--single` project keeps its Go module in `api/`, with the frontend owning the project root. Six places in the generator worked that out independently, and only one of them was right.

`grit sync` looked in `apps/api` and stopped at &ldquo;models directory not found&rdquo;. It did not run at all on a single project, and the scaffold's own CLAUDE.md calls that command not optional. `grit generate migration` wrote its pair into `<root>/migrations` while `grit migrate` reads `api/migrations`, so the migration could never run and nothing said why. `generate job`, `mail`, `saga` and `sequence` all wrote to the project root rather than into the module.

`Generator.APIRoot` had it right the whole time, and is now the only implementation: the rest call it. There is a test over the resolver rather than over each command, because one wrong answer is what produced six wrong commands.

#### The same shape, in the admin

`adminRootFrom` knew four layouts and not the one `grit new --single` has written since the SPA moved to the project root. Three commands read it.

So on every single project, `grit remove resource` deleted the Go side and left the admin definition and its page behind, **still registered**, so the panel kept a screen in its sidebar pointing at an endpoint that no longer existed. And `grit sync` never added a new model field to the admin table or form, silently, which is the feature that exists so those do not drift. `AdminCodeRoot`, which `grit generate` uses, had the case right, so generating worked and nothing else did.

#### And two paths that named files which were not there

`grit sync` wrote to the resolved shared root and printed a hardcoded `packages/shared/...`, so every success line on a single project named a file that does not exist, two inches above the error-catalogue lines printing the real `src/shared` path. `generate migration` and `generate sequence` carried a display prefix decided separately from the root, which is how a path can be one directory out. Both now derive the label from the directory they actually wrote to.

Found while starting grit#89, which asks for an admin without a public site. The plan there is to scaffold and then run `grit remove resource Blog`, reusing the one code path that knows every place the blog appears rather than building a second list. Checking that it worked is what turned this up.


## v3.515.0 - November 12, 2026

### A route that was forgotten fails open

grit#179, proposal 1, which the reporter called the strongest of their ten and which is their sentence above. A generated resource's routes carry their permission because the generator writes it. A route you write carries whatever you remembered, and a route with nothing in front of it is reachable by any signed-in account, which with open registration is anybody.

The failure is the wrong way round, and that is the whole argument: forgetting makes a route *more* permissive, so the mistake nobody notices is the one that costs something. They paid for it with a 364-line module guard and a 429-line catalog holding 105 per-route overrides, to get back a property the framework had no opinion about.

Now the route says what it needs, in a form a machine reads:

`{`m.Staff.POST("/payslips/:id/email", perm("payroll.edit"), h.EmailOne) m.Staff.GET("/payslips", perm("payroll.view", "payroll.admin"), h.List) m.Staff.POST("/payroll/run", role("FINANCE"), h.Run) m.Protected.GET("/payslips/mine", openToAnySignedIn("the handler scopes every row to the caller"), h.Mine)`}` `perm` is `RequireRole("ADMIN", "perm:x")` underneath, which is exactly what the generator writes, so there is one meaning of &ldquo;this route needs x&rdquo; rather than two spellings that drift. They are short on purpose: a declaration you have to spell out in full is one people shorten by leaving out.

`openToAnySignedIn` is the part that makes the check usable. It guards nothing and changes nothing at runtime. What it does is turn &ldquo;this route has no permission&rdquo; from something nobody wrote down into something somebody did, and it requires the reason, because almost every honest use is one of two sentences and if you cannot write either the route probably wants a `perm`.

#### And the build fails

`{`$ grit routes --check ✗ POST /api/v1/payslips/:id/void apps/api/internal/routes/payroll_routes.go → h.Void 1 route(s) stand behind authentication and demand no permission.`}` Exit code 1, so it belongs in CI beside the tests. It is a `grit doctor` check too, so the answer arrives without knowing the flag exists, and the routes table marks a declared-open route `signed in (declared)` rather than plain `signed in`.

#### Why it does not check every route

A freshly generated project has **67** routes behind authentication that demand no permission, and almost all of them are right: `/auth/me`, `/api-keys`, `/auth/passkeys/:id`. They are the caller's own things, scoped in the handler. Asking each to declare one would be 67 false positives on the first run, and a check that is mostly wrong is one people learn to pass with `--no-verify`.

So the default is the routes the project wrote, told apart by the manifest, which is exactly the reporter's situation with 105 hand-written routes in their own files. `--strict` checks all of them, and on a fresh project reports exactly those 67.

One thing worth recording about building it: the check needed to know which file a route was written in, and the first version grew a second per-file parser to work it out, with its own group seeding and its own guess at whether a route really came from that file. `ParseProject` already parses file by file with a seeded group table and was simply throwing the filename away. One line there replaced forty here.


## v3.514.0 - November 12, 2026

### A role the admin never heard of

Somebody asked on grit#89 how adding and removing roles could be made easier. Looking at it turned up a silent bug rather than a missing feature.

`grit add role` reached **four of its seven places** and reported success. It looked for `apps/admin/resources/users.ts`, and resources moved into a folder each some releases ago, so the real path is `apps/admin/resources/users/users.ts` and the old one simply did not exist. The check was `fileExists`, the answer was no, and the whole admin block was skipped without a word.

So the role reached the Go model, the Zod schema, the TypeScript union and the shared constants, and in the admin it had no badge, no filter and no option in the form's select. You could not give the new role to anybody from the screen that exists to give roles to people. The command printed &ldquo;added to 4 location(s)&rdquo; and looked like it had worked.

It resolves the definition now, with the same helper the admin sync already uses for the same lookup, and it says so when a count comes back short rather than letting the number pass as a detail.

#### And the command that was missing

`grit remove role`. Adding had no counterpart, so a role added by mistake had to be unpicked from seven places by hand, and missing one is quiet: a value left in the Zod enum that the Go model no longer accepts means the admin form offers a role the API refuses, and nothing looks wrong until somebody picks it.

Adding a role and removing it again leaves the project exactly as it was, byte for byte across all five files. That is the test, because it is the only assertion that catches a partial removal.

Three things it refuses to do. `ADMIN` and `USER` cannot be removed at all, not even with `--force`: the seeder creates an ADMIN, every generated route guard asks for one, registration assigns USER, and a project without them compiles and cannot sign anybody in. It stops if your own code still names the role, because a guard asking for a role that no longer exists asks for something nothing can be. And removing a role the project does not have says so instead of reporting a successful no-op.

It reads files and never your database, like `grit doctor`. The database may be Postgres, it may not be running, and &ldquo;could not connect&rdquo; would have become a silent skip of the only safety check there was. So it prints the query rather than pretending to know: an account left on a removed role cannot sign in, because the API refuses a role it cannot resolve.


## v3.513.0 - November 12, 2026

### One doomed request every thirty seconds, for ever

grit#215. A per-change refusal from `/sync/push` that was not a version conflict left the outbox row queued with no failed state, so the client re-sent it on every push for the rest of the install's life. With auto-sync on that is one request every thirty seconds that the server is guaranteed to refuse.

Three problems came out of one branch, and the report named all three. A 4xx was retried, when a 4xx for an unchanged payload is permanent. The row was indistinguishable from one simply waiting, because `PendingCount` counted it and `HasConflict` was the only flag there was. And the reason was stored in `conflict_msg`, a field named for conflicts, so a screen built from the field name would show a plan limit in a merge dialog.

The outbox has a state now. A permanent refusal moves the row to `failed` with the server's own `error_code` and `error_msg`, it stops being sent, and it stops counting as pending. `GetFailedChanges` and `FailedCount` are what a sync screen renders its second section from. A transient refusal is still retried and the attempts are counted, so a row refused thirty times reads differently from one on its first try.

Nothing retries by itself and nothing clears by itself. `RetryChange` puts a parked row back in the queue when the reason is gone, and it clears the old error rather than leaving it to be read as a fresh one.

#### The server says which refusals are permanent

`PushResult.Permanent()` and `.Transient()` set a `retryable` field on the wire. That is the reporter's own suggestion and it is the right place for the decision: the server is the only thing that knows what its own hooks answer. An entitlement guard refusing a row because the plan does not cover it is permanent for an unchanged payload, and no list compiled into a desktop build could know that code exists.

A client talking to a server too old to send it falls back to the codes the framework itself emits, and treats anything it does not recognise as worth retrying. Of the two ways to be wrong, wasting a request is recoverable and hiding somebody's work is not.

Five tests ship with every project, including the report's own measurement: four pushes of a change the server refuses, and the server is asked exactly once.

Also fixed: the push-chunking upgrade repair still described the loop as it was before this change, so it would have reported every project as not the file Grit wrote. That is the third anchor in two days to drift from the template it repairs.


## v3.512.0 - November 12, 2026

### A deployed site where every upload silently did nothing

grit#216. The generated Next.js Dockerfiles accepted one build argument, `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL`. The generated apps read eleven between them. The other ten could not be supplied to a production build at all, so they took their development defaults in the deployed image and nothing reported it.

One of them breaks every upload. `apps/web/next.config.ts` builds the Content-Security-Policy from `NEXT_PUBLIC_STORAGE_URL` and falls back to a MinIO on localhost, so a production image permits only the developer's laptop as a storage origin. Uploads are presigned PUTs the browser makes straight to object storage, and stored files are read from the same origin: both blocked. The API signs a good URL, the browser refuses it, and the trace is a console violation with no HTTP status and no server log line. There is nothing to grep for.

`.env.example` told you to set it. The Dockerfile had no way to accept it, so anybody following that advice put it in their platform's environment panel, where Next cannot see it: `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` is inlined at build time and an `ENV` on the running container is too late.

All eleven are build args now, generated from **one list** that the Dockerfiles and `docker-compose.prod.yml` are both written from. The drift was the bug: four places had to agree and they stopped agreeing without anything failing. A test scaffolds a project, greps the apps for every `NEXT_PUBLIC_` they read, and fails if one is not in that list, so the next variable somebody adds cannot repeat this.

`NEXT_PUBLIC_STORAGE_URL` is *required* in the compose file rather than defaulted, which matters more than it looks: an empty string is falsy, so `|| "http://localhost:9002"` fires on an empty value exactly as it does on an unset one, and a default of `""` would reintroduce the whole bug. Docker itself now stops the deploy and says why.

#### And an image that could not be built at all

The second half of the same report. pnpm's hoisted linker puts one copy of each dependency at the root, except where two packages need different versions, and then it nests one. A `packages/*` member whose dependency pins a peer more tightly than the root does therefore has its own `node_modules`, and the builder stage did not copy it.

The failure is forty lines of structural type mismatch naming two paths that are the same library at two versions, in a file nobody changed. It reads as a bug in your own code. It is fixed by one line, `COPY --from=deps /app/packages ./packages`, which has to come after `COPY . .` or the context copy puts a source tree with no `node_modules` back over it.

#### Two reasons this reached a user

`writeDockerFiles` was called from the two scaffold entry points and from nowhere else, so every fix written into a Dockerfile template reached new projects only. An existing project kept what it was scaffolded with until somebody tried a production deploy. `grit upgrade` writes them now, through the guard that holds back a file you have edited and names it rather than overwriting it, because a deployment file is one people genuinely do edit.

And `grit doctor` has two new checks, so this is a line of output rather than an afternoon: a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable the app reads and the Dockerfile cannot accept, and a `packages/` member whose `node_modules` the builder stage does not copy. Both read files, like every other check, so CI can run them.

#### What the tests did not catch

The first version of this fix put the ARG block at the wrong `%s` of a twelve-placeholder format string, which spliced it into the middle of a `COPY` line and left a bare `web` on a line of its own. Every test in the new file passed, because every string it looked for was present: they were simply in pieces. Found by generating a project and reading the Dockerfile. There is a structural test now, which asserts every line is an instruction, a comment or a continuation.

Sorting the build args also broke an unrelated upgrade repair that anchored on `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` being the only one, and inserted `API_INTERNAL_URL` after it. It anchors on `restart:` now, which does not move when the argument list changes.
