## v3.511.0 - November 12, 2026

### Billing belongs to the organisation, not to whoever clicked Checkout

grit#144. Installing the Stripe and multi-tenancy plugins together gave billing keyed to a **user**. One Stripe customer per person across every organisation they belonged to, so two organisations could not hold two plans, a payment made in A was readable while B was active, and the same reference in two organisations collided on one row. If the person who subscribed left, the organisation lost its subscription with them.

`Payment` and `Subscription` now carry a nullable `org_id`, stamped from the active organisation and left NULL without the plugin. Every read, refund, portal link, cancel and resume narrows to that scope, and each organisation gets its own Stripe customer, so two organisations hold two plans with two cards and two tax ids and one person can belong to both.

#### One implementation, not two

The report asked for this and it is the decision the rest follows from. There is no multitenant variant of the plugin. A variant would mean the security-critical half, webhook verification and event idempotency and the conditional state updates, existed twice and drifted, with the second copy getting less review. It would also make the install order load-bearing: add Stripe first and your billing is user-keyed for ever.

What makes one implementation possible is small. The multi-tenancy middleware does `c.Set("org_id", ...)`, so reading it back with `c.GetString` compiles in a project that has no tenant package at all and returns empty there. The plugins can be installed in either order, which is checked by generating a project each way and compiling it.

The default is narrow and the wide one is spelled out: `payments.Unscoped()` for a genuinely platform-wide path. That is the right way round, because the mistake that matters is reading another organisation's billing by accident, and it cannot happen without typing it.

#### The two that would have hurt

The admin payment list had no organisation filter, which is the easiest place to read somebody else's money by accident: the route exists, the operator has the role, and every organisation's rows arrive in one page with nothing saying so. And `Refund` took an id and nothing else, so an operator with B active could refund A's payment, which is not a thing you can take back. Both are scoped, and both have a test that fails if they stop being.

The webhook settles the right organisation with no header, because Stripe sends none: the organisation is written to the subscription's metadata at checkout and read once, when the row is created. A later event never moves a subscription between organisations.

Verified by generating a project both ways round, compiling it, and running the thirty tests the plugin ships inside it, including four new ones that are the report's own acceptance criteria. A project that already had payments before it had organisations has `org_id` NULL on those rows and only the project knows which organisation each belongs to, so the backfill is one line of SQL the install notes and the docs both hand you rather than something guessed at.


## v3.510.0 - November 12, 2026

### A rebuild button that reads the model, and pickers that work without a mouse

grit#87. A field added to a Go model reached the API, the shared types and the admin, and never reached the screens on a laptop or a phone. `grit sync` reported the drift and could not fix it, and the only route to a current screen was to regenerate the resource with its complete field list retyped.

Retyping that list is the part worth fixing. It is tedious, and it is quietly dangerous: a type remembered as `string` that was `text`, or a missing `unique`, silently becomes the new truth, and the first symptom is a column that changed under a table full of data. So `grit generate resource <Name> --force` no longer needs `--fields`: it reads the list off the model, which is the one list that cannot be wrong, and prints what it read before it uses it.

Not a second parser. The reader that already turns a model into a definition for `grit generate seeder` took a mode instead: a seeder must not invent a slug it computes or a foreign key pointing at nothing, and a rebuild must keep both, and that is the whole difference between them.

The desktop screen is updated in place rather than rebuilt. Its `COLUMNS` array now carries the same marker fences the admin resource file has had since v3.31.16, so a new field is appended inside the fence and a column somebody has customised is left exactly as it is. Insert-only: a field removed from the model keeps its column rather than being silently deleted, because a sync that removes things is a sync nobody can leave running.

The Expo list is deliberately not done this way, and `grit sync` says so rather than skipping it quietly. That screen renders a header block and a row block that have to line up underneath a summed table width: three things that must agree, where an insert getting one wrong puts the headers over the wrong columns. `--force` rebuilds it, which is exactly why --force stopped needing the field list in the same release.

#### What a byte comparison found

A rebuild of an unchanged model should produce the same model back. Diffing the two is how three faults turned up that the unit tests passed.

The rebuild dropped `required` from every column, and turned a required foreign key into `*string` with `default:null`, which is a migration that relaxes a NOT NULL nobody asked to relax. The cause is that `GoField.Required` reads a tag literally named `required:"true"`, and a generated model says `binding:"required"`. It also dropped the money column outright, because `money.Money` is embedded, two columns behind one field, and the type reader written for seeders answers "skip it" for anything it does not recognise. For a seeder a skip costs a duller demo. Here it regenerates the model without the column. An unreadable column now stops the rebuild and names itself.

The test fixture is the literal bytes of a real `grit generate resource` run rather than a model written by hand, because the hand-written one had money as a decimal float, which is a shape no generated project has.

#### The pickers, from grit#179

Proposal 5 asked for a searchable combobox on every `belongs_to` field and on an enum over about seven options. Most of it had shipped. What had not was everything around the search box.

The enum picker rendered its list as an absolutely positioned child of the form, so inside a dialog it clipped and near the bottom of a long form it opened past the edge of the window, which is the same as having no list. It is portalled and fixed now, like the date picker and the relationship pickers beside it, and it opens upward when there is more room above.

And neither single-choice picker was a listbox: `aria-haspopup` on the trigger and nothing else, so a screen reader got a pile of unlabelled buttons and the relationship picker had no arrow-key movement at all. Both now carry `role="listbox"`, `role="option"`, `aria-selected` and `aria-activedescendant`, with Arrow, Home, End, Enter and Escape, and focus handed back to the trigger on close. The multi-select picker was given this in the accessibility pass and these two were missed, which is the failure mode that stays invisible to everybody who is in the room when the feature is demonstrated.

The search box appears from eight options. Over three it is clutter; over forty it is the only way to use the control. With no search box the arrow keys work from the trigger, or the control could not be opened without a mouse.


## v3.509.0 - November 12, 2026

### An upgrade that quietly changed who could call two endpoints

grit#213, and this half is the one worth reading. An upgrade rewrote a route file somebody had written by hand and moved two student-facing endpoints behind an admin permission. The upgrade summary lists the files it declined to take, so a rewritten file reads as success, and nothing said the authorization had changed. The first symptom would have been a 403 in production.

The repair walks every `*_routes.go` and moves a resource's open routes behind a permission, which is a real fix for a real exposure. It decided what was generated code by looking for the text the generator writes, and the reasoning was that such an anchor cannot reach a developer's own code. That reasoning is wrong, and it is wrong for a reason worth stating: the generator's shape is the convention the documentation teaches, so hand-written code that follows the convention is indistinguishable from generated code by inspection. The file had a `handlers.XHandler`, and its two routes were `Import` and `Export`. Every anchor matched.

The manifest knows which files Grit wrote, and now it decides. Not on whether a file is unmodified, though: a generated route file somebody has added a route to is still Grit's file and still needs the fix. The question is whether Grit ever wrote it. A project from before the manifest existed has no entries at all, so the gate asks first whether the manifest knows about *any* route file, and stands aside when it does not. A gate that silently stops repairing the oldest projects would be the same bug pointing the other way.

And the summary names every route whose group or permission changed, in the files it did rewrite. A count was not enough: a project may have granted the old shape deliberately. When it declines to touch a file, it names the routes it would have moved, so the decision is the developer's rather than silence.

#### zod 4, in the one file nothing compiled

The other half of grit#213. `packages/shared/schemas/field-formats.ts` shipped with zod 3 syntax against the zod 4 pin for two releases, and every type-check in the repository passed throughout.

The reason is structural rather than an oversight. `schemas/index.ts` does not re-export field-formats, so the file is only compiled when a resource with a formatted field imports it, and `packages/shared` had a tsconfig and a typescript and *no script*, so `turbo type-check` walked past the package entirely. The CI workflow had a comment documenting that gap and working around it. The package now declares `type-check`, CI runs it, and putting the old code back reproduces both reported errors.

The schema itself is now `z.json()`, zod's own, in place of fifteen lines of hand-rolled recursive union. It was checked against the union it replaces on every case either accepts or refuses, NaN and Infinity and a nested undefined included. The three checked-in example apps were still pinned to zod 3 and are on 4 now.

#### The desktop sync engine knows what it may write

grit#214. The server declares every table's sync policy, enforces it on push and serves it at `GET /api/v1/sync/policy`. The desktop engine never asked, so it queued writes the server was guaranteed to refuse. The user then found a failed row in their sync screen about a record they did not create, cannot fix, and must not dismiss without being told what it was.

`LocalCreate`, `LocalUpdate` and `LocalDelete` now return a typed `*sync.PolicyError` and write nothing. The whole difficulty is that refusing only matters offline, because online the server would have said so anyway: a client that fetches the policy at startup and gives up when the fetch fails has implemented the half that never fires. So the table is persisted in the device's own SQLite, and under that sits a compiled-in copy that `grit sync` writes from the project's own registrations, which is what makes the refusal work on an install that has never reached the server. A table nobody has declared stays writable, so a resource generated after the installed build shipped is not broken offline. The web engine persists its table too, for the same reason.

`do()` returns a `*sync.APIError` holding the status code, with `Retryable()` on it. Every caller used to get a formatted string, which is fine for `/sync/push` and wrong for anything honouring the rule the offline guidance itself states: a 4xx will be a 4xx forever and must stop the retry, while a 5xx must back off and try again. Nobody should have to parse a status back out of an error message.

Two faults in this were found by running it on a real generated project rather than by the unit tests. A table registered bare in `routes.go` and given an explicit policy in a project's own file tied on strictness, and the tie went to whichever file was read first, so a declared `client_wins` and a declared `max_offline_age` were silently replaced by defaults. And `MaxOfflineAge` has three spellings in real code, including the raw nanoseconds the generator itself emits; reading only one of them returned zero, which means no limit.


## v3.508.0 - November 12, 2026

### Word documents, and why citations are not in the box

grit#212, both halves. Every project now has `internal/docx`, and it travels on `grit upgrade` rather than only reaching new projects.

It is a document writer, not a list export. A resource already exports its filtered list as CSV, XLSX and JSON, and a Word table of rows is that again in a format that holds it worse. What a list export cannot produce is a document with a page size, a named font at a given size, justified text, a line spacing and a page break before each chapter. Those are usually not preferences: a university department or a government office specifies them and marks against them, so getting them wrong costs the person submitting it something real. `docx.Submission()` returns that combination because it is asked for often enough that every project otherwise writes it out again.

Headings are named Word styles rather than bold text, so the navigation pane and an automatic table of contents work. `Chapter` uses `pageBreakBefore` rather than an empty paragraph, so the break moves with the heading when the text above it grows. `docx.Attachment` quotes a filename properly, because a filename holding a quote or a newline either truncates the response header or injects another one, and a filename is the first thing in a response to come from user input.

No dependency. A .docx is a zip of XML parts and this writes them with `archive/zip` and `encoding/xml`. The Go libraries for it are either thinly maintained or AGPL, and an AGPL dependency inside a framework other people build commercial products on is a licence decision nobody would choose deliberately.

#### The two bugs an independent reader found

The tests were written against python-docx reading the output back, rather than against the writer's own assertions, and that is what caught them. A test I write against my own output agrees with whatever I produced, correct or not.

`<w:tblGrid>` was missing. The schema requires it and Word silently tolerates its absence, so every table would have worked in Word and been refused by anything stricter. And the font and size lived only in `docDefaults`: Word honours that, but a reader asking the Normal style what font it is got nothing, which matters precisely because &ldquo;set in Times New Roman 12pt&rdquo; is the claim a marking scheme is checked against. Both are fixed, and both now have a test. Sixteen tests ship with the package so a project can run them.

#### Citations

The other half of grit#212 asked for a CSL formatter. It is not shipping, and [citations](https://gritframework.com/docs/frontend/citations) is the reason in full rather than a shrug: render on the client, lazily, and persist what the engine produced so the server reads it rather than deriving it a second time. That last part is the point. Two implementations of one rule in two languages drift quietly, which has already cost a day in a Grit project when an FNV hash written once in TypeScript and once in Go stopped agreeing and nothing failed.

The page carries the measurements rather than an opinion. citeproc-js under goja parses APA in 44 to 80 seconds against node's 0.61, and Chicago in 209; it is a cliff at about 45 KB of style, and APA and Chicago are the two styles most people ask for. A goja VM is not safe for concurrent use either, so a server would need one engine per style per worker. `v8go` would fix the speed and bring cgo, a C toolchain in the image and the end of cross-compiling; if that becomes necessary it should follow the vips image backend, which is pure Go by default and cgo behind a build tag. And citeproc-js is CPAL-1.0 or AGPL-1.0, which is a decision a project should make deliberately rather than inherit from its framework.

Two premises in the report did not hold, and the page says so rather than repeating them: nothing in Grit tells projects never to hand-roll a CSL formatter or a DOCX writer, and a resource exports CSV, XLSX and JSON rather than PDF.

## v3.507.0 - November 12, 2026

### The expert skills have a page, and the search box got looked at

`grit skills install` has shipped for a while and the pack it installs was private, so the docs could say it existed and not much else. It is public now, at [MUKE-coder/grit-expert-skills](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit-expert-skills) , which means you can read a skill before you let it tell an agent how to write code in your project.

So there is a page: [the expert skills](https://gritframework.com/docs/expert-skills), with all twenty-eight listed in groups, one line each on what they do and when they fire. Every line is the skill's own description out of its `SKILL.md` rather than a paraphrase, because twenty-eight paraphrases are twenty-eight chances to describe one wrongly and they all drift the first time a skill changes.

It also settles something that costs people time: four different things in this project are called a Grit skill, and the page says which is which.

The CLI said the pack held twenty-eight skills. Its own roster checker says twenty-seven, excluding `grit-references` as &ldquo;reference material the other skills read, not a skill&rdquo;. Both readings are defensible and the two surfaces disagreeing is not, so the help text now says twenty-seven plus the reference material, and a test counts it the way the pack counts it.

#### And the search box

Looking at the new page meant opening the search dialog, which turned out to have three things wrong with it that a token name explains:

shadcn's `accent` means &ldquo;hover surface&rdquo;. This design system's `accent` is the brand violet. The selected result row carried `bg-accent`, so it was a solid violet bar, with `text-accent-foreground`, which is not a utility this config defines and therefore set no colour at all. A muted grey section label on a violet fill is unreadable, and it was the only thing telling two identically titled results apart.

The search button in the header had the same violet at 30%, the one tinted control in a row of plain links, a document icon rather than a magnifier, and no `whitespace-nowrap`, so &ldquo;Search docs...&rdquo; broke across two lines at the widths the nav actually reaches.

And the dialog's close button is absolutely positioned at the top right corner, which is correct in a dialog with a heading and lands on top of the input in a command palette.

Fixed with tokens, so both themes follow: the selected row is the accent tint with its hairline and full-contrast text, the section is its own chip, the palette is wider and anchored near the top so the first result does not move as you type, and there is a footer saying it is keyboard driven. Results whose title is not unique now show their path, because searching &ldquo;deploy&rdquo; returned two rows both reading &ldquo;Deployment&rdquo;, both tagged Deployment, and picking one was a guess.

The global focus ring is a violet rectangle floating around whatever has focus. In the palette the input is focused for as long as the dialog is open and nothing else can take focus, so the ring was permanent furniture. It is a 2px accent underline across the input row there, and there only: still a visible keyboard focus indicator, at full accent contrast.

Both search surfaces index the new page: the embedded docs that `grit docs search` reads, and the website search. That needed the skill table written as data, because the index reader reads a const array a page maps over and does not read the text inside a hand-written table cell.

```text
This account uses two-factor sign-in. Complete it in the app,
```

## v3.506.0 - November 12, 2026

### zod 4, and a freshly generated project with no advisories at all

grit#175. zod 3 carries a HIGH advisory with no fix inside 3.x, GHSA-mrhx-c7xc-m3w5, and it was the last one left in a new project. A fresh scaffold now answers:

```text
$ pnpm audit
No known vulnerabilities found
```

Not just no HIGH. None, at any severity.

#### It cost less than the issue expected, and that was worth checking

The issue listed four API changes to work through and feared a sweep over every hand-written schema in the admin and web templates. Three of the four do not apply: there is not one `required_error` or `invalid_type_error` in the tree, and not one `z.string().datetime()`. The `z.string().email()` family is real and it was seven call sites in three files, because the admin and web schemas are generated from those.

Then the more useful finding, from installing zod 4.6.7 and asking it rather than reasoning about it: **every 3.x spelling still type-checks and still validates at runtime.** `z.string().email()`, `z.string().url()` and `z.string().uuid("message")` are deprecated in favour of `z.email()`, `z.url()` and `z.uuid()`, and they work, and they still reject bad input.

So this was a pin bump. The call sites were modernised because they should be, not because they had to be, and the eight separate `"zod"` pins at four different 3.x minors across eight files became one constant, which is its own small fix: a dependency the generator writes into every frontend is one fact.

#### Which is why grit upgrade does not scan your schemas

The plan was for `grit upgrade` to refuse to move the pin while a project's own schemas still used 3.x-only calls, and to name the files. That was the right design for the problem as described and it guards against nothing: there are no 3.x-only calls that break under 4, so the scanner would have refused no project and cost every upgrade a pass over every schema in the repository. It is not built.

The input-versus-output divergence around `.default()` is real in zod 4, and it does not reach Grit's own forms: `LoginSchema`, `RegisterSchema` and `ForgotPasswordSchema` declare no defaults, so `z.infer` and `z.input` are the same type for every schema handed to `useForm`. A schema of your own with defaults is still worth a look.

Verified on a generated triple project rather than on the templates: zod 4.6.7 resolved, and `type-check` clean on both the admin and the web app with the real compiler.


## v3.505.9 - November 12, 2026

### A generated test that passed here and failed in CI

CI went red on v3.505.8 while the same suite was green on this machine, which is the useful kind of disagreement.

```text
--- FAIL: TestTwoExchangesRaceAndOnlyOneWins
    0 of 2 exchanges succeeded, want exactly 1
    (errors: [no such table: o_auth_exchange_codes ...])
```

The table was missing, and it was missing locally too: the test passed here with the same error in its log. Every connection to `:memory:` gets its **own empty database**, and the pool opens a second as soon as two queries overlap. That test runs two goroutines through the same exchange on purpose, so one of them landed on a fresh database and found no tables at all. Pass or fail on timing, with an error that reads as a broken feature rather than a broken harness.

`internal/testkit` has capped its pool at one connection for exactly this reason, and says so in a comment that describes this symptom precisely. A helper that opens its own database is outside that, and a test in `internal/services` cannot use testkit anyway, because testkit imports services. So it caps its own pool now. Twenty consecutive runs, no errors.

Fifty-odd generated helpers open a bare `:memory:` database and exactly one of them runs a goroutine. The rest are sequential, where a second connection is never asked for, so sweeping them would be fifty files touched to prevent nothing. A test catches the first of them to grow a goroutine instead, which is the moment the bug becomes real.

### grit skills said twenty-seven and meant twenty-eight

Found while checking whether grit#160 was still open, which it mostly is not: `grit skills install` became visible in `--help` in v3.467.0, with the three artefacts people call a Grit skill spelled out and a refusal that names the repository rather than failing with an npm error.

What it still said was the wrong number. The help text counts the pack and the list of skills is beside it in the same file, so the two drift the moment a skill is added and the prose is not reread. `grit-teacher` arrived in v3.499.0 and made it twenty-eight.

A test counts the list and requires the help text to say that number, and requires it not to say any other, which is the half a search for the right word alone would miss. The shape of mistake nobody notices is the one where the sentence still reads correctly.


## v3.505.8 - November 12, 2026

### A logo that leaked, a race that answered 500, and a public route with no limit of its own

Three of the six follow-ups in grit#199, found by exercising the v3.486.0 invitation flow on real generated projects. The reporter named the first two as the ones to pick first.

#### Every replaced organization logo stayed in the bucket

Replacing or removing a logo cleared the column and left the object. The comment defending that said the storage driver owned its own cleanup, and nothing did: the orphan sweep reads the `uploads` table for rows nothing claimed, and a logo is uploaded straight to storage and never gets a row. So the justification named a mechanism that could not see these objects at all.

Both paths delete the superseded object now. The key is derived from the stored URL and then **verified**: the candidate is rendered back through the same `GetURL` that wrote the column, and only a byte-for-byte match is handed to a delete. A project whose storage has moved, or a driver whose URLs are not a base plus the key, declines and leaves the object exactly where the old behaviour left it. That is what makes a string operation on a URL safe here, and it is why this needed no new column.

Deleted after the column moves, never before: an object removed ahead of a write that then fails leaves the organization pointing at nothing. Best effort, because the column has already moved and failing the request over a bucket that refused the delete would report that the logo did not change when it did.

#### A slug or tax id race answered 500

Both were checked with a SELECT and then written, so a concurrent write hit the unique index and came back `500 INTERNAL_ERROR`. The index is the truth and the check is a courtesy, so a violation has to answer what the check would have:

```text
409  SLUG_TAKEN      That slug was taken while you were creating this organization.
409  TAX_ID_TAKEN    That tax id already belongs to another organization
```

Both write paths ask `respond.DuplicateKey`, which already recognised all four drivers and names the column when the driver says so, so an update racing the tax id is reported as a tax id rather than as a slug. Verified against a real driver rather than a mock: the index fires with `UNIQUE constraint failed: organizations.slug`, and that is what the helper recognises.

#### The invitation preview had only the global limit

`GET /organization-invitations/preview` is public by necessity, because the page has to say what a link is before anybody can sign in, and it takes a token. That puts it in the same class as every auth route with a per-route limit, and it had only the global per-IP one. It has its own now, listed whether or not the plugin is installed: a limit on a path the project does not serve never fires, and a limit added by an installer is one the next installer forgets.

The remaining three items are TOTP on the accept page, an Expo device pass, and the split-domain verification origin. All three are real and none is a one-liner.


## v3.505.7 - November 11, 2026

### The .custom file can take a button away

grit#211. `ResourceCustomisation` exists so a project's overrides outlive the generator, and it could patch `columns`, `fields`, `components` and `bulkActions`. It could not patch `table.actions`, so the one override a project genuinely needs, which buttons a resource offers, was the one that had to be edited in the generated file and was therefore lost on every `grit generate resource --force`. The reporter lost the same edit three times.

```tsx
// resources/audit-entries/audit-entries.custom.tsx
const custom: ResourceCustomisation<AuditEntry> = {
  // The server authors these rows: a create callback refuses clients, so the
  // generated New button could only ever 403.
  actions: ["view"],
}
```

Of the two fixes offered, this is the one the reporter called the honest one, and they were right: the framework cannot know about a project's own create callback. `--append-only` correctly drops `edit` and `delete` and keeps `create`, because appending to an append-only table is the point. A project whose own rules refuse that create is the only thing that knows, and a button that always fails teaches an operator the admin is broken.

Replaced rather than merged, unlike `columns` and `fields`: the point of setting it is almost always to take something away, and a patch that could only add would not do that.

Everything gated on an action follows from the one list, so nothing else had to change: `can()` is derived from it, which carries the override to the detail page's Edit and Delete and to the bulk toolbar. There is a test that it stays derived, because the failure mode if it stops is each surface being told separately and each one forgetting differently.

Verified against a real admin rather than the generated text alone: the three tiers resolving in order `["create", "view"]`, `["view"]` and the four defaults; the admin type-checking with the override set; and the override still in place after `grit generate resource --force` had rewritten the definition beside it.


## v3.505.6 - November 11, 2026

### A sync mode for rows the server authors

grit#210. Sync had two modes and needed a third. Anything the server writes on a user's behalf wants to be mirrored for reading and never written by a client: an append-only ledger, an audit or provenance row, a result computed by a job, anything written through a hook a client cannot reproduce. On the project that reported it, seven of twenty resources want exactly that.

```yaml
sync:
  mode: read_only
```

Neither existing mode fits. `online_only` means she cannot read a record about her own work offline, which is the wrong answer for a report she should be able to open on a train. `offline_first` declares the rows a client's to create, so the outbox queues a write that is guaranteed to fail and parks it in front of her with whatever the server said.

`conflict: server_wins` is the nearest available-looking answer and is not the same thing: it decides what happens when **versions** disagree, and a client-minted create has no version to disagree about, so it never runs.

Both halves, and the client half is the one that matters: the outbox refuses to accept the write rather than the server refusing to accept the push, because every queued-and-failed write is a row somebody has to look at and dismiss. The server refuses it too, with a `READ_ONLY` code, so an old client build is still told.

```text
sync: cannot create cost_ledgers: it is registered read_only. The server
writes these rows. Read them with useOfflineResource and call the API
directly for anything that changes them.

outbox entries after the refusal = 0
local rows written anyway        = 0
```

Checked before the local mirror is touched, not only before the queue: writing the row locally and then refusing to queue it would leave a row on the device that never reaches the server and never will, which is a worse lie than the one this replaces. `useOfflineResource` exposes `readOnly` so a screen hides the button rather than offering an action that throws.

#### And grit sync doctor has something real to check

```text
warning  audit_entries: is append-only and declared offline_first, so the outbox
         will queue updates and deletes the server and the database both refuse
         Declare `sync: {mode: read_only}` if the server authors these rows.
```

Its first check about what the server will actually accept, rather than whether a policy is internally coherent. That distinction is the reporter's, and it is the one that matters: in their project nothing was broken, because a GORM guard refused the push and a trigger refused the write under it, and `sync doctor` said everything checked out. A declaration that reads as though it took effect is the state the sync docs themselves call the worst one.

A warning rather than an error, because create is still legal on an append-only model: a client minting a ledger row is a real design, and only its updates and deletes are certain to fail.

#### One thing this nearly shipped broken

`internal/sync/policy.go` was written to new projects only, while `internal/handlers/sync.go` travels on upgrade. So giving `Policy` a `Writable()` method and calling it from the handler would have delivered, to every upgraded project with offline sync, a handler calling a method that project's own package does not declare. The package and its handler are one cluster now and travel together.

The test added in v3.505.0 for exactly this class did not catch it, because `internal/sync` was on its allowlist as a package every project already has. True, and not the question: an owned file calling into a package needs that package *refreshed*, not merely present. The allowlist now says so, and there is a test that the sync handler and the sync package arrive together.


## v3.505.5 - November 11, 2026

### Two relations to the same model named one variable twice

```text
grants-form.tsx(25,9): error TS2451: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'usersOpts'.
grants-form.tsx(26,9): error TS2451: Cannot redeclare block-scoped variable 'usersOpts'.
```

grit#209. The desktop form builder declared the options hook once per relation and named the variable after the *target* model, so a resource with two `belongs_to` fields pointing at the same model produced a form that did not compile, and `pnpm type-check` failed for the whole monorepo.

Not an exotic shape. &ldquo;A credit granted to one user by another&rdquo; is enough, and `--owned-by user` makes it three relations to one model, so the likeliest way to meet it is by accident.

```diff
- const usersOpts = useUsers().data ?? [];
- const usersOpts = useUsers().data ?? [];
+ const approvedByOpts = useUsers().data ?? [];
+ const requestedByOpts = useUsers().data ?? [];
```

Named after the field, which is the reporter's preferred fix and the readable one: two selects both reading `usersOpts` said nothing about which was which. Deduplicating by target model would also have compiled and is the wrong fix, because both selects would then share one hook result, right for User today and silently wrong the moment the two relations want different filtering.

#### The Expo form had it twice over

Not in the report: found by grepping for the pattern the desktop bug was an instance of. The mobile form builder declares two variables per relation, the query and the options, and both were named after the target. The admin and the web app are unaffected, as the reporter said: the admin resource files are declarative and have no local variable to collide.

The mobile half needed the form's text split from its write, which is the shape the desktop generator has always had. That is why one of the two was reachable by a unit test and the other was not.

Verified against the real toolchain rather than the generator's output alone: the reporter's exact command on a fresh triple-plus-desktop project, then `tsc` with zero errors, and the two old names put back by hand to confirm the same file still produces their TS2451 without the fix.


## v3.505.4 - November 11, 2026

### A project can declare its own error codes

grit#208. The catalogue had 123 codes and no way to add a 124th. `internal/respond/codes.go` is generated and says DO NOT EDIT, so an entry added there was lost on the next upgrade, and nothing said where to put one instead.

```yaml
# .grit/error-codes.yaml
codes:
  - code: PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED
    status: 402
    category: limit
    area: billing
    meaning: The account has used all three of its similarity checks.
    client: Show the upgrade prompt. Retrying will not help.
```

```bash
grit sync
```

Folded into the same two generated files the built-in codes come from, which is the property worth having: the typed Go constant and the `ApiErrorCode` union come from one list, so a switch over error codes in the frontend stays exhaustive for the errors the product actually raises. A Go-only extension file would have given the API its code and left the frontend unable to type a case for the one error the product most needs to handle well.

The file is refused rather than half-applied when it is wrong, and each refusal names the file and the code: a code that is not SHOUTING_SNAKE_CASE, a status that is not a 4xx or 5xx, a category that does not exist, a missing meaning or client line, the same code twice, or one that shadows a built-in:

```text
.grit/error-codes.yaml: VALIDATION_ERROR is already one of Grit's codes, at 422.
Pick another name: two entries for one code means its status depends on which
of them wins
```

`grit sync` refuses outright, since applying that file is its whole job. `grit new` and `grit upgrade` report it and carry on, because aborting an upgrade over a typo in a file the upgrade does not own is worse, and it is not silent in practice: the constant the handler wanted is then absent and the build fails right after the warning says why.

#### And the bug inside the gap

The workaround that suggests itself compiles:

```go
respond.Fail(c, respond.Code("PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED"), "You have used all 3 checks")
```

`Code` is a string type, so that is legal Go. `StatusOf` did not know the code, so the answer was **500**: every caller who reached their plan limit was told a server fault, the on-call was paged for it, and nothing in the response or the log said which code had done it. It still answers 500, because a code nothing documents is a bug in the handler, and now it says so once, by name, with what to do about it.

There is also the signal there was none of. Every project gets `internal/respond/codes_project_test.go`, which fails on any `respond.Code("...")` in the project that is not declared, so `go test ./...` finds it rather than production doing.

#### PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED, at 402

Shipped in the catalogue, because nearly every SaaS needs exactly it and the substitutes are each wrong in a way a client can feel. `RATE_LIMITED` is a 429, which means &ldquo;retry shortly&rdquo;: a client with backoff retries against a wall and the person is told the wrong thing. `FORBIDDEN` is indistinguishable from a permission failure, so a UI can only tell them apart by matching on the message string. There was no 402 in the catalogue at all, and 402 is what Stripe and GitHub answer for the same situation.

Which turned up a smaller thing: the map from a status to its Go constant was fifteen entries kept by hand, and 402 was not among them, so the new code came out as a bare `402` in a file whose stated point is to read like something a person wrote. It is now every 4xx and 5xx `net/http` declares, read out of `net/http`'s own source rather than typed: 418 is `StatusTeapot` and not StatusImATeapot, so a name derived from `http.StatusText` would have been wrong for it and the generated file would not have compiled.


## v3.505.3 - November 11, 2026

### A confidential resource with a parent generated a test package that did not compile

```text
vet.exe: internal/handlers/record_test.go:99:2: declared and not used: folder
```

grit#207, in this morning's v3.505.0. The two tests that flag added, `AnAdminSeesNothing` and `AGrantHolderSeesEveryRow`, create a row that belongs to somebody neither caller is. For a resource with a `belongs_to` they created the parent and then never pointed the row at it, so the parent was a declared and unused variable and the whole handlers package stopped building. Fifteen resources at once for the reporter, since every one of theirs has a parent.

The function that points a fixture row at the signed-in user works by replacing the owner's assignment, and it was called twice on one resource: the second call ran over the first call's output, could not find the assignment it was looking for, and fell into a branch that rebuilt the override from nothing. That branch discarded every other `belongs_to` assignment while leaving the lines that created those parents.

Both halves are fixed: each variant is now derived from what the fixture builder returned rather than from another variant, and the fallback adds the owner to an existing override instead of replacing it, so it cannot silently drop assignments again. The row is fully formed, which is what the reporter preferred: a test asserting an administrator sees nothing is more convincing when the row it cannot see is a real one, and on Postgres a row missing a required foreign key does not insert at all.

#### Why the tests that shipped with it did not catch this

Every fixture in them was a confidential resource whose only relation was the owner, and with one relation there is nothing to drop. The new ones take the two-parent shape, and they are built by running the words the reporter typed through the same parser the CLI uses rather than by writing a definition out by hand. The first attempt did write one by hand, left the parent relation optional, and so asserted the absence of an assignment the generator was never asked to make.

One of them parses the generated file and one checks that every variable it declares is read, which is the class of fault rather than this instance of it: an unused local is a type error, not a syntax error, so parsing alone does not see it.

For that fixture to be the real thing, `--owned-by` adding its own relation moved out of the CLI and into the resource definition as `EnsureOwnerField`. It was six lines in `cmd/grit`, which meant a definition assembled anywhere else was a different definition, and a test wanting the real shape had to copy them.


## v3.505.2 - November 11, 2026

### Upgrade past v3.505.1: it fixed one direction and broke a worse one

v3.505.1 made `manifest.Rel` resolve a relative path against the working directory, because `grit upgrade` hands its repairs `apps/api/...` and `filepath.Rel` errors on one absolute path and one relative one.

That resolved the path and left the root alone, and `grit new app` is the other way round: it opens the recording session with the relative directory it was given and then writes absolute paths. So the pair failed in the opposite direction and a freshly scaffolded project recorded nothing at all.

```text
grit new probe --api      # v3.505.0:  441 manifest entries
grit new probe --api      # v3.505.1:    0 manifest entries
grit new probe --api      # v3.505.2:  441 manifest entries
```

An empty manifest means every later `grit upgrade` has no record of what Grit wrote, so it cannot tell its own files from yours. Both sides are normalised now, and the test takes all four combinations rather than the one that happened to be broken at the time: that is what trading one for the other earns.

**If you scaffolded a project with v3.505.1**, run `grit upgrade` on this version. It rewrites the framework-owned files and records them as it goes, which took a probe project from 10 entries back to 329 and left it building. Files of your own were never in the manifest and are unaffected either way.

Worth saying plainly: v3.505.1 was green on all six workflows with this in it. Every test in the manifest package built its manifest by hand rather than through a session the way the commands do, so nothing exercised the path that broke. There is now a test that opens a session the way `grit new` opens one and counts what came back, and it fails against both v3.505.1 and the version before it.


## v3.505.1 - November 11, 2026

### A repair told the manifest nothing, so the file it fixed read as hand-edited

Found by following v3.505.0's own advice. The grid repair fixed a service, and `grit generate resource` then refused to touch that resource:

```text
Note has 1 file(s) you have edited since Grit wrote them:

  apps/api/internal/services/note.go
```

Nobody had edited it. The repair had, and the repair is Grit. Two things stacked up to produce that.

A repair writes through a helper that calls `manifest.Refresh`, so the file keeps reading as Grit's and keeps receiving later framework fixes. That call resolves the path against the project root, and every repair `grit upgrade` runs after the main pass hands it a relative path: `apps/api/...`. One absolute path and one relative path is an error from `filepath.Rel`, and the error read as &ldquo;this file is outside the project&rdquo;, so the record was dropped without a word. Underneath that, the recording session those refreshes needed was opened and closed inside the main pass, which had already returned.

So the file kept the hash it had before the repair. From then on the next upgrade skipped it as somebody's own work, and the generator declined to regenerate it. That is the exact failure the convention exists to prevent, and it has been true of every post-upgrade repair, not only the new one: the test that enforces the convention checks that `Refresh` is called, which they all did.

Relative paths resolve now, and the session is open while the repairs run. Verified by upgrading a real v3.504.0 project: the repair fires, the manifest entry moves to the new version and hash, regenerating the resource is allowed, its tests pass and `grit doctor` is clean.

Also, for an existing `--confidential` resource: its generated tests are the project's own files, so an upgrade does not rewrite them and they keep signing in as an administrator. `grit upgrade` now names those files and says to regenerate the resource, rather than leaving the tests red with nothing explaining why.


## v3.505.0 - November 11, 2026

### The grid was the one way into an owned table that ignored ownership

Found by reading the three tests grit#205 reported as failing, which turned out to be reporting something larger than a test bug. On every `--owned-by` resource, the bulk-edit grid took a list of row ids and loaded exactly those rows with no scope on the query at all.

```text
POST /api/v1/memos/bulk-edit    # the ids belong to another user
200 OK  {"data":{"affected":1},"message":"1 memo updated"}
```

The list refused those rows. The detail route answered 404. Patch refused the write. This one did it and reported success, so a caller holding nothing but `memos.edit` could rewrite any other account's row by putting its id in the grid. Nothing in a project would have noticed, because the response says how many rows were affected and not whose.

`BulkCreate` had the matching hole pointing the other way: it decoded the row it was handed, owner column included, and believed it, so the grid could file rows under somebody else's account. A single create has stamped the owner from the session since ownership shipped.

Both arrived with the grid in v3.372.0, and both were unchecked: `grit doctor` looked at List, Export, Bulk, GetByID and load, and not at the two newest methods in the file. It looks at all seven now.

There was also a comment directly above the unscoped query saying an owned resource is scoped to the caller here. That sentence is most of why nobody looked, so it is removed from existing projects too and not only from the generator.

#### It reaches projects that already exist

```bash
grit upgrade
```

A generator fix reaches resources generated from here on and nothing that exists, and a project with twenty owned resources is not going to regenerate twenty resources. So `grit upgrade` scopes the grid in every generated service it finds, reading the owner column out of the service's own List, and prints the name of any service it could not read so that one can be checked by hand. A repaired service is byte-identical to a generated one, which a test compares rather than trusts.

#### And three bugs in --confidential, one release old

- **grit#204:** `grit upgrade` wrote an `internal/authz/actor.go` that imports `internal/confidential` and never wrote the package, so an upgraded project did not compile: exactly one file referenced it and nothing provided it. A fresh `grit new` was fine, which is the shape of divergence that goes unnoticed. A test now reads every internal import in the set of files that travels on upgrade and fails if the set does not also write the package.
- **grit#205:** a `--confidential` resource generated three tests that sign in as an ADMIN and expect to see the row, which is exactly what the flag removes. So the generator wrote the contract into the resource and the opposite of the contract into its tests, and the flag was red on first use: fifteen resources adopted at once meant 45 failing tests. They act as the row's owner now, and two tests the flag always needed are generated beside them: an administrator gets an empty list and a 404, and a holder of `<resource>.confidential` sees every row. Both of those were asserted nowhere in a generated project.
- **grit#206:** the `owned-resource-unscoped` check knew `authz.ScopeOwned` and not `authz.ScopeConfidential`, so it reported every correctly scoped confidential resource as wide open. The check is an error and the docs present `grit doctor` as a CI gate, which made the quickest route to a green pipeline dropping the flag.

#### The part of grit#206 that was not about --confidential

The same report noticed `grit doctor` saying &ldquo;27 checks over 9 resource(s)&rdquo; on a project with nineteen. Every per-resource check was skipping every resource whose name is more than one word.

The handler and service maps dropped any file with an underscore in its name, on the reasoning that those are the generator's extra handlers: `product_import.go`, `page_tree.go`. It is also where a two-word resource lives. `CartItem` is `cart_item.go`, so it was discarded, and with it every ownership, PII, tenancy and append-only check that resource would have had. Which resources got checked depended on how they happened to be named, which is why the result looked arbitrary.

They are keyed by file name now and looked up by the resource's own, so an extra handler is still not mistaken for a resource and a two-word resource is no longer invisible. `grit doctor` on `examples/commerce` went from four resources to five.

Smaller, from the same report: adopting `--confidential` on an existing resource left two entries for it in the permission catalogue, because the injection is idempotent on the whole block and the block differs between flags only in its list of actions. The old entry is removed before the new one goes in.


## v3.504.0 - November 11, 2026

### An administrator who cannot read customer content

The second half of grit#203, and the harder half. Until now ADMIN was exempt from ownership scoping everywhere, so a product whose rows are medical records, legal files, tax papers or coursework had an operator who could read all of them, and the only way to change that was hand-editing framework files.

```bash
grit generate resource MedicalRecord \
  --fields "patient:belongs_to[User],notes:text,scan:file[pdf]" \
  --owned-by patient --confidential
```

Three tiers, where there used to be two:

Opt in, per resource. Nothing changes for an existing resource, and an administrator keeps full reach over Users, Roles and Settings, which they need to do the job at all.

#### It holds on every path out of the database, not just the table

A guarantee that covers the admin list and not the export is not a guarantee, so each way out was closed:

- **The service layer**, which is where the rule lives, so every route, job, command and test inherits it rather than only the routes somebody remembered.
- **Exports** fall out of that: the CSV is the list without pages, scoped the same way.
- **GORM Studio** browses tables directly, below the service layer, so a confidential model is never added to its list. In every environment, not only production: a development-only exemption is the kind that reaches production by accident.
- **Backup downloads.** An archive still holds every table, because a backup that omits them does not restore the application and nobody discovers that until the worst possible moment. So the control is on taking the file off the server, and it needs the grant for *every* confidential table: a caller who may read patient records and not payroll must not be handed a file containing payroll.

Two combinations are refused rather than generated, because both produce a resource nobody can read or one published to the internet: `--confidential` without `--owned-by`, and `--confidential` with `--public`. It implies `--audit-reads`, since the reason the grant goes to a named person rather than a role is that somebody can be asked afterwards who read what.

#### And the uploads table, which is where this started

```bash
UPLOADS_CONFIDENTIAL=true
```

Uploads are Grit's own table rather than a generated resource, so there is no flag to attach. One setting covers it, because a project with private files usually has only private files.

It also removes `uploads/` from the public storage prefixes, and that coupling is enforced in code rather than left to whoever edits `.env`. The default prefixes are `uploads/,thumbnails/`, which means a stored file is readable by anyone holding its URL with no signature. Hiding the rows from an administrator while leaving that on would have been no protection at all, and the person turning the setting on has no reason to know the two are connected.

#### One thing the compiler found that reading would not have

The registry of confidential tables started in `internal/authz`, which is where the scoping lives and looked like the obvious home. A model file registering itself from its own `init()` then imports authz, authz imports models, and the project does not build. It has its own leaf package now, for exactly the reason `internal/erasure` has one.


## v3.503.1 - November 11, 2026

### The Go floor moves to 1.26.11 for an HTTP/1 server crash

GO-2026-6859: a race in `net/http`'s `MaxBytesReader` header handling crashes an HTTP/1 server, fixed in Go 1.26.11. Reachable rather than theoretical: govulncheck named six traces through the CLI and failed both the repository scan and the scan of a freshly generated app.

A standard library advisory moves the toolchain pin rather than a module version, and that pin is mirrored in every workflow, both Dockerfiles, the desktop templates and the lint workflow the scaffold writes: twenty-six places. A new project pins `go 1.26.11`, and `grit upgrade` raises an older `go.mod` to it.


## v3.503.0 - November 11, 2026

### Erasure deleted the rows and left the files

grit#202. `erasure.Scrub` hard-deletes every registered row and anonymises the user, and had no awareness of storage at all. So a right-to-erasure request removed the `uploads` rows, left the objects they pointed at in the bucket, and the audit trail recorded a successful erasure. The objects were unreferenced by then, so nothing could find them to clean up later either.

For most projects that is an avatar. For the reporter it is a student's uploaded PDFs under Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, which is why the endpoint exists at all. Deleted that leaves the documents on disk is the one outcome the feature exists to prevent.

A model that owns something outside the database now says so once, and the cleanup runs inside the transaction and before the rows go, because what it needs is written on them:

```go
erasure.RegisterWithCleanup(&Upload{}, "user_id", deleteUploadObjects)
```

Grit's own `uploads` table uses it, so the common case needs no project code. A file column on one of your models is still yours to register the same way. An error fails the whole erasure deliberately: a request that reports success while the files are there is worse than one that fails.

### The upload allowlist could only ever grow

grit#201. `UPLOAD_ALLOWED_MIME` added to the baseline, so a project could accept more types than Grit chose and never fewer. The reporter accepts exactly four things and could not say so, while the baseline took RAR archives, seven audio types and three video ones. The alternative was editing the line in `routes.go` that builds the list, which means owning 1600 lines of central routing for an allowlist.

```bash
UPLOAD_ALLOWED_MIME=only:application/pdf,image/png,image/jpeg
```

A prefix rather than a second environment variable, because a second one needs a second config field, a second load line and a second constructor argument, and the repair that adds the first is gated on it being absent, so an existing project would never receive the second. An `only:` with nothing after it falls back to the baseline rather than refusing every upload, which is not what anybody meant to type.

And PowerPoint is in the baseline, which Word and Excel already were. That reads as an oversight rather than a decision, and it was an expensive one: the reporter's product exports a deck as PPTX and could not accept one back, while it could accept a RAR archive. Legacy `.ppt` and `image/tiff` went in beside it.

### Framework handlers attached no actor

grit#203. A generated resource handler builds its context with `authz.WithActor`. The framework handlers passed `c.Request.Context()` through untouched, so anything reading `authz.ActorFrom` below the handler saw a caller for generated resources and nothing for uploads. The reporter's GORM callback, which removes the admin exemption on tables holding customer content, worked for every generated resource and stood silently aside for the one table holding the actual files.

Standing aside for a context with no actor is right, because that is a job or a migration acting as the server. The bug was that a request-scoped call was indistinguishable from one. The actor is attached in the auth middleware now, once, after the role is resolved because that is what decides whether the caller is an admin. In `Identify` as well as `Auth`: fixing only the guarded routes would leave every signed-in reader of a public page invisible to the same check.

The second half of that issue, uploads carrying their own ownership logic with its own ADMIN exemption rather than sharing `--owned-by`, is still open.


## v3.502.0 - November 11, 2026

### An error page that can fix the error

Reported from this site: a black screen and one line of unstyled text, "Application error: a client-side exception has occurred while loading gritframework.dev". That is Next's own fallback, and it appears when an app has no `error.tsx`. Every project `grit new` scaffolds ships one, and a `global-error.tsx` beside it. The site that generates them had neither.

Both exist now, in the site's own dark styling rather than the browser's default. But the interesting half is what put somebody there, because three releases went out that day.

#### A deploy breaks every tab that was already open

Next splits an app into hashed chunks and a deploy replaces them. A tab open across one asks for a filename that no longer exists, gets a 404, and throws. Nothing is wrong with the app: the page is simply built by a version that is gone.

The generated error page already handled this badly, and the reason is worth stating because it looked fine. Its one button called `reset()`, and `reset` re-renders the same tree, which asks for the same missing file. The only action on the page could not fix the likeliest reason for seeing it. Only a reload fetches the new filenames.

```ts
// Matched on the message, not the class: it has been through a minifier,
// and three runtimes word it three ways.
function isStaleChunk(error: Error): boolean {
  const text = (error.name + " " + error.message).toLowerCase();
  return (
    text.includes("chunkloaderror") ||
    text.includes("loading chunk") ||
    text.includes("failed to fetch dynamically imported module") ||
    text.includes("importing a module script failed")
  );
}
```

When it matches, the page reloads itself once and says what happened rather than calling it an unexpected error, because nothing was unexpected: the app was updated. Once, and guarded in `sessionStorage`, because an automatic reload with no guard turns any error this misidentifies into an infinite refresh, which is worse than the error. And "Try again" is not offered on that branch at all: a button that cannot work is worse than no button.

This landed in `apps/web` and `apps/admin` as well as on this site, from one copy of the check shared by both templates, because two lists of substrings drift and the drift is silent. Both paths were verified in a browser: a generic throw renders the page, and a chunk-shaped throw reloads once and then stops.

### And the docs nav stopped changing under you

The header shows the docs' own sections inside `/docs` and the product nav everywhere else, which is deliberate. One link in the docs set pointed at `/blueprints`, the marketing catalogue, so clicking it left the docs and swapped the whole header. Every other link in that set keeps you inside, so the one that did not read as a second navbar appearing from nowhere, which is exactly how it was reported.

It points at `/docs/blueprints` now, which already existed, is already in the sidebar, and links to the catalogue from a page that first explains what a blueprint is. `check-nav.py` fails CI on any docs-nav link that leaves `/docs`, and on a section missing from `DOCS_SECTIONS`, which would underline two entries at once.


## v3.501.0 - November 10, 2026

### An upload that failed in the grid said nothing at all

Reported as a silent failure when storage is not configured, and it is worse than that: *every* upload failure in the bulk grid was invisible, whatever the cause. The cell caught the error and rendered it into `<span role="alert" className="sr-only">`, which announces to a screen reader and shows a sighted operator nothing. The spinner stopped, the button went back to saying "Choose", and that was the whole of it.

Reproduced against a real API answering 503 to the presign: the grid was pixel-identical before and after. It now marks the cell and puts the API's own sentence in the dialog's error bar, which is the sentence worth reading because it names the setting that is wrong:

```text
File storage is not configured. Set STORAGE_DRIVER=local in .env to keep
uploads in a folder on this server, or point the bucket settings at a
running object store.
```

The first fix showed "Request failed with status code 503", which is what an axios rejection's `message` says. The admin already has `getApiErrorMessage` for exactly this and the cell was not using it.

### And a column of integers had no thousands separators

`unit_price:int` rendered as `1750000`. The cell was `<input type="number">`, and the spec requires that element's value to be a valid floating-point number, so a grouped string assigned to it is discarded and the field goes blank. No amount of formatting around the cell could have worked: the input type had to change. It is now a text input with `inputMode="decimal"`, grouped when the cell is not being edited and raw while it is, because a separator appearing under the caret moves the caret and this grid exists to be typed in quickly. Money had the same input type and the same problem.

Looking at it turned up the half that was losing data rather than only looking wrong. Pasting a column out of a spreadsheet, which is the likeliest way anybody fills this grid, ran `Number("1,250,000")`. That is `NaN`, and `JSON.stringify` writes `NaN` as `null`, so every pasted value over 999 was silently emptied on the way to the server.

One mistake of mine in the first version: the replacement cell carried `role="spinbutton"` to keep the old semantics, and the accessibility tree then reported `aria-valuenow 0` for every empty cell. A text input with a label is honest; a text input claiming to be a spinbutton announces a number that is not there.

### grit new asks where uploads go

Every project was scaffolded with `STORAGE_DRIVER=minio`, and the only way to learn there were five drivers was to scaffold one and then read a comment in `.env`. The one most new projects actually want needs no Docker, no bucket and no credentials, and it was the hardest to find:

```bash
grit new myapp --storage local
```

`minio` (the default), `local`, `s3`, `r2` or `b2`, with the usual spellings accepted (`aws`, `cloudflare`, `backblaze`, `disk`). `grit new` with no flags asks for one, in a picker built from the same list the flag validates against, so the two cannot drift: that is how every driver but minio came to be invisible to the people who use the prompt.

A project scaffolded without the flag gets exactly the `.env` it got before, which is what `TestNoStorageChoiceKeepsMinio` is for.

Both were asked for in the same sentence, and both are the question somebody has about ten minutes after their first `grit generate resource`: I made the thing in the admin panel, now how does a stranger see it, and then how do I put a page behind a sign-in.

```text
# A marker cookie opens the gate, which is all it does.
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -b "shop_session=1" localhost:3000/account
200

# And the API is not fooled by it.
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -b "shop_session=1" localhost:8080/api/auth/me
401
```

The gate decides what HTML to send. The API decides what data to return. Only the second is a security boundary, and confusing the two produces a site that looks locked and is not.

Both pages were written by building what they describe: a triple project, a seeded `Product` resource, the five components, `pnpm build`, and every `curl` in them run against it. That page said Grit "ships three pre-built auth pages" in `apps/web`, and listed `/login`, `/register` and `/forgot-password`. It does not and never did: only the admin panel gets an `(auth)` route group, and a freshly scaffolded web app has no login page and no `hooks/use-auth.ts`.

Sending a reader to look for a file that is not there is the most expensive sort of documentation error, because they have no way to tell whether the file is missing or they are. ## v3.499.0 - November 10, 2026

### A twenty-seventh expert, which writes the tutorial

The expert pack gains `grit-teacher`. It takes one feature that has shipped and writes the tutorial that would have let somebody build it themselves, one markdown file per lesson into `.grit/tutorials/`.

It names its reader rather than imagining one: somebody who reads React without effort and has never written Go in anger. That single decision settles most of the others. The struct tag and the returned error get explained and the `useQuery` does not, every file it touches is named by full path because the reader has not opened most of the folders yet, and the words "simply" and "just" are banned, because a reader who is stuck reads those as evidence they are too slow for this.

Two things are required rather than encouraged. The scenario comes before step one, names a product rather than a category, and says when *not* to use the feature: a technique nobody knows the occasion for is a technique nobody uses, and that section is the difference between teaching and documentation. And every step ends in a checkpoint saying what the reader will see and what it means if they see something else, because a reader who cannot tell whether step four worked stops learning at step four.

The rule that keeps it honest is the same shape as the advocate's rule about numbers: every command in the file was actually run, in order, in a project built while writing it. A flag that does not exist is worse than no tutorial, because the reader cannot tell whether they typed it wrong or the document is wrong, and most beginners decide it was them and stop.

`grit skills status` was also reporting five fewer skills than the pack ships. Its list is a copy, kept local so the command works with no network, and it had fallen four behind before anybody looked: `grit-adopt`, `grit-blueprints`, `grit-design-review` and `grit-plugins` were installed, working and invisible.

### And the two things writing the first lesson found

This is the part of the new skill that pays for it. Teaching a feature means following your own steps as if you had never seen it, and the steps that fail are the ones a reader would have failed at. The lesson was the vector field type from v3.491.0, and it found two.

#### The package said that working code was broken

`internal/vectors` told you to pass `Nearest` to `Clauses`, and gave as the reason that `Order()` "would compile and do nothing". The advice is right. The reason was wrong:

```text
Clauses(Nearest)         ORDER BY present: true   ... ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
Order(Nearest)           ORDER BY present: true   ... ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
Order(CosineDistance)    ORDER BY present: false  SELECT * FROM "support_tickets" WHERE ...
```

GORM's `Order` handles a `clause.OrderBy`, which is exactly what the three `Nearest` helpers return. What it drops without a word is a `clause.Expression`, which is what the three raw distance helpers return. So the trap is real and the comment was pointing at the wrong thing, which is worse than pointing at nothing: the first reader to check finds the framework lying about its own API, and the one who believes it learns a rule about `Order` when the rule is about the type.

The generated project now asserts both halves, so the recommendation and its reason cannot drift apart again:

```go
func TestOrderDropsAnExpressionAndKeepsAnOrderBy(t *testing.T) {
	// Order(Nearest) keeps the ordering. Order(CosineDistance) loses it.
	// The recommendation to use Clauses only makes sense once both are pinned.
}
```

#### A test that passed against a query with no ORDER BY

The tutorial's own test, written the obvious way, was vacuous. Three tickets, nearest first, assert they come back nearest first. It passed. It also passed with the ordering removed from the query altogether, because rows with no `ORDER BY` arrive in scan order, scan order was insertion order, and insertion order was the answer.

The fix is one line of fixture ordering and it is now part of what the lesson teaches: insert the rows in the reverse of the order they should come back in. The same test then fails loudly against a query that is not sorting. It is the third time this month a green test turned out to be green for a reason unconnected to the thing it named, and the cheapest defence remains asking what would have to break for this to go red.


## v3.498.0 - November 9, 2026

### A constraint test that passed without a constraint

grit#198, and the third instance of one shape: the test schema is built by AutoMigrate, and AutoMigrate is not what `grit migrate` does. v3.494.0 added the append-only triggers. This adds the checked-in SQL pairs, which is everything a project expresses that AutoMigrate cannot: a CHECK, a partial index, a trigger, a backfill, an extension.

The reporter's argument for why this instance is the worst of the three is the one that decided the design. A missing trigger fails loudly, because a test for it asserts that an UPDATE is *refused* and gets an accepted UPDATE. A missing CHECK fails silently, because a test for it can just as naturally assert that a valid row is *accepted*, and that goes green against a schema with no constraint in it at all.

```go
// Without the constraint in the schema this passes, having proved nothing.
db.Create(&models.Reference{Doi: "10.1000/abc"})
```

#### Applied on Postgres, and declared on SQLite

The pairs run on the Postgres path only, because most of what a pair is for cannot run on SQLite: no `ADD CONSTRAINT`, no `CONCURRENTLY`, no extensions. So a test whose subject is something a pair creates says so, and `RequireSQLMigrations` fails rather than skips:

```go
func TestAReferenceNeedsAStableIdentifier(t *testing.T) {
	testkit.RequireSQLMigrations(t)
	db := testkit.DB(t)
	// ...
}
```

Failing rather than skipping is the reporter's point again: a skipped guarantee reads in a CI log exactly like a guarantee that held, and SQLite is the default, so a full-suite run would skip quietly for ever. They had added a CI step to fail the job on a skip, which should not be necessary.

On cost, which they also raised, the default goes the other way from their suggestion: applied unless turned off, not opt-in. `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` per test is genuinely not free, but the default has to be the one that cannot lie, and the cost is measurable while the silence is not. `GRIT_TEST_SKIP_SQL_MIGRATIONS=true` turns them off, and the guard then catches every test that needed them.

The testing docs now say what the suite covers on each database, because the reporter is right that it changes silently with one environment variable and that was written down nowhere.

#### One mistake of mine worth recording

The first version of the guard read a package-level flag that `testkit.DB` set. That is wrong twice: a guard placed first, which is where a guard belongs and where the reporter put it, always failed because the flag is only set once the database exists; and a global mutated by `DB` is not safe under `t.Parallel`. It reads the environment instead, which is answerable before any database is built, and the same predicate decides the behaviour so the two cannot disagree.

### And --force wrote a second copy of the index migration

grit#197, mine from v3.491.0. The existence check asked whether *this run's* timestamped filename was there, and the timestamp is new every run, so it only ever caught a collision inside the same second. Regenerating wrote another pair; regenerating three times wrote three.

The up side was harmless, being `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS`. The down side was not: both pairs record as applied and either one's down drops the index they share, so `grit migrate down --sql` leaves the history saying the older pair is applied while the index is gone. On a table big enough to want an hnsw index, that is a retrieval path quietly becoming a sequential scan rather than an error anybody sees.

An existing pair is now found by its derived name whatever timestamp it carries. And the generator says which of the two things happened, because `--force` promises to rewrite this resource's files and the migrations directory is not one of them:

```text
• apps/api/migrations/20261109032626_index_source_chunks_embedding.{up,down}.sql exists, left alone
    the hnsw index for embedding is already a migration. Edit that pair
    rather than regenerating: a second copy would drop the shared index on rollback
```

Both verified against a real Postgres, including each counterfactual: the reporter's constraint test passes in both directions with the pairs applied and fails loudly without them, and reverting the duplicate fix produces four migration files where there should be two.

### The desktop app type-checks for every field type

grit#196. A `--desktop` project failed `tsc -b` for any resource using one of six field types: money, percent, json, country, toggle or vector. Ten resources of nineteen on the reporter's project, sixteen errors. `vite build` was fine, so it was quiet until CI.

#### Two unions for one format

```text
src/routes/app/ai_runs.index.tsx(32,33): Type '"money"' is not assignable
  to type 'ColumnFormat | undefined'.
```

The generator emits one `ColumnFormat` per field type and writes it into both frontends. The admin's union has twenty-three members and the desktop's had nine, so the desktop silently stopped accepting what the generator emits. It takes the same list now, and `money`, `percent` and `json` render rather than falling through to the default.

On the reporter's question of whether `currency` or `money` wins: money, because it is the field type and the thing the generator writes. `currency` stays as an alias through the same case, because it is what the desktop has said for several releases and somebody may have written it by hand.

#### Three fields the form held as strings

```text
ai-runs-form.tsx(69,7):       Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'Money'.
ai-runs-form.tsx(70,7):       Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'boolean | undefined'.
source-chunks-form.tsx(57,7): Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number[]'.
```

Three separate causes, all falling through to the string default: money had no case at all, toggle was missed because the boolean case tested only `bool` and toggle is its own type, and vector had no case and should not have a form field.

A money field is now a number and a currency, and the conversion goes through the shared `toMajor` and `fromMajor` rather than a second exponent table. The reporter's point there is the one that mattered: the minor unit is per-currency, and a desktop form dividing by 100 shows a 50,000 shilling price as 500 in the currency this product actually bills in. The table already exists on the frontend for exactly that reason, so the form uses it rather than a copy that can disagree.

A vector gets no form field, which is what the admin already does: nobody types a 384-dimension embedding, the ingest pipeline writes it.

#### And a package.json that pointed at nothing

`@repo/shared` set `main` and `types` to `./index.ts`, which has never existed, while `exports` listed only subpaths. The fields are gone rather than the barrel written: this package is subpath-only on purpose, because `./types` carries no runtime dependency while `./schemas` pulls in zod and libphonenumber-js, and a root barrel would hand both to every consumer that wanted a type. The reason is in the file now, so the next reader does not add the barrel back.

Verified the way the reporter verified it: `pnpm build` on a generated `--triple --next --desktop` project with a resource carrying all six types plus a vector, which runs `vite build && tsc -b`.
