```ts
export const useProducts = products.useList;
export const useCreateProduct = products.useCreate;
```

Which buys the thing the issue asked for. The compiler now answers a question it could not before:

```bash
error TS2353: Object literal may only specify known properties, and
'title' does not exist in type '{ name: string; price?: number; active?: boolean }'
```

**The exported names are unchanged.** The issue sketches `useList` and `useCreate` destructured at the call site, and `useProducts` and `useCreateProduct` are what somebody's pages already import, so renaming them would be a breaking change in exchange for a tidier shape. They are three-line aliases over the generic.

The generic also fixes something the old copy got wrong every time: an update invalidated the list and not the row, so a detail page kept showing what was there before the edit it had just made. And a filter whose value is `undefined` is now "not filtering" rather than `?status=undefined`, which is what `String(value)` would have sent.

Not shared with the admin's, which the issue suggests and which I looked at. `apps/admin/hooks/use-resource.ts` is 429 lines and is wired to the admin's own api client, its resource registry, its optimistic-update conventions and its toast surface. Moving it to `packages/shared` would mean a package importing from both apps, or a third set of conventions neither uses. Two small generics that each know their own app is the cheaper truth.


## v3.472.0 - November 5, 2026

### A user's role had two stores, and the answer depended on who asked

grit#154. `users.role` is a string column; `user_roles` is the join table behind the grants. Grant resolution reads the join table and falls back to the column. A route guarded by a *role name* read the column outright. So where the two disagree, `RequireRole("ADMIN")` and `RequireRole("perm:users.delete")` answered from different data, and which you got depended on how the route happened to be written.

Fixed by resolution rather than by migration. `authz.RoleNamesFor` answers "which roles does this user hold" with exactly the precedence grant resolution uses, the middleware sets the role from it, and the column becomes an *input* to that answer instead of a second source of it. No data change, no upgrade decision about rows that disagree, and where the two agree nothing changes.

```go
// internal/authz/grants.go
names, err := authz.RoleNamesFor(db, user.ID)   // the join table, then the column
c.Set("user_role", names[0])
c.Set("user_roles", names)
```

`RequireRole` checks every role the caller holds rather than one, because the join table is many to many and matching only the first would refuse somebody whose ADMIN is their second assignment: a new way to be wrong in exchange for fixing an old one.

The writer had the matching trap. `UserService.Update` takes the column write in `updates` and the assignment in a separate `roleName`, so a caller could set `updates["role"] = "ADMIN"` with `roleName` empty and write a column saying ADMIN beside grants saying otherwise, silently. A role in `updates` now implies the assignment: one input, whichever way a caller reaches for it.

Three tests ship into the project, and the first was checked by putting the old behaviour back, where it reported `RoleNamesFor = [ADMIN], want [USER]`.

### On the default theme, a failed sign-in said nothing

grit#149 asked for one `AuthShell` instead of nine, on the grounds that the same markup is copied per theme. Half of that was already done and the other half was not the problem.

The eight shells are eight genuinely different layouts, keyed by `theme.authLayout`: centered, split-carousel, modal, boxed, banner, showcase, quote, split-static. Collapsing them is not a fix. And five of the eight were already built from one shared preamble plus a per-layout body, with a comment saying why: "Five copies of a token list is five chances for one theme to quietly stop publishing --auth-radius."

Three predated that and were never moved. Which would be housekeeping, except that the shared preamble's `ErrorBanner` carries `role="alert"` and the three inline copies did not. So on **Atlas, the default theme**, a failed sign-in was not announced to a screen reader. Precisely the failure the issue predicted: the one that gets missed is whichever theme nobody is looking at.

Atlas and Aurora are on the shared helper now. Pulse is not, and that is a decision with a test on it: it has its own cross-link copy ("New here?", "Create an account") and its own imports for the rotating hero, so moving it would either change its copy or complicate the helper for one caller. It gets `role="alert"` without the refactor.

A test now reads all eight and fails on any that renders its error without the role. The login page was looked at in a browser afterwards rather than only type-checked, because the change moved a visual component.

One thing found while measuring and not fixed here: the login form's email field has no `autoComplete`, while the password beside it says `current-password`, so a password manager cannot reliably save the pair. It is 29 sites, and which attribute each needs depends on the form, so it is grit#180 rather than a sweep. That count is also the measured version of grit#149's argument: a one-attribute fix to a sign-in form is a 29-file diff.


## v3.471.0 - November 5, 2026

### A freshly generated project had five critical advisories

grit#148 was filed as dependency hygiene: stale floors, two unused packages, a `components.json` pointing at a file that does not exist. Running `pnpm audit` on a new project to check the work found something else.

```bash
19 vulnerabilities found
Severity: 1 low | 10 moderate | 3 high | 5 critical

critical  vitest    patched >=3.2.6    arbitrary file read via the UI server
critical  tinypool  patched >=2.1.2    prototype pollution gadget to RCE
critical  next      patched >=16.4.1   unauthenticated remote code execution
high      zod       patched >=4.6.6    memory exhaustion on oversized input
```

**Next was pinned below its own security fix.** The pin exists for a good reason, written out at length in `next_version.go`: a project once installed a 16.4.0 published eighteen hours earlier whose layout-router threw on every page. Pinning made the version a decision. It also meant the decision had to be revisited, and two unauthenticated RCEs landed in 16.4.1 while the pin stayed at 16.3.8.

It is 16.4.3 now, not the newest. 16.4.4 and 16.4.5 were three and two days old, inside the release-age window that file already argues for; 16.4.3 is thirteen days old and carries the same fixes.

`vitest` was `^2.0.0`, resolving to 2.1.9, and the critical is fixed in 3.2.6. It is `^4.1.12`, which also takes `tinypool`, `vite` and `esbuild` past their advisories, since all three arrive through it. Nineteen down to one.

### The issue's own advice would have shipped two more

It said to move `xlsx` from a SheetJS CDN tarball to a registry version and unpin pnpm in the same change. The registry's newest `xlsx` is 0.18.5, which is where SheetJS stopped publishing to npm, and it carries two HIGH advisories: prototype pollution, fixed in 0.19.3, and a ReDoS, fixed in 0.20.2. Checked rather than assumed, with `npm audit` on a one-line package.json.

So the tarball stays, and the pnpm pin stays with it, which is the right way round: a pinned toolchain is a smaller cost than two known vulnerabilities. What was actually wrong is that the **single architecture was on the registry version** while every other shape used the patched tarball. That is fixed, and the reasoning is now a comment beside it so the next person does not fix it back.

### Floors, and what broke when they moved

`@hookform/resolvers` went from `^3.3.0` to `^5.9.0` and `zod` to `^3.25.0`, which is what resolvers 5 needs. That broke one page, and it is worth saying how:

```ts
// ProfessionalInfoSchema's fields are .optional().default(""), so its
// INPUT type is string | undefined and its OUTPUT type is string.
// Resolvers 5 distinguishes the two; useForm<ProfessionalInfoValues>
// asserts both are the output type and does not compile.
const professionalForm = useForm({            // inference gets both right
  resolver: zodResolver(ProfessionalInfoSchema),
  defaultValues: { job_title: "", bio: "" },
});
```

Two type errors, in one file, found by type-checking a real project rather than by reading. And the first fix went into the wrong file: there are two copies of that account page in the scaffold and only one of them is the one a project gets.

`@vitejs/plugin-react` is the other story. `^6.2.0` looked right, passed the Next admin's tests, and broke the single architecture's build outright: plugin-react 6 peers on `vite ^8` and imports `vite/internal`, which Vite 6 does not export. The Next admin never noticed because Next does not use the Vite plugin to build, only to test, and vitest 4 brings its own Vite. It is `^5.2.0`, which supports Vite 4 through 7. Vite 8 is a separate decision for a release that is not about security.

### Three smaller ones

`js-cookie` and `@types/js-cookie` are gone from the web app: they are left over from the OAuth flow that read tokens out of a callback URL, and that flow does not exist any more. `dompurify` goes with them from the Next web app, after checking that the TanStack one genuinely uses it and that the Next blog page does not need it, because the API sanitises rich text on write and on read.

`components.json` said `"config": "tailwind.config.ts"`, a file a generated project does not have under Tailwind v4, so `shadcn add` was pointed at nothing. It is empty now, which is the shadcn CLI's own convention for v4.

And the admin's public-IP hint is opt-in behind `NEXT_PUBLIC_IP_HINT=1`. It fetched `api.ipify.org` on page load in development, to put a nicer value in a log line nobody had asked about. Correctly guarded to development and still not something a generated app should do unasked. Adding that read also broke the single architecture, where Vite has no `process`, and the test for that caught it in the same minute.

The one left is `zod`: patched only in 4.6.6, and zod 4 is an API migration across every emitted schema rather than a floor. Filed as grit#175 rather than rushed into a release that is already this long.


## v3.470.0 - November 5, 2026

### The mobile app's Google button has never worked

grit#174. Every generated Expo app shipped a "Continue with Google" button on its login screen that could not work, in three ways that compounded.

It asked the API to send it back to `myapp://callback`, hard-coded. `app.json` registers the project name as the app's scheme, so the app was not listening on that URL at all. It then read `access_token` and `refresh_token` out of the query string, which is the thing nobody should build. And the API ignored `redirect_uri` entirely: the callback finished the handshake, set HttpOnly cookies and redirected to the web frontend, so the in-app browser landed on a web page, the app never got its tokens, and cookies are no use to a client that authenticates with a bearer token.

A native client now gets a **one-time code**:

```text
GET  /api/auth/oauth/google?redirect_uri=myapp://callback
          ... the provider handshake ...
302  myapp://callback?code=<single-use, 60 seconds>

POST /api/auth/oauth/exchange   { "code": "..." }
200  { "data": { "user": {...}, "tokens": { access_token, refresh_token } } }
```

Not the tokens in the redirect, which is the fix that suggests itself. A URL lands in browser history, in the `Referer` of the next request and in any proxy log on the way, and a refresh token in any of those is a standing key to the account. The code is single-use, lives for sixty seconds, is stored only as a SHA-256, and is spent by a conditional update so two exchanges arriving together cannot both succeed. The app retries on a lost response, so that race is ordinary rather than hostile, and it has to resolve to one session rather than two.

### redirect_uri is an allowlist, and it is checked first

`OAUTH_NATIVE_REDIRECTS` lists the deep links the callback may send a code to. Anything else is refused.

An allowlist rather than a pattern, because a callback that redirects wherever the query string says, carrying a sign-in code, is an account takeover: the attacker starts the flow with their own redirect, the victim signs in, and the code arrives at the attacker's app. Empty means no native sign-in, which is the right default for a project with no mobile app, and a generated project ships with its own Expo app's scheme in `.env.example` and nothing else.

Checked at the *start* of the flow, and there is a test that fails if that order is ever reversed. Refusing after `gothic.BeginAuthHandler` has already redirected to the provider is not refusing: the response is gone. The test compares the two positions in the emitted handler and was verified by swapping them.

The app builds its callback URL with `Linking.createURL("callback")` instead of a literal, so it cannot drift from the scheme `app.json` registers, and if the allowlist does not match the error names the URL it asked for rather than saying sign-in failed.

Four tests ship into the project and five guard the templates, including one that fails if an access or refresh token ever appears in a redirect URL again. A model added to the scaffold also has to be reserved against `grit generate resource`, and the test that enforces that caught me forgetting.

### A docs page describing behaviour that had been fixed

Found next door. The OAuth page said the frontend callback page "extracts `access_token` and `refresh_token` from the URL". It does not, and should not: the callback sets HttpOnly cookies on its own response and redirects with no query parameters, which is the right behaviour and has been for a while. A security page describing the insecure thing it replaced is the worst way for documentation to be out of date.


## v3.469.0 - November 5, 2026

### grit upgrade --to: one release at a time

grit#158. `grit upgrade` had one speed. It applied the CLI's own templates, so pinning a project's framework version meant pinning the binary on every machine and in CI, and moving forward one step at a time was not possible. With several releases a week and six hundred tags since v3.0.0, "latest" is a long way from wherever an older project is.

```bash
$ grit upgrade --to 3.465.0 --dry-run

  Upgrading project to Grit v3.465.0

  This CLI is v3.468.0. Fetching v3.465.0 to do the upgrade.
  The binary is verified against the release's signed checksums and
  cached in C:\Users\you\.grit\versions. It is not installed on your PATH.

Looking for v3.465.0...
Downloading:    grit-windows-amd64.zip (9.2 MiB)
Verifying signature...
Verified:       grit-windows-amd64.zip, signed by the release workflow
```

It runs that release's own binary rather than trying to apply its templates from this one, because the templates *are* the binary: there is no archive of past templates to read, and pretending otherwise would mean applying this version's files under another version's name. The download is checked against the release's signed checksums, reusing the verification `grit update` already does rather than a second copy of it, cached under `~/.grit/versions`, and never put on your PATH. Every other flag passes through, so `--to 3.455.0 --dry-run` is a dry run of that version.

That passthrough is the part with a test on it. A flag added to `grit upgrade` and forgotten in the passthrough is dropped in silence, and the failure mode is `--to 3.455.0 --dry-run` upgrading the project for real. So the test reads the command's own flag set rather than a list written beside it, and fails on a flag it has never heard of.

### A deprecation policy, so something can be retired

There was none, which meant nothing could be removed: v3.467.0 found a genuine duplicate command and the only options were leave it for ever, or break somebody's script with no notice. A stated window is what makes the third option exist.

A deprecated command or flag keeps working for at least **90 days and 30 releases**, whichever is longer, and in practice until the next major. Both numbers, because this project ships several releases a week: thirty of them can pass in under a month, which is not notice. It is on [the versioning page](https://gritframework.com/docs/versioning#deprecation) with the three things it deliberately does not cover, generated code among them.

### A breaking marker in the changelog

The versioning page is honest that these numbers are not SemVer. They still look like SemVer to everybody who has not read that page, and with 641 unmarked entries the only way to find out whether a release changes behaviour was to read all of them.

```tsx
{/* v3.470.0 breaking */}
```

One word in the comment that already carries the version, so writing an entry and marking it are the same edit. A marker nobody has to remember separately is a marker that gets used. The weekly rollup carries it through as a badge.

Nothing before this release is marked, and nothing will be marked retroactively. Guessing which of six hundred past releases were breaking would be inventing a record rather than reading one, so the rollup says that out loud instead.


## v3.468.0 - November 5, 2026

### Removing the Blog cost you framework fixes to four files

grit#173, and the last place where the framework asked you to choose between a clean project and a maintained one.

Four framework-owned files hard-coded the built-in Blog example: the web navbar, the seeder, the landing page, and a doc comment on the trash screen. Removing the resource meant editing them, and `grit upgrade` leaves an edited file alone, so the removal survived and those four files never received another framework fix. The alternative, recording the edits, was tried and reverted in v3.462.0: the upgrade then rewrote them from templates that still contained the Blog, so the navbar links came back as 404s and `seed.go` stopped compiling on `undefined: SeedBlogs`.

Both halves of that trade were wrong because the templates were wrong. They ask now:

```go
// internal/scaffold/web_files.go
filepath.Join(webRoot, "lib", "nav-menu.ts"): webNavMenuConfig(opts, !blogRemoved(root, opts)),
```

Through `blogRemoved`, which already existed for the Blog's own files and carries the gate that matters: on a new project the model has not been written when these maps are built, so asking the filesystem directly answers "the blog is gone" for every project Grit creates, and no project would ever get one. I had written exactly that bug before finding the function.

Then the file the removal leaves behind *is* the file the template produces, and the upgrade guard already adopts a file whose contents match what it would write. So the manifest becomes truthful again by itself, with no new repair step. What that turned on was a blank line: cutting a block with a blank line each side left two, the bytes differed from the template by that one line, and the file stayed held back. Cuts collapse the run now.

The trash screen needed no condition at all. Its Blog reference was `/** blog_posts -> Blog posts. */`, an illustration of what a helper does, and naming a removable resource in an example cost that file every later framework fix. The example is `order_items`.

One bug found while testing it, which the issue did not mention: `grit remove resource Blog` left five `/blog` links in the navbar. The nav menu belongs to the web app rather than to the resource, so the removal never knew about it, and only `grit setup --starter blank` cleaned up afterwards. A project where somebody ran the removal themselves kept four 404s in its navigation. The removal re-renders those files from the template now.

### The generator's tests read the Go it writes

grit#159. The templates are raw Go strings and the tests assert on them with around 1,600 `strings.Contains` calls. A `Contains` that passes says the substring is there. It says nothing about whether the file is valid Go, so a template emitting a syntax error passed every test and was found by CI compiling a scaffolded project, ten minutes later, with a failure pointing at a generated project rather than at the template.

Two sweeps now parse what gets written: 30 files from the generator, and 231 from the scaffold across four architectures. Both print the offending line, numbered, rather than a column number.

**Two resources, not one**, in the generator sweep, and that is the point of the second. Every test in that package generated a single resource, so a template declaring a package-level function without the resource name in it looked fine: the redeclaration only appears on the second resource. That shipped in v3.451.0 and nothing could see it.

`codefmt.Go` made it quieter than it needed to be. It parses the source, so on a syntax error it already knows, and it returned the text unformatted and said nothing. That is right for a write, because a file on disk somebody can read beats a scaffolding failure with nothing written, and it is wrong for a test. There is a `GoChecked` that returns the error, and `Go` is now one line over it.

Both sweeps were verified by breaking a template on purpose, because a sweep that finds nothing is indistinguishable from one that ran over nothing, and this project has shipped the second kind. They also fail if they read fewer files than expected, for the same reason.


## v3.467.0 - November 5, 2026

### grit own: whose file is this

grit#161. Ownership is the idea the whole framework rests on and the thing people get wrong first, and the answer was already exact: the manifest records what Grit wrote, and `grit upgrade` reads it. There was no way to ask. You read the manifest by hand, ran an upgrade with `--dry-run`, or guessed from the directory, and guessing from the directory is how it goes wrong.

```bash
$ grit own apps/admin/components/tables/data-table.tsx

  apps/admin/components/tables/data-table.tsx
  framework-owned, and unchanged since Grit wrote it
    grit upgrade will replace it. Keep your changes somewhere it will not:
    a *.custom overlay where one exists, or a file of your own that imports this one.
```

Four answers: framework-owned and unchanged, framework-owned and edited, yours, and deleted. The last one reads the directory, as the upgrade does: a file gone from a directory that is still there was deleted and comes back, while a directory gone with it is a feature the project does not have. A project with no manifest, which is anything from before v3.147.0, is told so rather than guessed at. `grit own --all` groups every file Grit has written by what an upgrade will do to it.

The part that needed care is that this has to predict what the upgrade actually does, and the decision lives in the upgrade guard. Mirrored rather than shared, because the guard counts and records as it decides while this answers a question, and then one test drives both over the same five files and fails if they disagree. A test per side would pass while the pair was broken, which is the shape of bug this project keeps finding. Checked by breaking the mirror: it reported the disagreement by name.

### The changelog is greppable from a checkout

grit#167. The canonical changelog is a 37,000-line TSX page and `CHANGELOG.md` was a pointer to the website, so the history of this project could not be grepped from a checkout, diffed between two tags, or read offline. `CHANGELOG.md` is now 639 releases of prose, generated from the page.

Generated, never maintained beside it. A hand-written mirror is two changelogs within a week and the second one is always the stale one, so the release regenerates it and CI fails if it is behind, naming the versions that differ.

Two faults in the first version of the generator, both of them the quiet kind. Its regex for a code block stopped at the first escaped backtick, so a TSX snippet containing `{`Remove ${file.name}`}` was truncated mid-line. And one block on the page is written with a single-quoted `code=` rather than a template literal, so it was dropped entirely, and the only reason anybody noticed was counting the fences afterwards. The generator now counts every `CodeBlock` on the page against the number it understood, and fails on a form it does not recognise rather than letting the block vanish.

### Two CLI tidies

grit#157. `grit new-desktop` and `grit new --desktop` produce the same project, which is the only genuine double the CLI review found: `update` and `upgrade` replace different things, `version` and `versions` answer different questions. Deprecated rather than deleted, because somebody has it in a README: it is out of `--help`, still works, and says what to use instead.

grit#160. `grit skills install` was hidden, and it installs an agent skill from a private repository into your agent's own configuration. The reasoning for hiding it was sound as far as it went, since a command most people cannot run is noise in the help output, and what it produced was worse: a command that writes to your agent config, from a source you cannot read, that you cannot find. It is visible now, its help says which of the three things called a Grit skill it installs, and it checks access to the pack before npx does, so the failure is a sentence naming the repository rather than an npm 404.


## v3.466.0 - November 5, 2026

### The matrix and the stability page disagreed about the same features

grit#166. Two-factor, passkeys and RBAC are `beta` on [the stability page](https://gritframework.com/docs/stability), and counted towards "ready on first run" in the capability matrix with nothing said about it. Both are this project's own claims, in two files, and which one a reader believed depended on which page they found.

The statuses now live in one config that both read. A capability row points at a stability area by id, the matrix shows that area's badge beside the label, and a row cannot be settled in one place and young in the other because there is only one place.

```ts
// docs/config/capabilities.ts
{
  id: 'twofa',
  stability: 'twofa',   // -> the area on /docs/stability, whose badge renders here
  label: 'Two-factor with backup codes',
}
```

Eleven of the thirty-three rows point at an area. The other twenty-two do not, because no stability area covers them, and inventing a pointer would put a badge on a claim nothing backs. A pointer that resolves to nothing renders no badge and says nothing, which is the original bug returning by a rename, so CI now reads both files and fails on a pointer with no area.

The matrix also says how it was scored, which a self-scored table should: the rows are Grit's own list, some of them exist because Grit has them, the count includes beta and new features, and the file is linked with an invitation to send a pull request against a single cell. A comparison that invites corrections is more persuasive than one that does not.

### No third-party security audit has been performed

grit#165. Nothing said so, and for a project that ships a security dashboard, an audit log with a written threat model and an OWASP page, silence on that point reads as the other answer. It is now stated in `SECURITY.md` and on the security page, along with which subsystems have a written threat model and which do not.

"WAF" is the other word. Sentinel blocks known probe patterns and rate-limits by IP and route, with account-level lockout. That is useful and it is not ModSecurity with the OWASP Core Rule Set, so somebody reading "WAF" and expecting the second one was being surprised in the wrong direction. The README and the batteries diagram now say request filtering, and the security page qualifies the word where it still appears.

Also softened: "defends every category of the OWASP Top 10:2025 by default" is now "every category has a named defence in the scaffold", which is what the page actually demonstrates, file path by file path. And "GDPR tools" is GDPR tooling, with a line saying it is a mechanism rather than a compliance programme.

### "No down-migrations" reads as "you cannot roll back"

Three places on the coming-from page said it. What is true is that there are no hand-written up and down files, because AutoMigrate works the change out from the models. Rolling back exists: `grit migrate down` reverses a run from the record of what that run actually changed, and CI exercises it. Telling somebody arriving from Laravel that a migration cannot be undone is the most alarming thing you can say about a migration system, and it was not the case.

### The policies feature had no documentation page

grit#169. `internal/policies` is generated into every project, `grit generate resource` writes the file and registers it, and nothing under `/docs` mentioned it. There is a page now, beside authorization: where a rule goes, what it receives, which paths consult it, what a refusal looks like over HTTP, and a worked example that is not a stub.

Writing it caught two things. `authz.Actor` holds `UserID` and `Admin` and nothing else, so the first draft's example read `actor.OrganizationID` and would not have compiled, in a code block on a page whose whole purpose is that nobody could find out how this works. And `authz.Abilities()` carries a comment saying it is for `grit doctor`, which does not call it: the only caller is the gate's own test.

### The benchmark nobody else could rebuild

grit#164. Every side of the benchmark is in the repository except the Grit one. `grit-bench/` is gitignored, which was the right call, since committing scaffold output lets it drift from what the CLI emits today, and the wrong one at the same time: the single side whose numbers the page makes a claim about was the side nobody could reproduce.

`benchmarks/grit-bench.sh` builds it from a pinned CLI version. The app is still not committed and anybody can produce it, which also demonstrates the claim the benchmark rests on: there is nothing bespoke in it, no tuned handler and no benchmark-only shortcut. The README's reference to a `run.sh` that does not exist is now `pair.sh`, which does.

Two things about the numbers. The tabs opened on `show`, where the ratio is 26x, and `show` is one indexed read: the request an API serves least often. `mixed` is 5.6x against the same Laravel and is 85% list, 10% read, 5% write. Leading with 26x invited exactly the reading the methodology section asks against, three paragraphs after asking, so `mixed` leads now.

And **Grit never saturated its own container in any pair, in any scenario**, sitting at 287 to 310% of its 400% allowance even on `show`. The page said that about the read-heavy rows and not about `show`, so the cleanest row read as a ceiling when it is a floor too. That is a favourable fact being left out, which is the worst kind to leave out. The host hardware was never recorded with the runs, so `pair.sh` now writes a `host.txt` beside every result set, and the page says the existing figures predate that.


## v3.465.0 - November 5, 2026

### The upload control said "button", five times

grit#151. The review said `dropzone.tsx` has no keyboard handling of its own. Half of that was wrong, and the half that was right is worse than it sounds.

It is operable. react-dropzone's `getRootProps` gives the drop zone its tabIndex and its Enter and Space, and every control is a real `<button>`, so Tab reaches it and Enter fires it. What it was not is legible: every one of those buttons is an icon and nothing else, so a screen reader announced "button", once per file, with no way to tell which file each one removed.

That is the same fault as the thirteen form fields this project shipped with a label attached to nothing. Fine with a mouse, unusable otherwise, and invisible in a demo because the person demonstrating it can see.

```tsx
aria-label={`Remove ${file.name}`}
aria-label={`Move ${fileLabel} up, position ${index + 1} of ${total}`}
```

Six controls, each naming its file, and the reorder buttons also saying where in the list they are, which is the other thing somebody who cannot see the list has no way to know. The move buttons had a `title`, which is a tooltip: announced inconsistently and not at all on a touch device.

Two tests ship with it. One reads every `<button>` in the component and fails on any without an accessible name; the other checks the names say which file. The first version of that test reported six labelled buttons as unnamed, because it matched the tag with a regex ending at the first `>` and these buttons carry `onClick={(e) => ...}`, so it stopped reading three lines before the label. It steps over braces now.

### A Google button that cannot work

Found while closing grit#156, which claimed the OAuth and SSO callbacks put the refresh token in the redirect URL. They do not: both set HttpOnly cookies and redirect with no query parameters. That issue was filed from a stale note and is closed as wrong.

What is real is next door. Every generated Expo app has a "Continue with Google" button that asks the API to send it back to `myapp://callback`, and the API ignores `redirect_uri` entirely. The in-app browser lands on a web page, the app never gets its tokens, and cookies are no use to a bearer client. It has never worked.

Filed as grit#174 with the one-time code design written out, rather than fixed in a hurry, because the obvious fix is to put the tokens in the redirect and that is how a refresh token ends up in browser history. It also needs `redirect_uri` validated against an allowlist, since a callback that redirects to whatever the query string says is worse than the dead button it replaces.


## v3.464.0 - November 5, 2026

### Two tabs signed you out of every device

grit#153. Refresh tokens rotate, and a second presentation of a rotated token is read as a captured token being replayed, so the session is killed. That is right for a thief. It is also what happens when two tabs' access tokens expire in the same second, or a phone retries a request whose response never arrived: both present the token they hold, which by then is the previous one.

There is a ten second grace now. Inside it, presenting the previous token rotates normally instead of revoking:

```go
// Inside the grace window: two refreshes raced, which is ordinary.
// Rotate as though the current token had been presented, and leave
// prev_token_hash and rotated_at where they are, so the window stays
// anchored to the first rotation and presenting the same old token
// repeatedly cannot keep it alive.
if replayed.RotatedAt != nil &&
    now.Sub(*replayed.RotatedAt) <= SessionRotationGrace &&
    replayed.Active(now, SessionIdleTimeout) {
```

Ten seconds because the real window is one request in flight: the refresh token is a cookie every tab shares, so the second tab holds the old one only until the first response lands. A thief who waits is still caught. A thief already racing the victim gets one refresh, which rotation alone never prevented either.

What it does not do, since the issue asked for more: the two callers get different new tokens and the client keeps whichever it stores last. A browser resolves that by itself, sharing one cookie. A native client that processes both responses orphans one token, and the orphan's next refresh is refused rather than fatal: the session survives and the other devices keep working. Handing both callers the same pair would mean keeping the issued token retrievable for the window, which is a new secret at rest.

Two of the existing tests asserted the old behaviour and now age the rotation past the window before asserting it, which is the case the protection is actually for. Three new tests cover the race, and one covers the window not sliding: presenting the old token repeatedly must not keep pushing its deadline out.

### A refresh storm instead of one sign-out

grit#147. The admin's 401 interceptor has two paths that replay a request and marked only one of them. A request that queued behind an in-flight refresh was replayed without `_retry`, so a second 401 on that replay read as a first attempt and started the refresh again.

The desktop client already had it right, setting the flag before the branch, so the fix is the two agreeing rather than a rule invented for the occasion. There is now a test that reads both clients and fails if either marks after it branches.

### Stored XSS in the commerce example

grit#150. The product page wrote JSON-LD into a `<script>` element with `JSON.stringify`, which escapes what JSON needs and nothing HTML needs. A product titled `</script><img onerror=...>` closed the element and the rest was parsed as markup. The title comes from the database, so that is whoever can edit a product.

```ts
function jsonLd(data: unknown): string {
  return JSON.stringify(data).replace(/</g, "\u003c");
}
```

Escaping `<` rather than the literal `</script>` is deliberate: the variants are many and the escape is one. `\\u003c` is a valid JSON string escape, so every consumer reads it back as `<` and the structured data is unchanged. Verified against the payload, not by reading it.


## v3.463.0 - November 5, 2026

### go test did not compile in a new project

`grit new`, then `go test ./...`, and the services package did not build:

```text
internal/services/webhook_event_test.go:143:51:
  not enough arguments in call to events.ByExternalID
    have (context.Context, string, string)
    want (context.Context, string, string, string)
```

`ByExternalID` gained a tenant parameter in the fix for grit#138, and it gained it for a good reason: without the tenant, a redelivery lookup can return another organization's row, and the caller then claims and re-runs somebody else's delivery. The handler was updated. The test that calls it was not.

So every project scaffolded between that release and this one ships a services package whose tests do not build. The fix is one argument. What it cost to find is the interesting part.

### Why nothing caught it

Three checks had the chance and each missed it for a different reason:

- ** `go build ./...` does not compile test files. ** That is the check this project runs on a generated app before calling a release verified, and it is blind to anything that is wrong only in a `_test.go`.
- **The checked-in examples are committed output.** `examples/library` and `examples/saas` are vetted and tested on every push, and they carry the templates as they were when somebody generated them. Their service and their test agree with each other, at the old signature, so they pass.
- **The nightly canary did catch it.** It scaffolds fresh and runs the tests, and it had been red for five nights saying exactly this. Nobody read it.

CI now scaffolds a project on every push and runs `go vet` over it, which compiles the test files and takes seconds. The canary keeps running the full suite overnight. A template change that breaks only the generated tests now fails the push that makes it.

### And the assertion the fix deserved

Nothing tested that `ByExternalID` scopes by tenant, which is the whole point of grit#138. The dedup tests prove two organizations may store the same reference, which is the database constraint rather than the lookup. Generated projects now carry `TestByExternalIDIsScopedToItsTenant`: two tenants, one provider, one external id, and each lookup has to return its own row.


## v3.462.0 - November 1, 2026

### grit setup, the guided installer

Contributed by [daljo25](https://github.com/daljo25) in [#170](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/pull/170) , the second contribution from the same person this week.

```text
$ grit setup myapp

  the architecture, the frontend, a starter, a database,
  Redis, storage, mail, the plugins that fit the shape

  then: dependencies, local services, migrate, seed,
  the first commit, and grit start if you want it
```

It is a separate command from `grit new` on purpose, and the reasoning in the PR is the part worth repeating: `grit new` is the fast, scriptable scaffold and its behaviour is frozen, so a build script that runs it keeps working. A wizard that could change that command's output would be a liability. Setup is the guided path, and it only creates new projects.

A starter is the example content a project begins with, and there is no separate template repository: `blank` is the same scaffold with the built-in Blog removed, `blog` keeps it as `grit new` writes it. The hard part of that is the leftovers, and the PR found four kinds nobody had looked for: public TanStack routes importing a deleted hook, admin routes importing deleted pages, Expo Blog screens with their discover entries, and a desktop quick-access card pointing at a removed screen. All four have tests.

Documented at [/docs/getting-started/setup](https://gritframework.com/docs/getting-started/setup) . The `--yes` form takes every answer as a flag, for CI.

### A review note I had to take back

Reviewing that PR, I asked for the starter's cleanup to record its edits in the manifest. The cleanup edits files the scaffold owns, so without that the first `grit upgrade` read four of them as hand-edited and stopped maintaining them, the nav menu among them. That much was measured and true.

The fix was wrong, and so was the same fix I wrote for `grit remove resource` alongside it. Refreshing an edited file's hash hands the file back to the template, and the template still contains the Blog:

```text
$ grit setup blankapp --starter blank    # no Blog anywhere
$ grit upgrade
$ grep blog apps/web/lib/nav-menu.ts
            title: "Blog",
            href: "/blog",                   # a 404

# and on the remover, worse:
$ grit remove resource Blog --force
$ grit upgrade && go build ./...
internal/database/seed.go:21:12: undefined: SeedBlogs
```

The stale hash was not a bug. It is the only thing preserving a removal against a template that still knows about the resource. The same goes for the fourteen recorded-but-absent manifest entries I filed as [#171](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/171) : a recorded file that is absent is how the upgrade guard knows the project removed a feature. Dropping those entries made the Blog's public pages come back.

Both halves are reverted, and both now carry a test that fails if somebody re-applies the idea, because it is an attractive one: refreshing looks obviously right until you run the upgrade. The real fix is for the templates that mention a demo resource to ask whether the project still has it, which is [#173](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/173) . Until then a blank project has a handful of files that stop receiving framework fixes, and the setup page says so.

### An upgrade put back a resource you had removed

[#172](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/172) , and mine from yesterday. v3.460.0 moved `blog` and `upload` onto the list of shared types a new project ships, so the comparator test would cover them. That list is also what the upgrade's repair walks, and the repair creates every entry that is missing. So a `blog.ts` absent because somebody removed the resource looked exactly like one absent because the project predates the list.

The model is what tells those apart: if `internal/models/blog.go` is not there, `grit sync` would not write the type either. The repair asks now, and a tree with no models directory at all is read as a question that cannot be answered rather than as a removal, so a frontend-only checkout still gets its types.


## v3.461.0 - October 31, 2026

### grit plugin new

[Issue #143](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/143) , from `daljo25`. Writing a community plugin meant starting from an empty directory. The authoring page described the manifest and then pointed at `internal/plugin/multitenant.go`, which is inside the CLI and written in Go, so a reader who followed the page had the shape described to them and nothing to copy.

```text
$ grit plugin new audit-trail

  ✓ audit-trail/plugin.json
  ✓ audit-trail/files/api/audittrail.go
  ✓ audit-trail/files/api/audittrail_test.go
  ✓ audit-trail/files/admin/audit-trail-card.tsx
  ✓ audit-trail/README.md
  ✓ audit-trail/.github/workflows/plugin.yml
```

It installs as it stands, which is the point: get the loop working before the plugin does anything interesting. It exercises the list the issue asked for, one file written always, one behind a `when` clause, a Go test that runs in the installing project, and two injections, because a route needs its import and neither compiles alone.

### Generated, not a template repository

The issue offered either and made the case for the command: "so the skeleton cannot drift from the manifest schema". That is right, and it is the same problem the two releases before this one were about. A repository falls behind the first time the schema gains a field. A skeleton generated from templates inside the CLI can be held to it by the CLI's own tests:

- the skeleton is written to a temporary directory and loaded with `LoadDir`, the same function `grit plugin add ./dir` calls, so a schema change it does not follow fails a build here rather than in somebody's terminal
- the markers it injects at are compared against the `routes.go` the scaffold actually writes. This is the one mistake in a manifest with no error message: an injection at a marker that is not in the file is not refused, it simply does not happen, and the first sign is a route answering 404
- every marker the README names is checked the same way, since a list of markers in prose is a list that goes stale

The README is most of the value. It covers the placeholders, `when`, the markers, `codeFrom`, dependencies, and a "what not to do" section. And it leads with the loop, because the loop is the part that cannot be inferred from the manifest:

```bash
grit new testbed --triple
cd testbed
grit plugin add ../audit-trail

cd apps/api && go build ./... && go test ./...
cd ../.. && pnpm install && cd apps/admin && npx tsc --noEmit

cd ../.. && grit plugin remove audit-trail --force
cd apps/api && go build ./...
```

That last build is the one worth running and the one people skip. Removal replays the lockfile backwards, so it cannot take back an edit the lockfile has no record of: a plugin that changed a file outside an injection installs cleanly and leaves the project broken on the way out. The generated CI workflow runs the whole thing on every push, for `--triple` and for `--api`, which is where a missing `when` clause shows up.

Measured by running it: installed into a fresh triple, the Go side builds and its test passes, the admin type-checks, and after `grit plugin remove` the project builds again with nothing left behind. On an `--api` project the admin component is correctly not written at all.


## v3.460.0 - October 31, 2026

### grit sync undid what grit generate had just written

Review 2.14. Two writers produced `packages/shared/types/<model>.ts`, and the second one to run won. `grit generate resource` prints "run grit sync" as a next step, so the second one was usually sync.

What each got wrong was the opposite of the other, which is why neither looked broken on its own:

```diff
  // generate wrote this        sync rewrote it as this
- price: Money;                 + price: unknown;
- cover: FileRef | null;        + cover: unknown | null;
- status: "draft" | "live";     + status: string;
- author?: Author;              + author: unknown | null;

  // and sync knew six columns generate had never heard of
+ version: number;              // the admin sends it on every update
+ archived_at?: string | null;  // bulk archive reads it
+ path, depth, position,
+ children                      // on every --tree resource
```

The generator built the interface from the definition, which is the list of fields somebody asked for. The model is the list the API serialises, and those are not the same list: a request returned six fields the TypeScript said did not exist. Sync read the model, so it had all six, and mapped their Go types with a function that knows the builtins and nothing else.

Neither is fixed by a second set of rules. There is one writer now. The generator reads the model it has just written and calls the same emitter sync calls, which reconstructs the field each column was generated from and asks it for its own type. That mechanism already existed: it is what fixed the Zod schemas in v3.421.0, and the TypeScript was left out of it.

```text
$ grit generate resource Article title:string author_id:belongs_to:Author ...
$ grit sync
$ git diff --stat packages/shared
(nothing)
```

### A resource with two relationships to one model would not compile

Found by generating one, which no fixture had. A `belongs_to` and a `many_to_many` naming the same model each emitted the import, and two imports of one name is TS2300, which fails the type-check of the whole workspace rather than one file:

```text
$ grit generate resource Article author_id:belongs_to:Author tags:many_to_many:Author
$ npx tsc --noEmit
packages/shared/types/article.ts(1,15): error TS2300: Duplicate identifier 'Author'.
packages/shared/types/article.ts(2,15): error TS2300: Duplicate identifier 'Author'.
```

### A tree's create form asked for a materialised path

`path`, `depth` and `position` are the tree service's to write, and sync put all three in `CreateNodeSchema`: a form built from it wanted a path before the row had an id. They carry `server:"true"` now, the tag a slug and an owner column already use, so the schema that describes what you may send leaves them out and the one that describes what comes back keeps them.

### And one latent rule, now written down

Adding two models to the list the scaffold ships shared types from broke a test three files away, with a diff of a whole index file and no hint of the cause. The template writes those export lines in list order; the repair that adds a missing one writes it in sorted order; the two produce the same file only while the list is alphabetical. It had been alphabetical by accident, every entry appended in a release whose model name happened to come next. There is a test for it now, and another that compares what the template writes against what the repair would write.


## v3.459.0 - October 31, 2026

### The admin panel loaded for people who were not signed in

Review 2.15. Type `/system/api-keys` into a browser that had never signed in and the whole page arrived: the JavaScript, the sidebar, the route names. React then mounted, asked the API who you were, got a 401 and replaced the route with the login. Nothing leaked, because the API refuses every request behind that panel and that is the check that decides anything. But the panel was sent to a stranger, its shape was readable in the response, and the first thing they saw was a dashboard they could not use.

The panel inside a web app has had a gate since v3.391.0, because the app it lives in has a file to put one in. `apps/admin` had no such file at all. It does now.

```text
$ curl -i localhost:3001/system/api-keys
HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect
location: /login

$ curl -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" localhost:3001/grit_logo.png
200
```

The gate denies by default. Its matcher is every path except Next's own output and anything that looks like a file, so a page added later, by `grit generate` or by a plugin, is protected the day it lands rather than the day somebody remembers a list. The pages that let you sign in are let through from one short list inside the file, and the framework's own test suite derives that list from the panel's file map: a missing auth page would be a page nobody can open, and that is the one mistake this file can make which does not correct itself.

The second line of that output matters as much as the first. The logo on the login page is served out of `public/`, so a gate that covered it would send a stranger to a login page with a hole where the logo goes.

### What opens the gate

A cookie with no secret in it, written on the admin's own origin whenever the API hands back a session. It is forgeable from the console, and that is fine: forging it buys you the HTML of a panel whose every request is refused. It is not the session. The session is still the HttpOnly pair the API sets, which JavaScript cannot read.

It is written in one place, the admin's API client, from a list of the endpoints that answer with a session. The alternative was a call in each of the four auth mutations plus the OAuth callback page plus the magic-link page, and the next sign-in route added would have been the one that forgot. A 200 carrying `totp_required` does not count: that is a challenge, not a session, and stamping it would open the panel to a browser that stopped at the second factor.

The cookie's name is declared once and imported by both files. Two copies of a cookie name is this project's recurring bug: the gate reads one spelling, the thing that opens it writes another, and each file is correct when you read it on its own.

### middleware.ts is now proxy.ts

Found while measuring the above, which is the argument for measuring: Next 16 renamed this file convention, and a project with a `middleware.ts` prints a deprecation notice on every dev server start. Rather than ship the new gate under the deprecated name, both files moved.

```text
before   ⚠ The "middleware" file convention is deprecated.
                   Please use "proxy" instead.

after    GET /dashboard 200 in 14.0s (proxy.ts: 36ms)
```

It is the same file: same request object, same matcher, and the function it exports is called `proxy`. `grit upgrade` moves an existing one, keeping its contents exactly, so any protected paths you added to it move with it. A file whose export is not the one Grit wrote is left alone with the one line it takes to do by hand, because renaming that one would give Next a file to read and no function behind it.

```markdown
# My project

Never touch the billing module without asking Sarah.

...Grit's rules, replaced on every refresh...
```

Text on either side survives a refresh, a file with no marked section yet gets the block appended below what is already there, and running it twice changes nothing. None of those loses anything, so the merge needs no flag and `grit init` is now safe to re-run. `--force` still replaces the whole file, which is what a destructive flag should mean and is now the only thing it means.

Review 2.20. There was a note about this, in yellow, at the very bottom of the migrations page, after the section on rolling back. It undersold the limit as being about "development and simple schemas", when additive migration is a perfectly good production strategy, and it left out the one that actually bites.

It is a section of its own now, near the top, and it names all five things that do not happen: renames, type changes, drops, data moves, and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`. That last one is the one worth reading twice: an index is added with a plain `CREATE INDEX`, which takes a lock, so adding one to a large busy table is an outage rather than a migration.
