## v3.456.0 - October 30, 2026

### The audit chain protected against nobody

Review 2.7. Every row of the activity log is hashed over the row before it, so changing one row breaks every hash after it. The hash was `SHA-256(prev_hash || row)` with no key, over values anybody can read off the source. So the attack is: edit a row, recompute the rest, and verification passes.

The package comment said it defended against "a DBA covering tracks". That is precisely the one person it did not defend against. The docs were honest about the missing external anchoring and overstated everything else.

```text
hash = SHA-256( prev_hash || canonical(row) )          before
hash = HMAC-SHA256( key, prev_hash || canonical(row) )  now
```

The key is `AUDIT_CHAIN_KEY`, and it derives from `JWT_SECRET` through SHA-256 when unset, so no project has to set a second secret to get a keyed chain and the two are never the same bytes. Set it explicitly when the chain should outlive a `JWT_SECRET` rotation, or when the two should be held by different people. Keep it somewhere your database administrator is not, because that separation is the entire mechanism.

#### The chain has to verify across the day it was keyed

Every row records which algorithm hashed it. A project that upgrades has unkeyed rows before the key and keyed rows after it, and a chain that reported every historical row as tampered would be a chain nobody looks at again. So verification honours each row's own algorithm, with one rule that is the whole point: once a keyed row has been seen, an unkeyed row after it fails. A chain does not go back to being unkeyed, so that is tampering whatever its hash says, and it closes the obvious way around the key.

What this proves and what it does not is now written down rather than implied. It stops someone with database access. It does not stop someone who also holds the key, there is still no external anchoring, and rows written before the key prove only that nothing has changed them *since*.

Three tests ship with every project and one of them is the attack: edit a row, re-link every row after it, and verify. Run against an unkeyed chain that test passes the forgery, which is what makes it worth having. Measured on a generated project, with and without the key:

```text
a row edited and the chain re-linked after it

unkeyed    the whole chain verifies          the attack works
keyed      refused at the first edited row   the attack fails
```

### The admin runtime stays copied into your project

Review 2.13, considered and declined. The admin is 36-38k lines generated into your repository rather than imported from a package, and the review is right that editing one of those files stops framework fixes reaching it.

What was missing is anybody saying so. The admin overview now says what the trade costs, points at `grit upgrade --dry-run` and `--diff` for seeing what is being held back, and says where to put changes so they survive: a resource's definition and its `*.custom.tsx` overlay, which are never overwritten.

A versioned `@gritframework/admin` package would cut the surface you carry and would also take these files out of your hands. The data table and the form builder are the two things people most often need to change, and a dependency you cannot edit is worse than a file that stops updating.


## v3.455.0 - October 30, 2026

### Searching for "50%" returned every row

Review 2.19. A search term went into a `LIKE` pattern exactly as typed, so the wildcards in it were the pattern's wildcards:

```text
search      matched

50%         every row, because % is the wildcard
a_b         "axb", because _ is any character
%%%%        every row, after a full scan
```

The term is a bound parameter, so this was never injection. It was a wrong answer, and on a large table a pattern of nothing but wildcards is work the database does for no result.

Terms are escaped now, and the clause declares the escape character it uses, because SQLite has no default one. `!` rather than a backslash: in Postgres with `standard_conforming_strings` on, `ESCAPE '\'` is a single backslash, and in MySQL the same literal escapes the closing quote and the statement does not parse.

### And the export searched differently from the screen

The same finding's other half, and the reason the first one could not be fixed in one place. The clause builder was unexported, so the generated `Export` carried its own copy of it. Two copies of a query builder drift, and this pair had already drifted into the same bug twice over: fixing one would have left an export of a search for "50%" returning every row while the list screen beside it showed the right ones.

`Export` now calls `paginate.BuildSearchClause`, the same function `List` uses. `grit upgrade` replaces the copy in every service that has one, and a test holds the repaired service to byte equality with a freshly generated one so the two cannot drift again.

### Repairs in the generator package wrote behind the manifest too

v3.454.0 fixed eleven of these in `internal/scaffold` and added a test to keep them fixed. The test looked in one package; `internal/generate` holds repairs as well, and the money repair had the same three raw writes. It now scans both, and fails if it finds no repair files in either, so a renamed directory cannot make it pass by checking nothing.


## v3.454.0 - October 30, 2026

### An injection could launder your edit into Grit's

Review 2.6. The manifest exists so `grit upgrade` can overwrite the files nobody has touched and leave the rest alone. `manifest.Refresh` re-hashes a file after Grit injects into it, which is right: adding a route to `routes.go` is an edit Grit made, and without it every injected file would read as hand-edited from then on.

It was wrong when the file had **already** been edited. Change `routes.go`, run `grit generate resource`, and the injection recorded your work as Grit's; the next upgrade saw an untouched file and overwrote it without a word. The one thing the manifest is for.

Fixed inside `Refresh` rather than at its thirty-seven call sites, because the answer it needs is the status before the write and that is gone by the time it runs. A session now records which tracked files were already edited when the command started, and `Refresh` declines to re-hash those. One pass over the project's own source at startup, 829 files and 4.9 MB in a real project, against a command that writes thirty files and runs gofmt.

### grit upgrade is now run twice in CI, and diffed

Review 2.5. "A repair is idempotent or it is a bug" is rule 8 in the scaffold's own AGENTS.md, and across ninety-six repair passes it was enforced by convention alone. A repair that appends on every run, or rewrites a line it rewrote last time, is invisible to every other test: the project still builds, the tests still pass, and a file quietly grows a duplicate block per upgrade.

CI now upgrades the checked-in `examples/library` once, upgrades a second copy twice, and diffs them. It found two real bugs on its first run, and neither was cosmetic.

#### Upgrading removed optimistic locking from the browser

The repair that adds `If-Match` to the CORS allow list and exposes `ETag` ran 350 lines before the repair that turns the old string literal into that list. So on a project from before the list shape it found nothing to insert into and did nothing, the list was then built without `If-Match`, and the upgrade reported success.

A browser on another origin then could not use optimistic locking at all: the preflight stripped the header it needed to send, and `ETag` was invisible to `fetch()` so it had no version to send anyway. That is grit#124, reintroduced by the upgrade meant to carry its fix. Running `grit upgrade` a second time fixed it, which is exactly why nobody had noticed.

#### The access table was six routes short

`internal/access/registry.go` is read out of the route files, and it was written at the end of the upgrade. Three steps that add routes run after that: the money repair, which adds the grid's bulk-create and bulk-edit routes, the write-checks repair, and the plugin update, which rewrites `routes.go` outright.

So an upgraded project recorded 219 routes where it has 225. That table is what the admin's routes screen reads and what `grit add scout` hands the scanner, so six routes were invisible to both. It is now written after the last thing that writes code, in the same place and for the same reason as the build check.

### Eleven repairs wrote behind the manifest

The other half of 2.5. Most repairs go through one helper that checks the manifest before writing and refreshes it after. Eleven used `os.WriteFile` and told the manifest nothing, which cost in both directions: the file read as hand-edited afterwards, so every later framework fix to it was skipped, and nothing consulted the upgrade guard. A repair poisoned the file it fixed.

There are now two helpers, one for editing a file that exists and one for a whole framework-owned file arriving, and a test that scans all ninety-six repair files and names any that write around them. A convention with a hundred call sites is enforced by a test or it is not enforced.

### A regenerate says which columns it stops reading

Review 2.23. A model somebody has edited is refused rather than overwritten, which is the good half. The unedited case is the likelier one: you generate `Contact` with name, email and company, and a week later run the same command from your shell history with name alone, because that is the line you still have. The model was rewritten with one field and nothing said so, because the output of the second run looks exactly like the output of the first.

```text
$ grit generate resource Widget --fields "name:string"

  ! This regenerate stops reading 2 columns: Price, Qty
    They are still in the database with their data, because migrations
    are additive. Nothing in the API, the admin or the types will read
    them after this. If that is not what you meant, the previous model
    is in git, and the field list to pass is the one in it.
```

Not a refusal: regenerating with fewer fields is a legitimate thing to do and the files are in git. The framework's own columns are never named, because no definition mentions them and a warning that fires on every run is a warning nobody reads.


## v3.453.0 - October 30, 2026

### A provider sign-in trusted an address the provider never verified

Review 2.9. goth puts the provider's userinfo response in `RawData`, `email_verified` is in there, and nothing read it. An address a provider has not verified is an address anybody can claim, and the callback treated the address as proof of who was signing in. Three things followed from one missing check:

- a new account was created with `EmailVerifiedAt` set, turning "somebody typed this address into a provider" into "this address is confirmed"
- an existing account had the provider linked to it, which is account takeover with one more step
- an existing account whose address was never confirmed had its password removed and its sessions revoked, which is account takeover outright

Now one predicate decides all three. Google says so in the payload. GitHub does not need to, because it does not expose an unverified address: the public profile email must be a verified one, and when that is empty goth falls back to `/user/emails` and takes the address that is primary and verified. Any other provider counts as unverified until a rule is written for it, so adding one cannot quietly reopen this.

An unverified claim no longer reaches an account that already exists. The refusal says what to do instead: sign in with your password, then connect the provider from your profile. A returning user whose provider account is already linked is not affected, because the link was established deliberately and is not being claimed now.

And when a password is removed, the person is told. In the case that step exists for, whoever had the password was not the owner; in the far more common case somebody registered, never confirmed, and later used the provider, and their password silently stopped working. The mail is how they find out why.

### Rate limiting on the sign-in routes needed Sentinel

Review 2.8. Every limit on the routes that take a password or a code lived inside `mountSentinel`, behind a check on `SENTINEL_ENABLED`. That is off by default in development and one environment variable in production, and with it off `/auth/login`, `/auth/forgot-password`, `/auth/totp/verify` and the passkey routes had no limiter at all. The per-account lockout still barred a single account, so guessing one password was bounded; nothing bounded credential stuffing across many accounts from one address, or a forgot-password loop pointed at one mailbox.

There is now a limiter in the project itself, reading the same table, mounted whether or not Sentinel is. It is in-process and per-instance, so it is the floor rather than the ceiling: Sentinel keeps its counters in shared storage and is still what you want in front of several replicas. The point is that turning Sentinel off downgrades the protection instead of removing it.

```text
SENTINEL_ENABLED=false, 110 POSTs to /api/v1/auth/login

                     before   after
attempts 1-100         401      401
attempts 101-110       401      429  Retry-After: 31
```

Measured on a running project. The table also gained seven routes it never had: a magic link costs an email per request, backup codes and passkey logins are credential checks, and the SSO callbacks are a sign-in. Development relaxes the numbers now rather than dropping all but two, because a route with no entry is a route with no limit, and a limit nobody exercises in development is a limit that surprises somebody in production.

### The refresh token went to browsers in a readable body

Review 2.10. The refresh token is the long-lived credential: it mints access tokens for days. It was returned in the JSON body to every client, next to the `HttpOnly` cookie carrying the same value, while the docs said a script never sees it. For a browser those cannot both be true, and the cookie is the one worth keeping.

The single architecture's frontend was the worse half: it read the token out of that body and put it in `localStorage`, which is the one place a long-lived credential should never be. It now refreshes with the cookie and an empty body, and clears whatever an older version of itself stored.

```text
POST /api/v1/auth/login        tokens in the body

Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin    access_token, expires_at
X-Grit-Client: native          access_token, expires_at, refresh_token
no browser headers at all      access_token, expires_at, refresh_token
```

A native client asks, rather than being guessed at: the desktop app runs in a webview and looks exactly like a browser, and it keeps the token in the OS keychain, which is better than a cookie. The Expo app keeps it in `SecureStore`. Both generated clients send the header already. A request with no browser signal at all, which is a CLI or a server-to-server call, still gets the token, so nothing that worked before this stopped working.

`grit upgrade` carries all three. The token change is two repairs in a deliberate order, because the sign-in repair writes a `Login` that calls `tokens.ForClient(c)` and a project whose `TokenPair` has no such method would stop compiling on an upgrade that reported success.


## v3.452.0 - October 30, 2026

### grit deploy was a first deploy only

Enterprise review 2.2. Seven faults in one command, and the thing they have in common is that the first deploy to a fresh box worked, so none of them showed up until the second one.

```text
the shell          every value interpolated unquoted, from .env
the second deploy  scp over a running binary is ETXTBSY on Linux
the restart        nothing checked whether the app came back
a bad deploy       nothing to roll back to
the schema         no migration step at all
the environment    EnvironmentFile named a .env nothing uploaded
the web server     the whole /etc/caddy/Caddyfile overwritten
```

#### Releases and a symlink

Most of the list is answered by one change of shape. A release is a directory of its own and `current` is a symlink to it:

```text
/opt/app/releases/20261030-150405/{app,grit-migrate,.env}
/opt/app/current -> releases/20261030-150405
```

Nothing is written over a running binary, so the second deploy works. The switch is one symlink, so a request in flight sees the old release or the new one and never half of a copy. The previous directory is still there, so a rollback is the same move backwards. The systemd unit names `current` rather than a release, so it is written once instead of rewritten on every deploy.

#### A deploy that does not come up undoes itself

After the restart, `grit deploy` fetches the health endpoint on the server through the app's own port, for up to a minute. From the server deliberately: a deploy that works and a certificate that has not issued yet are different problems and should not look the same. A release that never answers is put back and the failure says how to read the logs, with the broken release left on disk to read them against. `grit deploy --rollback` does the same thing on demand, without building or uploading anything.

#### The schema travels with the code

The deploy builds `cmd/migrate` alongside the server, uploads both, and runs the migration before the symlink moves. Before the move, because the old binary is still serving and a migration that fails must not leave the new one running against a schema it does not expect. A project with no `cmd/migrate` skips the step rather than failing on it.

#### The .env the unit always named

The unit has said `EnvironmentFile=<path>/.env` since the command shipped and nothing ever put one there, so the service started with none of the project's configuration: no database URL, no secrets, defaults everywhere. systemd does not complain about a missing `EnvironmentFile`, so it looked fine. It is now uploaded into each release at 0600, owned by the service user, over SSH rather than scp so the mode is never briefly wider.

#### Your other sites survive

`setupCaddy` wrote the whole `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`. Deploying a second app to a box, or a first one to a box that already served anything, threw the other site away without a word. For a command whose pitch is a server you own, that is the opposite of owning it. This app's site block now lives in `/etc/caddy/sites/<app>.caddy`, the main Caddyfile gets one `import` line appended if it does not have one, and the configuration is validated before the reload, because a Caddyfile that does not parse takes every site on the box down.

#### Two defences on the shell

`AppName`, `RemotePath`, `Domain` and the ports went straight into `ssh host "...%s..."` by string interpolation, and `DEPLOY_HOST` and `DEPLOY_DOMAIN` come from `.env`. Every interpolated value is now single-quoted, and every value that becomes a path, a unit name, a domain or a port is checked against what it is allowed to be before a single command is built. Two defences rather than one, because quoting alone is a single point of failure in code that assembles shell strings, and a deploy that refuses is recoverable while one that has already run is not.

Files go over SSH inside a heredoc, so their contents are never a shell argument and a `.env` holding `$(id)` or a backtick arrives as written. The one thing that breaks a heredoc is its own delimiter alone on a line, and the `.env` is the project's file rather than ours, so that case is refused with a message naming the line to change.

#### And the dry run tells the truth

`--dry-run` printed the old plan: one scp, the whole Caddyfile, no migration, no .env, no health check. A dry run that lies is worse than no dry run, so it now prints the release path, every artifact, the env upload, the migration, the symlink move, the site file, the validate, and what happens if the health check fails.

`--keep` sets how many old releases stay on the server, five by default, and they are pruned only after the new release has answered: a tidy-up that runs first is one that deletes the release you are about to need.

### The release build set a version variable that does not exist

Review 2.26. `release.yml` built every binary with `-X main.Version=${TAG}`, and the variable is `version`, lowercase. The ldflag set nothing, silently, so a released binary reported whatever the source constant said. That was right every time, because the release ritual bumps the constant by hand, which is the kind of correctness that holds until the one time somebody forgets.

The ldflag is gone rather than fixed: the constant is what the ritual bumps, so it should be what the binary reports. In its place, the release build refuses a tag that disagrees with the constant, and a test compares the three places in the source that carry the version. A release ritual with four spots and nothing comparing them was one typo from shipping a binary that lies about which version it is.


## v3.451.0 - October 30, 2026

### Every policy rule was dead

`policies.Register()` had no call site. Not in `main`, not in `routes`, nowhere in a generated project. Every rule anybody wrote in `internal/policies` was registered into a map that nothing ever filled, so no rule ran on any path: a `PATCH` on a row a rule denied answered 200.

That is the worst shape an authorization feature can fail in, because everything about it looks finished. The package is generated beside the resource, it is documented, it carries a worked example, and each resource injects its own registration into a marker inside it. The only missing piece was the one nobody looks at twice.

The call cannot be written into `main.go` at scaffold time, because the package only exists once a resource has been generated and a project with none would stop compiling. So `main.go` carries a `grit:main:boot` marker and the generator injects the call beside the registry it already creates. `grit upgrade` adds it to every project that has the package, which is every project that has ever run `grit generate resource`.

Found while testing the next item, which reported the rules as evadable through a bulk action. They were evadable through everything.

### Patch, BulkEdit and Bulk wrote maps nothing had checked

Enterprise review 2.4. `Create` and `Update` bind into the model, so gin runs the binding tags, and they load their row through `s.load`, which consults a policy. The three map-shaped paths did neither. A column whitelist answers "may this column be written at all" and nothing else, so `binding:"required"` never fired, a money value was never checked, and `{"count":"x"}` reached the database as a type error and came back a 500.

All three now apply the whitelisted patch onto a copy of the row and run the model's own rules over the result. Onto a copy of the row rather than an empty struct, so a rule about a field the patch does not mention still sees the value already stored; the copy is thrown away, and the write is still the map, so a column nobody sent is not zeroed. Before the money expansion, which rewrites a field into two columns whose names are not json tags.

And both bulk paths run the policy per row. The ability follows the action, so a rule that refuses a delete and allows an edit is asked the right question, and a refusal is a 403 rather than the 422 it would otherwise have been: a client branching on the status should not see one code for one row and another for twelve.

```text
                     before   after
single PATCH, denied    200      403
bulk patch, denied      200      403
bulk delete, denied     200      403
{"count":"x"}           500      422  count must be a whole number
{"label":""} required   200      422  label: This field is required
```

Measured on a running project with a real rule defined. The first line is the one worth looking at twice: the single path was never supposed to be affected, and it was, because of the finding above.

`grit upgrade` applies all of it to services that already exist. A security fix only the generator carries reaches resources nobody has generated yet, which is the one set that was never at risk. The repair and the generator are held together by a test that runs the repair over a service the generator wrote before any of this and compares the result to what the generator writes now, byte for byte, so the two cannot drift into an upgraded project being checked less than a new one.


## v3.450.0 - October 30, 2026

### grit update verifies what it is about to run

It did not. The updater downloaded the release artifact and handed it straight to `update.Apply` with no checksum and no signature, while the release workflow had been publishing `SHA256SUMS`, a cosign signature over it and the certificate all along. Everything needed to check the download existed and nothing read it. This is the first command the README suggests after install.

Now, before a byte is written over the running binary:

- the certificate chains to Fulcio's root, pinned in the binary rather than fetched, because a trust root you download at verification time is not one;
- its subject is this repository's release workflow *on a tag*, so a run from a branch cannot sign a release;
- its issuer extension is GitHub's OIDC provider;
- the signature over the checksums verifies;
- the artifact's SHA-256 is one of those checksums.

```text
Downloading:    grit-windows-amd64.zip (9.0 MiB)
Verifying signature...
Verified:       grit-windows-amd64.zip, signed by the release workflow
```

What is *not* checked, said plainly because the alternative is implying more than is true: there is no Rekor inclusion proof, so there is no trusted timestamp for the signature. Adding sigstore-go would take this CLI from 56 modules to 129, which is a poor trade in the binary whose supply chain this protects, and the property that matters is held without it: forging a signature needs Fulcio's CA key or control of this repository's release workflow.

Tested against the real artifacts of the real v3.448.0 release. A genuine release verifies; tampered checksums, a signature over other content, and a self-signed certificate claiming to be the release workflow are each refused with a reason.

### And it will not take you backwards

`grit update` refuses a release older than the one running, because moving backwards silently is how a fixed vulnerability comes back. `--version 3.440.0` installs a named release, and `--allow-downgrade` is how you mean it. The refusal prints the exact command.

### A bearer client's logout left the session alive

Logout revoked the server-side session only when the `grit_refresh` cookie was there. A browser has one; a mobile or desktop client holding a bearer token does not, so its logout cleared nothing and answered "Logged out successfully" while the session stayed usable until the idle or absolute timeout.

The access token already carried its session as the `sid` claim and `Refresh` already read it; the middleware simply never passed it on. It does now, and Logout falls back to it. Measured on a running project: `GET /auth/me` answers 200 before a bearer-only logout and 401 with the same token after it.

### Two headers, and the cache they nearly broke

The CSRF cookie set its `Secure` flag from `c.Request.TLS` alone while every auth cookie honoured `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Behind the usual TLS-terminating proxy that left the double-submit token as the one cookie without `Secure`. Four places, not the one reported.

CORS now sets `Vary: Origin`, before the allow decision rather than inside it, because a refusal is also a response that varies by origin.

That second one would have switched the URL cache off for every response at once, silently: `shareableResponse` refuses to store anything whose `Vary` names a header its key does not include, which is correct. It is safe to cache here for a specific reason, not a general one: a cache hit replays the status, the content type and the body and nothing else, so the origin-dependent header is written per request by middleware that runs ahead of the cache on a hit as well as a miss. The test asserts that replay stays header-free, and says to take the exception back out if it ever does not.

### The error, above the flags

`SilenceUsage` was set inside nine individual command bodies, which is too late for anything that fails before reaching the line. The sentence worth reading landed under twenty lines of flags. It is set on the root now, and a genuine usage error gets a one-line pointer after the message instead of the table before it.


## v3.449.0 - October 30, 2026

### An organization switcher, because nothing set the header

[#141](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/141). The multitenant plugin resolves the active organization from `X-Organization-ID`, and nothing in a generated client ever set it. A user who belongs to one organization is fine, because the middleware activates it automatically. A user who belongs to two had no way to choose, which is the case the plugin exists for.

The admin gets a switcher now. It renders nothing at all below two organizations: a control offering one choice is furniture that implies a decision nobody has, and a single-tenant project looks exactly as it did.

### The header is the framework's, the choice is the plugin's

`lib/active-org.ts` and the `api-core` interceptor ship in every project, with or without the plugin, and send nothing until something sets a value. That split is deliberate: `api-client.ts` is rewritten by every upgrade, so a plugin that injected the header into it would make the file read as the developer's own edit. The injection would survive and the file would stop receiving the fixes that actually matter in it, which are CSRF, token refresh and the 401 retry.

It is in `api-core.ts` specifically, which the admin and the web app share. One writer, two consumers.

### Switching clears the cache rather than invalidating it

An invalidated query serves its old data while it refetches, and that data belongs to the organization being left: React Query would go on rendering one tenant's rows under another tenant's name. Showing a spinner is better.

And a stored id for an organization the reader no longer belongs to is dropped when the list comes back without it. A membership can be revoked while the id sits in a browser; sending it then means every request carries an organization the API refuses, and the reader sees an app that is broken rather than one that moved them back.

### Found by running it

The hook called `/organizations`, and `versionedPath` only rewrites a path that starts with `/api/`, so the request went to the host root and answered 404. It compiled, `tsc --noEmit` passed, and six new tests passed. The browser did not. There is a seventh test now.

Verified end to end in a browser against a running project: the switcher appears with two organizations and not with one, switching changes the label and clears the cache, the choice survives a reload, and `x-organization-id` is on the request headers of calls the app makes by itself.

Still open in #141: the invitation flow. `POST /organizations/:id/members` takes a user id, so somebody must already have an account and you must already know their id.


## v3.448.0 - October 30, 2026

### grit new --multitenant

[#62](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/62). Everything the flag needs has existed since the multitenant plugin did: organizations, memberships, the middleware, the scoping callbacks, and per-organization roles since v3.442.0. What was missing is the flag, so the way in was to scaffold and then remember a second command, and the reporter had six starter kits that need it from the first one.

```bash
grit new acme --triple --next --multitenant
```

Installed by calling the same function `grit plugin add multitenant` calls, the way `--i18n` calls `AddI18n`. Two code paths that write the same project are how they start writing different ones, which this codebase has learned more than once.

It runs before the access table is read out of the route files, so the nine organization routes are in it on a brand new project rather than appearing only after the next `grit generate`.

Models stay shared until you say otherwise, which is the one thing the original request asked to be automatic and Grit deliberately does not do. Putting `org_id` on every table is a schema decision no framework should make on your behalf: add `tenant.Owned` to the models that belong to an organization, or generate them with `--tenant-owned`. The flag says so when it finishes.


## v3.447.0 - October 30, 2026

### An import could not skip a row that was already there

[#140](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/140). The generated importer writes rows with `clause.OnConflict{DoNothing: true}`, which only does something when the database has a constraint to conflict with. A generated resource had a unique index on its primary key and nothing else, and the importer assigns a fresh id per row, so nothing ever conflicted: the same CSV imported twice produced two copies of every row, and the job reported `Imported 4, skipped 0` where the 0 was structural rather than a fact.

Every part of the machinery was already there and correct. What was missing is the constraint, and which columns it covers is a decision per resource that no generator can make: a contact might be unique by email, by phone, or by name within a company. So `--unique` names them.

```bash
grit generate resource Contact \
  --fields "name:string,email:email,company:belongs_to:Company" \
  --unique email

grit generate resource Member \
  --fields "name:string,company:belongs_to:Company" \
  --unique "name,company"      # unique within a company
```

One composite index over the columns in the order named, so a foreign key can be part of it, which is how "unique within a company" is spelled. The relation keeps its ordinary index as well: the unique one is composite, so it does not serve a lookup by company alone.

Measured on a running project, importing the same two-row file twice: `Imported 2, skipped 0` then `Imported 0, skipped 2`, with two rows in the table. A duplicate write through the API answers `409 CONFLICT` with the field named, which the framework already did and had no index to do it on.

### What it refuses, and why at generation time

A unique index that fails to create leaves a resource whose importer silently duplicates every row, which is the bug the flag exists to fix. So the spellings that cannot work are refused when the resource is generated rather than when it is migrated: a many-to-many, which has no column on this table; a money field, which is two; a list stored in one column, where two rows holding the same values in a different order would be distinct; rich text, which most databases refuse to index; and the same column named twice, including once as `company` and once as `company_id`. Each refusal says which column and why, and a column that is not there at all lists the ones that are.

New resources only, deliberately. Adding the index to a resource that already has rows has to say what it will do about the duplicates already in there, which is a migration and a conversation rather than a flag.


## v3.446.0 - October 30, 2026

### A webhook secret that differs per tenant

[#138](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/138). A `Provider` carried `SecretEnv`, one environment variable for the whole deployment, and the receiver read it with `os.Getenv` at request time. That is right for Stripe and GitHub, where the deployment has one account. It is impossible for a gateway where every organization connects its own, with its own signing secret in its own row, and the route was `POST /webhooks/:provider` with no further segment, so the handler could not tell which tenant a delivery was for before verifying it. The reporter hand-wrote a separate route and lost the stored deliveries, the dedupe and the admin replay along with it.

`Provider.Secret` resolves the secret for *one* delivery and takes precedence over `SecretEnv`. It gets the route's path parameters, so it can read the tenant out of `POST /webhooks/:provider/:tenant`, and the headers, for a provider that names the account in one instead. An error refuses the delivery rather than verifying it against the wrong secret, and the receiver answers that the same way it answers a bad signature: the resolver runs before verification, so it is reachable by anybody who can post to the route, and "no such tenant" is worth more to somebody probing than it is to you. The reason goes to the log.

### The dedupe key needed the tenant

Not in the report, and necessary for the feature to work: two organizations on one gateway can each receive a reference `INV-001`, because their accounts are their own and the references are theirs to choose. Under the old `(provider, external_id)` key the second is refused as a duplicate it is not, answered with a `status=skipped` 200, and that payment is never recorded. The key is `(provider, tenant, external_id)` now, and `Tenant` is the empty string for a provider that has none, so Stripe and GitHub behave exactly as they did.

The new index has a different NAME on purpose. AutoMigrate decides by name, so reusing `idx_webhook_provider_external` with different columns would have left the old two-column index in place and never created the new one: the feature present and not working. The old one is dropped after the replacement exists, never before, because between the two there is no idempotency at all and a redelivery arriving in that window runs twice.

And the drop had to go somewhere an upgrade reaches. `Migrate` lives in `models/user.go`, which `writeAPIFiles` writes for new projects only, so a migration put there reaches nobody who needs it. That is the trap this exact shape sprang in v3.441.0. The drop lives in `models/webhook_event.go`, which upgrades do deliver, and a repair injects the call. Verified against a database holding the old index.

### And one thing the docs never said

The reporter's second point, which has no code fix: a payment gateway posts several events about one transaction, first `pending` and later `completed`, both carrying the same reference. An extractor that returns the reference makes the second a duplicate of the first, so the event that actually matters is dropped with a `status=skipped` 200 and nothing looks wrong. The extractor has to return something unique per event, and the deduplication section now says so.


## v3.445.0 - October 30, 2026

### An import resolved an owner against every user on the platform

[#139](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/139). A generated importer looked a user up with `db.Where("email = ?", v)` and nothing narrowed it. In a multitenant project that is a cross-tenant read through an importer: somebody importing a spreadsheet into one organization could file rows under a user who belongs only to another, by knowing or guessing their address, and the row error told them whether that address exists on the platform at all.

The ceiling that did exist, `canAssignOwner`, asks whether the caller may name an owner. Nothing asked whether the owner they named is somebody this organization can see. It is the shape GHSA-4j45-98gm-mv9v is about: a path that checks a key rather than who owns the row.

Narrowed to the active organization's members, read from the context at runtime rather than assumed, because an administrator importing platform-wide has no active organization and must still be able to. A project without the multitenant plugin keeps the lookup it has, where there is no members table to narrow against and the current behaviour is correct.

The refusal says the same thing either way, which is the point: a user who exists in another organization and an address that exists nowhere both answer `no user with email "x@y.com" in this organization`. Measured on a running project with two organizations, one row imported and one refused.

### One reader, and one writer

Two things had to agree about this and lived in packages that cannot import each other: the generator, deciding what to write for a new resource, and the upgrade, deciding what to repair in a project that already has one.

`PluginInstalled` moved to `internal/project`, which both read, so there is one answer to "is this project multitenant". It had been sitting in `internal/generate` with no callers at all since it was written; this is its first. And the lookup itself moved to `internal/scaffold` beside the other import codegen, which is where `ImportNameResolver` already lives for exactly this reason, so a project generated today and one upgraded today get the same bytes.

The upgrade rewrites the lookup in importers that already have it, matching the generated text, because an unscoped cross-tenant read is not something to leave in place for projects that exist. An importer somebody rewrote by hand no longer matches and is left alone.


## v3.444.0 - October 30, 2026

### The upgrade stops overwriting files it never wrote

[#125](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/125), and the only one of the batch that destroyed work rather than failing to do some. The guard held back a file Grit had written and the project had since edited. Everything else it wrote, including a file Grit had never written at all, because "no record" and "mine to overwrite" were the same answer.

An Expo app copied into a project has no records, because copying it was the only way in: `grit add` had no `expo`, and `--expo` lives only on `grit new`. So the next upgrade replaced the tab bar, the API client that adds the organization header, the auth provider and the query client, wrote back six screens the project had deleted, and said `Updated 603 files`. The app still compiled, against endpoints the project does not have.

### Four answers where there were two

The reason the unrecorded case was not simply protected still holds: a project generated before v3.147.0 has no records for anything, and refusing to update all of it would be worse than the problem. So the question is not whether the file has an entry, it is whether the project has a manifest at all.

- Grit wrote it and it has changed: held back, as since v3.147.0, under "you have edited these".
- Grit wrote it and it is gone, *along with the directory it lived in*: the project removed a feature, so it is not put back. "Missing" and "never written" used to be the same answer here, which is why six deleted screens returned on every upgrade.
- Grit wrote it, it is gone, and its directory is still there: written. Deleting one framework file out of a directory full of them is how you ask for the stock version back, and has been since v3.147.0.
- No record, in a project that has a manifest: the file is not Grit's. If it differs from the template it is held back and listed under a heading that says so, because "you have edited this" is the wrong sentence for a file Grit never wrote. If it is identical there is nothing to decide, so it is written and adopted.
- No record and no manifest: written, exactly as before v3.147.0.

The directory is the discriminator, and it exists because a test already in the suite said why the first version of this was wrong: deleting a framework component is how people ask for the stock one back, documented since v3.147.0. Two wanted behaviours in direct conflict, told apart by the only thing that differs between the two reports. Removing a directory is a bigger statement than removing a file, and the only one of the two that reads as "I do not want this".

`grit upgrade --force` writes a removed directory back, and the upgrade lists what it left absent, so it is a decision rather than a silence. Grit's own deletions now forget their manifest entries as they go, so a file the framework removed is never reported as one you did.

### grit add expo, grit add desktop

The guard is a safety net for however the files got there. It cannot fix the first upgrade after a manual copy, because a file with no record and nothing on disk is indistinguishable from one this version has newly added, so a deleted screen comes back once.

These two commands remove the copying. They write the app with the same function `grit new` uses, set the flag in `grit.json` so the upgrade maintains it, rewire `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, the root `package.json` and `grit.config.ts`, and record every file as it goes. With records the provenance is right from the first upgrade rather than the second.

`grit.json` is edited as text, not decoded and re-encoded, because a round trip through a struct drops every key this version of Grit does not know about, including a project's own.

Verified by reproducing the report, then by the proper route. A copied-in app keeps its edited tab bar and reports it; added with `grit add expo`, an edited screen is left alone and a deleted one stays deleted on the very first upgrade.


## v3.443.0 - October 30, 2026

### An import stops creating a parent it cannot fill in

[#129](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/129). A generated CSV importer resolves a `belongs_to` column by the related record's natural key and created a missing record from that key alone. For a lookup table whose only column is a name that is exactly right. For a model that requires anything else it is a constraint violation per row: `Company.OwnerID` is `binding:"required"` with a foreign key to users, so an imported contact naming a company that does not exist yet failed. In the reporter's CRM that was 4 of 4 rows, and in a real contact list it is nearly every row.

The generator reads the related model before it writes the resolver. If the natural key is all that model needs, a missing record is still created, so a name-only lookup table imports exactly as before. If it needs anything else, nothing is created and the row is refused with something a person can act on:

```text
company "Gulu Agro" does not exist. An import cannot create one,
because Company requires owner_id, which this file has no column for.
Add the Company first, or import company records before this one
```

It refuses rather than guesses. The only value an importer could invent for an owner column is "whoever is running the import", which is right for an owner and wrong for anything else, and a wrong foreign key is worse than a refused row because nobody finds out. On Postgres the old behaviour was a visible failure; on SQLite, where the column is not `NOT NULL`, it quietly wrote a company nobody owns.

One function decides it, read from the model file on disk because that model was generated earlier and may have been edited since. The generator and `grit upgrade` both call that one function, so they cannot answer differently, which is how two copies of generated code start to disagree.

The upgrade replaces the resolver in projects that already have it, because a resolver that cannot succeed does not become correct by being old. Only where the model on disk says so: a lookup table's resolver is left creating records, and a resolver somebody edited by hand no longer matches the generated text and is left alone.

Verified by reproducing the report: the same two resources, the same four-row CSV, four refused rows with that message and no company written, then the same file importing cleanly once the companies exist.


## v3.442.0 - October 30, 2026

### An organization manages its own roles

[#130](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/130). v3.441.0 gave an organization roles of its own and left out the endpoints, because who inside an organization may author a role is a product decision rather than a technical one. It has been made: the organization's owner, a platform administrator, or a member holding `orgroles.manage`. Four routes under `/organizations/:id/roles`, and any member may read the list, because picking a role for a colleague means seeing the names.

A read is scoped by owner and not only by id, so another organization's role answers "not found" rather than "forbidden": a different answer tells the caller the id is real. A role somebody still holds is refused rather than deleted.

### Three keys that could never be held

A permission key is `<feature>.<action>`, two segments, and `authz.Keys()` builds every valid one from the catalogue. The key v3.438.0 invented for member management had three. No catalogue entry could produce it, so the roles UI called it an unknown permission; the prefix list v3.441.0 added refused it in an organization role; and it was never in the catalogue at all. Three layers disagreeing about one string, and the role the feature existed for could not be saved.

It is `orgmembers.manage` now, with `orgroles.manage` beside it. Nothing can be holding the old name, because every path that writes a role rejected it. A test in the plugin reads the forbidden prefixes out of the role service and the keys out of the handler, and fails on a key that cannot be held.

### What an owner may hand out, and why the schema decides

The ceiling on authoring a role is the author's own grants, which is right on the platform and wrong for an organization: an owner holds no role by default, so that ceiling refused them every role they tried to write. The first fix was "the two organization keys and nothing else", which is safe and useless, because a customer wanting an Editor with `blogs.edit` could not have one.

The real test was already in the project, in the only place that knows: `tenant.Owned`. A permission on a model carrying `org_id` is scoped by the tenant callback to the organization in the request, so handing it to a member gives them their own rows. Without that column nothing scopes the query and the same grant hands them every organization's. Same permission, same role, opposite blast radius, and only the schema knows which. So the schema is asked, per permission, at the moment the role is written.

The refusal says that, at length, because the first version of it said "you cannot grant permissions you do not hold": true, not the reason, and the fix it implies is to grant the owner that permission, which opens the very hole the refusal exists to close.

### Two ceilings that between them made it impossible

One decided what an owner could write into a role. The other decided what they could hand out. Each was defensible alone. Together they meant the owner could author the role that delegates member management and then could not give it to anybody, because handing it out was measured against grants they personally hold. The feature existed and refused its only user, and a test per ceiling passed throughout.

There is one ceiling now, with two call sites, and a test that asserts both reach it. Closing that also closed something the old version allowed: the role was read by id alone, so one customer could hand their member a role another customer owns, and that customer's next edit changed what the first one's people could do, which is the complaint #130 opens with arriving by a different door.

### And the upgrade

A plugin's files are written at install time, so `grit upgrade` carries a second copy of this API and delivers it to projects that already exist, along with the renamed key and `tenant.ColumnName`, which the handler reads and an older `internal/tenant` does not have. Two copies of security-shaped code is the thing that goes wrong quietly, so the repair's copy is sliced out of the plugin and a test fails when the two drift.

Verified by putting a generated project back into the shape v3.438.0 left it in, upgrading it, and compiling. Every fault above was found by running the flow, not by a test.

### A checker that could not see the plugins

`VALIDATION_ERROR` is 422 in the catalogue and this handler returned it with 400, in two places before today and four more added with the role endpoints. The test that keeps one code to one status walked `internal/scaffold` and `internal/generate`, so every plugin's error codes went unchecked since plugins existed. It walks `internal/plugin` now, and the ten mismatches it found are fixed. A checker blind to a directory reports success about it, which is worse than not having one.


## v3.441.0 - October 29, 2026

### An organization can have roles of its own

[#130](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/130). A role's name was unique across the whole platform, so if one customer created an "Accountant" nobody else could, and giving a second customer the same role meant every edit by the first changed the second's permissions. The multitenant plugin promises "an Editor in one organization and a Viewer in another", which was true of the assignment and not of the role.

`Role` carries an owner now. Empty means the platform defines it; an organization's id means that organization does, and the name is unique per owner.

### Not called org_id, and that matters

The reporter's warning, which is worth repeating: the multitenant plugin scopes every query on a model carrying `org_id` to the active organization. A column of that name on `roles` would hide every platform role from every request made inside an organization. The table would read as empty mid-request and every permission lookup would fail closed. It is `owner_org_id`.

### Six lookups, not four

Every lookup of a role by name had to say whose role it meant, because "the role called ADMIN" now has as many answers as there are organizations. The report listed four places; there were six. They go through `models.PlatformRoles` now, and a test enumerates them rather than a person: it reads every template for a lookup by name and fails on one that does not narrow to an owner. It found five I had missed.

### What an organization role may hold

Nothing marked that before, and the default was everything. A customer's role holding `users.view` reads the whole platform's user table, because a membership role's grants are merged into the request and the platform routes check the key rather than who owns the role.

An organization role may hold permissions about its own resources and never `*`, `users.`, `roles.`, `apikeys.`, `settings.`, `organizations.`, `audit.` or the rest of the platform's own administration. A forbidden list rather than an allowed one, so a resource generated tomorrow works in an organization role the day it exists and a new piece of platform administration does not. Checked where a role is written, because the ceiling at grant time sees the role somebody chose and not the one they wrote a moment earlier.

### And two gaps the work exposed

`internal/models/role.go` was never delivered on an upgrade: `writeSecurityFiles` writes it and only new projects call that. It went unnoticed while nothing depended on the file. When `ceiling.go`, which *is* delivered, started calling `models.PlatformRoles`, an upgraded project got the caller without the function and stopped compiling.

The old unique index needed dropping too, and the first place I put that was `Migrate`, which lives in `models/user.go` and has the same problem: it would have reached only projects that never had the old index in the first place. It runs from `SeedRoles` now, after AutoMigrate has created the replacement, because between dropping one and creating the other there is no uniqueness at all.


## v3.440.0 - October 29, 2026

### Generated tests passed on SQLite and failed on Postgres

[#137](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/137). Every resource with a `belongs_to` had a handler test that failed on the database the project actually runs on:

`{`insert or update on table "books" violates foreign key constraint "fk_books_author" (SQLSTATE 23503)`}` The factory leaves a `belongs_to` column empty on purpose, and its doc comment says to pass the parent in. The generated test did not: it called `factory.CreateBook(t, db)` and the row went in with `author_id = ""`, an empty string rather than NULL, because the column is a string. The test now creates each parent first and points the record at it.

### And the reason nobody saw it

SQLite does not enforce foreign keys unless the connection asks, and the test database never asked. So the suite was green on the database nobody ships and red on the one everybody does, which is the worst way round for a test suite to be wrong.

`testkit.DB` sets `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON` now, before migrating, so the tables are built with it on. With the old fixture put back, SQLite reports what Postgres reported: `FOREIGN KEY constraint failed`.

This is the more useful half. A test database that cannot see a broken foreign key is worth less than it looks, and every future bug of this shape now fails where people actually run their tests rather than waiting for a deployment.

A self-reference is left alone: a resource whose parent is its own kind is created with none, because making one first would need the same override and recurse. A resource with several parents gets one fixture each.


## v3.439.0 - October 29, 2026

### grit upgrade --dry-run, because --diff was not one

[#133](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/133). `--plan`'s help said "Not a dry run: use --diff for that", and `--diff` applies the upgrade. On a real project it rewrote 46 tracked files and added about 40. A flag that promises a look and writes is the worst shape a flag can have.

`--dry-run` runs the real upgrade on a copy of the project and diffs the two trees. A dry-run switch threaded through every writer was the other option, and there are 54 places that write a file without passing through the guard: a dry run that still wrote some of them would be the same bug wearing a different name. Running the real thing somewhere else cannot drift from what an upgrade does, because it is what an upgrade does.

`--diff` still applies the upgrade, deliberately: what it prints is what the upgrade would have changed in the files it leaves alone, and that is only knowable while the upgrade runs. Its help says so now, and so does `--plan`'s.

### brand.css showed Grit's colours under a heading saying yours

[#135](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/135) reported an upgrade repainting a themed project purple. It does not: the file is 1714 bytes and zero after stripping comments, in both apps, and a project's own accent in `globals.css` survives the upgrade intact.

What is real is why it read that way. The upgrade said "your colours", the example then showed Grit's purple, and the comment markers sit on their own lines where they are easy to miss. The example is now seeded from what the app renders today, read out of its own `globals.css`, and a token the app does not set is left out rather than filled in from Grit's palette. The web app has no dark palette at all, so a dark block seeded from defaults was showing a colour that app has never rendered.

Writing that found a second thing, in the fix: a note placed inside the commented block ended the comment early, because CSS comments do not nest, and the closing brace became live CSS. Four bytes of it, in a file whose whole promise is that it declares nothing. A test now asserts the file is inert for every shape of input, and that its comment markers balance.

### Every invoice PDF was two pages

[#136](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/136). The second held nothing but the footer line. fpdf breaks 20mm from the bottom, which is 277mm on A4; `Doc.Footer` moved to 272 and wrote a 5mm cell, ending at exactly 277, so fpdf started a new page to write it. One millimetre either way and nobody would have noticed for another year.

The automatic break is off around the footer and restored after, so a document that genuinely needs more pages still gets them. Two tests ship with every project: a one-line invoice is one page, and a 120-line invoice is more than one.


## v3.438.0 - October 29, 2026

### Two privilege escalations in the multitenant plugin

** Upgrade if you have `grit plugin add multitenant` installed. ** Both were found while working on [#130](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/130), and both were reproduced on a freshly scaffolded project.

### Creating an organization made you a platform administrator

This one needed no attack. It was the happy path.

`OrganizationHandler.Create` assigned the **platform ADMIN role** as the creator's membership role, and `addOrgGrants` merges a membership role's grants into every request made with that organization active. ADMIN holds `*`. So anybody who created an organization could read every user on the platform, not only their own members.

Measured on a fresh project: `GET /api/users` was 403 for a new account, and 200 returning the whole table after that account created an organization. The creator is the organization's owner, which is all they need, and they are given no role now.

### Any member could grant themselves any role

`POST /organizations/:id/members` checked that the caller was a member and nothing else, then wrote whatever `role_id` it was sent. An ordinary member could post their own user id with the ADMIN role's id: the same `GET /api/users` answered 403 before the call and 200 after it.

Two guards now, deliberately both, because they fail independently. `canManageMembers` is who may change the membership at all: a platform administrator, the organization's owner, or a member holding `organizations.members.manage`, which nothing grants by default. `roleBeyondCaller` is what they may hand out, bounded by their own grants, and only a platform administrator may hand out ADMIN. The second is the one that still holds if a project relaxes the first, which is a thing projects do.

This is the shape GHSA-4j45-98gm-mv9v describes, a membership role holding a platform grant, and the plugin was doing it to itself by default. `grit upgrade` repairs an existing project and says what it changed; a project that has rewritten the handler is told so rather than silently skipped, because an upgrade that looks like it fixed something is worse than one that admits it could not.

### And a repair of mine that broke the build

The benchmark repair added in v3.433.0 substituted `{{PROJECT}}` and not `{{MODULE}}`, so an upgrade wrote a literal `{{MODULE}}/internal/config` import into `bench_test.go` and the project stopped compiling. Found by running an upgrade on a real project, which is the only place it shows.

A test now reads every repair and fails when one renders a template with a placeholder it does not substitute.


## v3.437.0 - October 29, 2026

### An SSO sign-in you can act on

[#127](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/127). Social sign-in has `OnOAuthLogin`, run after the account is resolved. Enterprise SSO had nothing equivalent: the OIDC callback and the SAML ACS went from `applyGroupRoles` straight to the token pair, so a project had no supported place to act on an SSO sign-in. The only way in was to edit a handler Grit owns and rewrites on upgrade.

That matters most in a multi-tenant app, where the obvious thing to do there is put the person in their company's organisation: an SSO connection belongs to one customer. `applyGroupRoles` only writes platform roles and an `SSOConnection` has no organisation of its own, so every SSO user landed with none, which is what `grit doctor`'s `tenant-sso-no-organization` warning is about.

`services.OnSSOLogin` takes the connection, the user and the groups the IdP asserted, which are what an app needs and what the OAuth hook's `goth.User` does not carry. It runs from both ways in, after the group roles, on every sign-in rather than only the first. A failing hook is logged and the rest still run, the same choice `applyGroupRoles` makes a line earlier.

A registry nothing calls is the failure worth guarding against, so a test asserts both callbacks run it and that they run it after the group roles.


## v3.436.0 - October 29, 2026

### A deep page was fast once and slow every time after

[#123](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/123), a follow-up to #121. The deferred join reads the primary key out of the statement's schema, and a statement's schema is filled when something runs on it. Counting used to fill it incidentally. With the count cache installed, which is what `database.Connect` does on every real project, a cache *hit* counts on a dry-run copy and nothing touches the caller's statement, so the schema was still nil and `fetchPage` fell back to a plain OFFSET.

On 499,975 rows that is 2.4s a page, every time the same deep page is opened twice inside the cache's lifetime. The schema is parsed now rather than inherited from a side effect.

The reporter's own note is the more useful half: "the paginate tests do not install the cache, which is why they pass". Every deferred-join test in the scaffolded file ran without it, which is a configuration no project runs. The test that would have caught this now ships with every project, and was confirmed by putting the bug back.

### Every organization drew invoice numbers from one counter

[#131](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/131). A sequence counter is keyed by name and bucket, and the generated hook passed a fixed name, so on a multitenant project organization A got INV-202610-0001, B got 0002, and A's next invoice was 0003. A sees a gap it cannot explain, and each organization can work out how many invoices the others issue.

Gap-free numbering per business is a legal requirement in many countries, Uganda's EFRIS among them, which is most of what `auto` is for.

On a `--tenant-owned` resource the counter now carries the organization, read from the context rather than the struct so it does not depend on which hook stamps first. It fails closed: with no organization the write is refused, because a number drawn from somebody else's counter is worse than a write that did not happen. Verified with two organizations issuing interleaved: 0001, 0002, 0003 and 0001, 0002, no gaps.


## v3.435.0 - October 29, 2026

### Five reported bugs, all of them invisible from inside the app

Every one of these was reported from a real project with a repro and a cause, and every one of them failed in a way the application could not see.

### A sequence that never resets issued exactly one number

[#132](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/132). With `--reset never` the counter's bucket is the empty string, which is the zero value of the string half of its primary key, and GORM's `Save` treats a zero primary key as a new row. So the second call INSERTed a duplicate and hit the unique constraint, and with the generated `BeforeCreate` hook the second record of that resource could not be created at all. Monthly and yearly counters have a non-empty bucket, which is why only "never" broke. It is an explicit update now, inside the same lock: C-0001, C-0002, C-0003.

### Downloads answered 404 with the file in the body

[#128](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/128). Every generated `/export` through the unversioned `/api` path. The alias is a `NoRoute` handler, so gin has already set the writer to 404 on the way in, and `HandleContext` does not reset it. A handler answering with `c.JSON` sets its own status and was fine; the export handler sets headers and streams the CSV, so the first write flushed the leftover 404. axios rejected the download as an error and a browser saved a failed request. Verified on a running API: 200 on both paths, same bytes.

### No browser could use optimistic locking

[#124](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/124). `If-Match` was missing from the CORS allow-list, so the preflight stripped it and the write was never sent: no status, no log line, and a bare `TypeError: Failed to fetch` in the page, which is also what a lost connection looks like. The same call worked under curl.

Allowing it is half the fix. Cross-origin JavaScript can only read a response header named in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, and there was no such header at all, so a client could not read the `ETag` that carries the version it must send back. `ETag`, `Deprecation` and `Link` are exposed now, with an `ExposeResponseHeader` to extend the list the way `AllowRequestHeader` already does.

### The SMTP driver threw away a Message-ID

[#122](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/122). `Message-Id` is in `reservedHeaders`, so the MIME builder always wrote a generated one, while the API drivers passed the caller's through. The same `mail.Message` therefore kept its id on Resend and lost it on SMTP. An app that stores the id to match replies by `In-Reply-To` stored one that was never sent.

A caller-set id is kept when it is well formed, and generated otherwise. Well formed means `<local@domain>` with no CR or LF: a header value carrying either is header injection, so a malformed one is replaced rather than written.

### Every accent tint on the desktop app rendered as nothing

[#126](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/126). Tailwind 3 cannot apply an opacity to a colour given as a bare CSS variable: it emits no rule at all for `bg-accent/10`. The class was on the element, the variable was set, and the stylesheet held nothing. The scaffold tints the accent 25 times: the sidebar's active item, the avatar, badges, the command palette's selected row, table selection, filter chips.

`text-accent-fg` was used on three accent fills and never defined, so every primary button kept the inherited dark text on a dark purple fill. Both are fixed, in the config `grit new --desktop` writes and in the separate one `grit new-desktop` writes, because a fix in one of two copies is how a bug comes back. ### The web app has no tailwind.config.ts

The frontend page showed a Tailwind 3 config: a TypeScript default export with content globs and `require("tailwindcss-animate")`. Scaffolded projects are on Tailwind 4, which is configured in CSS. Anyone following that page created a file Tailwind ignores. Twenty-nine paths are deliberately left: they are tutorials telling you to *create* a file, and pointing those at existing framework files would be wrong. Telling a stale claim from an instruction needs the prose read one page at a time, and `docs/AUDIT.md` says where to start.

### Em dashes, on a ratchet

Banned in this project's writing, and there were 3,457 of them. A check that simply fails on the first run is a check somebody disables, so `docs/scripts/check-em-dashes.py` holds a budget per area and fails when an area goes *up*. The rule is enforceable today and the backlog can only shrink.

It cannot be a find and replace. An em dash does several jobs: an appositive wants a colon, a consequence wants a comma and a conjunction, an independent clause wants a full stop, and a *pair* of them wants commas or brackets and is ruined by a colon. A lone one in a table cell is not punctuation at all, it means "no value", and the checker ignores those 32.

The site title went first, since it is the browser tab and the search result, then the pages a new reader hits before any other: quick start, create a project, project structure, troubleshooting. 2,735 remain outside the changelog, which is excluded because rewriting past entries is rewriting history.


## v3.429.0 - October 29, 2026

### Cross-tenant reads through Scan, in the multitenant plugin

** If your project uses the multitenant plugin, update it: ** `grit plugin update multitenant`. The plugin reports 1.0.1 once you have the fix; 1.0.0 is affected.

`RegisterScoping` installed the organization filter on GORM's Query, Update, Delete and Create callbacks. GORM has a fifth processor, Row, and it is the one `Scan` goes through:

` func (db *DB) Scan(dest any) *DB { ... tx.Rows() ... } ` ` func (db *DB) Rows() (*sql.Rows, error) { tx.callbacks.Row().Execute(tx) } `

So `db.Model(&Order{}).Scan(&out)` on a tenant-owned model ran with no organization filter and returned every organization's rows. `Find`, `First` and `Pluck` were all scoped correctly, and that is what hid it: the ordinary reads behave, and only the aggregate paths leak.

Which is the bad case, because the aggregates are what the admin shows. The generated per-resource insights use `Scan` twice, in `paginate/insights.go`: once for the time series and once per breakdown column. On a tenant-owned model, an organization's own insights counted every organization's rows.

The fix is one callback. `scope` was already generic, so it does the right thing on Row unchanged. Raw SQL has no parsed schema and stays unscoped, exactly as before: `db.Raw(...).Scan(...)` is still yours to filter, and there is now a test pinning that so the two are never confused.

Four regression tests ship with the plugin, so they run in your project against your copy of the scoping: Scan, Rows, an insights-shaped grouped count, and raw SQL staying unscoped.

** Reported privately by [daljo25](https://github.com/daljo25) ** , who found it while testing an organization switcher in their own project and asked that it be treated as a user report rather than an expert finding. It was correct in every particular: the missing callback, the Scan path, and the insights queries as the place it shows. Thank you.

Twenty places where a chapter's code used something a later chapter teaches, and the prose never mentioned it. Chapter 4 uses structs, slices, interfaces, errors.Is and defer before any of their chapters; chapter 7 reaches for sync.Mutex, which is eight chapters away.

## v3.421.0 - October 29, 2026

### The spinner never span

Reported as the scaffolder hanging on "Go dependencies" for half an hour, and the report was right about everything except the cause.

`Stepper.Start` drew `Frames()[0]` once. Nothing ever drew the second frame. Two files carried a comment saying "the step that is running animates", and it had never been true. At 600ms a stage nobody noticed. On a cold Go module cache the dependency stage really does take minutes, and a motionless glyph over a silent terminal is indistinguishable from a dead process.

It animates now, counts the seconds once there are two of them, and says what it is doing: `Go dependencies downloading github.com/gin-gonic/gin (23)`. Those lines were always there. `go mod tidy` prints one per module to stderr and the scaffolder was calling `CombinedOutput()`, which swallows every byte until the command is over and then throws them away unless it failed.

Nothing here makes the download faster. Measured on a cold cache, an API-only project spends 283 seconds in that stage, and that time is Go's, over whatever connection you have. A scaffolder that quietly changed your GOPROXY to improve the number would be a worse tool than a slow one. The bug was the silence.

### brand.css: somewhere to put your own colours

Giving an app its own accent meant editing `globals.css`, which Grit owns and rewrites on every upgrade. The manifest guard then held that file back for ever: the app kept its colours, stopped receiving every later fix to the same file, and was told so on every upgrade. Ten blueprints were about to hit this at once.

Every frontend now has `app/brand.css` (or `src/brand.css` on Vite): created once, never written again, deliberately absent from the manifest, and imported after `globals.css` so what it sets wins. It ships with every rule commented out, so a project that never opens it renders identically.

Four uncommented lines turn a scaffolded app WhatsApp green, logo and buttons and icons, in both modes, while globals.css keeps arriving with fixes.

### The CLI and the website are one palette again

The brand violet already matched. Five of the other six roles had drifted: close enough to look deliberate, far enough to be two palettes. The comparator that was meant to stop this held two hex strings copied out of `globals.css`, covered the accent alone, and a copy is the thing that drifts.

It reads `docs/app/globals.css` now, for every text role. `muted` and dark `warning` moved onto the site's tokens exactly. Four values cannot: the site holds its colours to two backgrounds, its own, and the CLI holds them to nine, because a terminal has no zoom and no high-contrast mode. Each exception carries the measured ratio that forced it, and the test now fails if an exception becomes unnecessary.

`opts.IncludeDesktop` was never set during an upgrade. The line directly above it does exactly this for Expo. `injectBefore` is idempotent against the lines directly above its own marker, which is the right question for a snippet that may legitimately repeat and the wrong one for `x := ...`: that can exist once in a scope. It now refuses to inject a short variable declaration the file already declares, names it, and carries on rather than failing the install.

It moved twice yesterday and was still not at the end: plugins are updated by the command after `Upgrade()` returns, and a plugin rewrites routes.go. That is how the storefront was told its API compiled and then had a duplicate declaration injected into it.

Blueprints is in the documentation navbar too. It was on the marketing header and nowhere inside /docs, which is where a reader actually is.
