** Every generated project shipped Grit's description of itself as its own meta description. ** The tag read &ldquo;A full-stack framework that combines Go backend with Next.js frontend. Build fast, ship faster&rdquo;, and it is the sentence a search result and a link preview read out under your project's name. It now names the project.

The home page under it was fixed a while ago, and the `<head>` above it was missed, which is the shape this keeps taking: the visible half gets corrected and the half that only a crawler reads does not. `TestRootLayoutMetaDescriptionIsAboutTheProject` now sits beside the home page's test and fails on the exact string that shipped.

Existing projects take it on `grit upgrade`, which already rewrites the root layout. The `<meta name="generator" content="Grit">` tag stays: it is the convention every static site generator uses, it carries no version, and the comment beside it says how to delete it.

Found by opening the WhatsApp blueprint and reading its front page, which is the only way this class of thing gets found.

### grit upgrade tells you when it has broken your build

** An upgrade can leave a project that does not compile, and until now it did not say so. ** Upgrading that same blueprint from 3.306.0 produced four compiler errors from three separate causes, and reported success. The next command somebody types is the one that tells them.

`grit upgrade` now ends by running `go build ./...` and printing what broke, where, and that the previous files are in `.grit/backups`. It fixes nothing: telling the truth at the end of an upgrade is the whole job. A missing Go toolchain or a build that runs long is reported as &ldquo;could not check&rdquo;, never as a failure.

The reason this class exists at all: `internal/config/config.go` is yours, not the framework's, so every field added to it since your project was scaffolded arrives through an anchored repair. The file that *uses* the field is framework-owned and gets rewritten regardless. A repair whose anchor has drifted warns and moves on, and the warning scrolls past in a thousand-line upgrade.

Four of them are fixed where they were caused:

- The auto-ban config repair anchored on a `SentinelTurnstileSecret` field that older projects never had. It falls back to the end of the struct and the end of the loader's literal, which are there whatever the fields have done since.
- The auto-ban worker repair added a `*services.SecurityAutoBan` field without adding the import (`undefined: services`), wrote its half-applied result when an anchor was missing, and, because its guard was a string only the missing half carried, declared the handler again on every later upgrade. It is all-or-nothing now, imports what it names, and the module path comes off a sibling import rather than a guess.
- The Sentinel exempt-list repair returned early on a project with neither list, reasoning that nothing would miss them. routes.go names both and is rewritten from the template every time, so such a project got two undefined fields. It adds both.
- The Pulse profiling repair anchored on `resolveSQLitePath(getEnv("PULSE_STORAGE_DSN"` , and `repairSQLitePath`, which is what wraps that line in `resolveSQLitePath`, ran seventy lines later. One upgrade left the project broken and a second one fixed it, which is not a thing anybody does. The order is swapped, with a comment saying it is load-bearing.

**And two writers the upgrade never called at all.** `writeTOTPFiles` and `writeSecurityObservabilityFiles` ran when scaffolding a new project and nowhere else, so everything they own was frozen at whatever version a project started on: the two-factor models and service, the security and observability handlers, the Sentinel and Pulse bridge, its poller, and the ban sweep itself. Other paths kept refreshing the code that calls them, which is how it surfaced, as `s.Bridge.SentinelPost undefined` and `pending.CodeHash undefined`. Both are delivered on upgrade now, and two tests hold it: one that the ban sweep only calls bridge methods the bridge template defines, and one that upgrade calls both writers.

The build check exists because the seventh one will not be in that list. An anchor is a guess about a file somebody else owns, and guesses go stale.

Also: the upgrade runs `go mod tidy` for you. It adds the modules its new files import to go.mod and left go.sum behind, so `grit migrate` failed with &ldquo;missing go.sum entry&rdquo;. The instruction existed, a few hundred lines up, where it scrolled past. It is printed at the end now, and only when the tidy could not be run, because a check that reports a wall of go.sum errors as a broken build is one people learn to ignore.


## v3.418.0 - October 28, 2026

### Blueprints have a page, a price and a way to buy them

** Every blueprint now has its own page, and the paid ones can be bought. ** $10 buys one blueprint permanently. $20 a month, $200 a year or $400 once buys every one of them, including the ones still on the list. A year costs ten months; lifetime costs two years.

Access is a GitHub repository invitation, and it is automatic. Checkout asks for your GitHub username, and a Stripe webhook adds you as a collaborator, usually within a minute of paying. Ending a membership takes that access back; a single purchase is never revoked, which is what &ldquo;permanently&rdquo; means on the page.

There is no database behind any of it. Stripe is the record of who paid, and both GitHub calls are idempotent (adding a collaborator who is already one changes nothing, removing one who is already gone returns 404), so a redelivered event is harmless. That property is what lets the whole thing be stateless.

**Each page says how to run it.** What has to be on the machine first, the exact commands in order, what each one does, where to open it, and which account to sign in as, taken from the blueprint's own README rather than written again. A Go test fails if an available blueprint has no install steps: a page that takes $10 and then does not say what to type is worse than no page.

**And three screenshots each.** Real ones, from the running application with its demo data: each blueprint repository already shipped mockups for its README, and `scripts/blueprint-shots.py` crops and resizes them into the site. A card fans three phone screens or stacks three browser windows; the detail page lays them out flat with captions.

**Ten blueprints in the catalogue**, up from six: Airbnb (an availability calendar that cannot double-book), Notion (a block tree that loads in one query), Udemy (video that has been paid for) and Zendesk (an SLA clock that pauses) join the list. Three are built and seven are named rather than hinted at, so it is obvious which is which.

The CLI prints the same numbers. `grit blueprint info instagram` says what it costs and links to the page that sells it, and `TestBlueprintPricesMatchTheWebsite` compares the Go constants with the website's. A price the CLI prints and a price the checkout charges are two writers for one number, and the drift between them is an argument with a customer holding a screenshot.


## v3.417.0 - October 28, 2026

### A deep page no longer reads the whole table

**Page 20,000 of a list took 1.6 seconds.** `LIMIT 25 OFFSET 499950` makes the database fetch every one of those 499,950 earlier rows *from the table*, not just from the index, and throw them away. An index on the sort column does not help, because the planner still visits the heap for each row it skips. Page 1 was 9ms; the last page of a large list was 1.6s cold, and every &ldquo;go to page&rdquo; click paid it ([grit#121](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/121)).

Past an offset of 1,000, `paginate.List` now fetches a page in two queries: the primary keys first, which touches only the index, then the rows by key. Same page, same order, about a tenth of the time. Shallow pages stay a single query, because below that threshold the extra round trip costs more than the rows OFFSET discards. Nothing to switch on and nothing to configure.

Two queries rather than one join against a subquery, deliberately: your query arrives with its own scopes, conditions and `Preload` chains already set, and reusing it as-is means the second query is exactly the one your handler asked for. It also works unchanged on SQLite.

**It needs a partial index to actually be faster.** The gain depends on the key query being answerable from an index alone, and every generated list carries `deleted_at IS NULL`, so a plain index on the sort columns still visits the table to check it. The [scaling guide](https://gritframework.com/docs/scaling#deep-pages) now says so, with the index to create and the `EXPLAIN` output that tells you whether it worked.

Five tests ship with every project and run against SQLite: a deep page matches the plain OFFSET query row for row across three sort orders, the pages partition the table with no row repeated or missing, preloads arrive on a deep page, a filter applies to both queries, and a page past the end is empty. The preload one is not hypothetical. The first implementation shared the caller's GORM statement, so clearing preloads for the key query cleared them for the row query too and every association came back empty; that test is what caught it.


## v3.416.0 - October 28, 2026

### Two reported bugs, light mode, and the CLI finally looks like the website

**Every Google sign-in created a user called &ldquo;User&rdquo;.** The scaffold called goth's `google.New` with no scopes, and goth falls back to `["email"]` when none are given. With only that, Google returns no name and no picture, so the callback : which was always written to copy them : had nothing to copy and fell through to its placeholder. Anything listing people showed a column of &ldquo;User&rdquo;. New projects ask for `profile` as well, and `grit upgrade` adds it to an existing one ([grit#120](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/120)).

**`docker compose up` could not pull MinIO.** MinIO took their image off Docker Hub, so Grit moved to `quay.io/minio/minio`; Quay now answers 401 for it even with an anonymous pull token. A fresh machine got a registry error that says nothing about which part of the project is wrong. Compose now uses a pinned image that still pulls without a login, and a test resolves it against the registry on every run, because this has broken twice and both times only a user found out ([grit#109](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/109)). Local development needs none of it: `STORAGE_DRIVER=local` writes to disk and starts no container.

**Light mode.** The design system's component CSS hard-codes thirteen dark colours. Nine are deliberate, because a terminal stays dark in both themes so a screenshot of one is stable. Four were not: the rails, the grid, the dot field and the highlight gradient are atmosphere, and atmosphere in near-black reads as a cage on a white page. The gradient was the worst, starting at a near-white that made the first half of every emphasised phrase invisible.

**The CLI was still cobalt.** You ran `grit new`, watched a blue CLI scaffold your project, then opened a violet website about it. `internal/ui` carries the website's accent now, and the contrast claim it has always made in a comment is a test: every text role against the nine terminal backgrounds it names. It found a violation on its first run, in a colour nobody had touched.

**Blueprints have a page.** The registry has pointed at `gritframework.dev/blueprints` since it shipped, and that URL was a 404. Plugins and Blueprints are both in the nav now, and `/docs/plugins` : which was a page about optional Go modules, a different thing from the plugin system : redirects to the marketplace.


## v3.415.0 - October 28, 2026

### Three reported bugs, a worked example on every plugin page, and a way to see how far behind a project is

**A batch insert panicked.** The multitenant plugin's stamp callback reached straight for GORM's `Statement.ReflectValue`, which is a struct for `Create(&row)` and a slice for `Create(&rows)`. Passing a slice to `field.Set` panics inside reflect rather than returning an error, so a batch insert of any tenant-owned model took the process down: an import, a join table, any hand-written code doing the ordinary thing. It handles both now, and dereferences pointer elements so a slice of pointers works too ([grit#117](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/117)).

**A record page showed a dash where a name should be.** A belongs_to column is generated with a dotted key, `board.name`, because the API returns the related object rather than a flattened field. The list table resolved it and the record page did not, so on a CRM a deal's page showed a dash for Pipeline, Stage, Contact, Company and Owner while the list beside it showed all five. Nothing failed: a missing nested property is undefined, and undefined renders as a dash. The resolver now lives in one place that both surfaces import ([grit#118](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/118)).

**A date read "just now".** Both `date` and `datetime` columns were formatted relative to the current moment, so a calendar date with no time showed "just now" today and "18h ago" yesterday, on a column whose own form field said `date`. The deeper problem was two choosers disagreeing: the one `grit sync` uses for hand-written models had always told dates from timestamps. They share one rule now, and a test asserts they agree ([grit#119](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/119)).

**Every plugin page now carries a worked example.** The marketplace sends people to a plugin's page to find out how to use it, and those pages only said what each plugin was. All nine have a step-by-step run through on a real project, each step with the command and what it actually does, and a Related plugins block where every entry says why it is related rather than just naming it.

Writing them found a hole in the CLI's own documentation indexer. It only extracted arrays a page rendered with `.map(`, so a page rendering its data through a shared component was invisible to `grit docs search` while looking perfectly fine in a browser. It recognises the prop form too now.

**grit versions** is new. `grit doctor` warns when something is wrong, which means it is silent about everything that is merely old. Somebody deciding whether to bring an existing project up to a newer Grit needs the opposite: the whole picture, including the parts that are fine, because what they are weighing is the size of the move rather than any one fault. It prints the project's Grit version against this CLI's, every library the generated API mounts (Sentinel, Pulse, GORM Studio and the rest) against the version this CLI expects, and every installed plugin. Each line reads current, behind, ahead or absent, and a behind line says why the newer version matters. It changes nothing; `grit upgrade` is what raises them.


## v3.414.0 - October 28, 2026

### A Kanban board you can install, and the marketplace to find it in

`grit plugin add kanban` gives a project boards, columns and cards, with dragging by pointer, by finger and by keyboard. It is also the worked example the [authoring guide](https://gritframework.com/docs/plugins/authoring) is now written around, because a board turns out to be the smallest feature that needs every part of the plugin system at once: models and migrations, a service with real logic, routes, React Query hooks, two admin pages, a nav entry, an npm dependency, and injections into six existing files.

**The part worth stealing is the ordering.** An integer `position` column is the obvious design and the wrong one. Moving a card means rewriting every card below it, two people dragging at once interleave those rewrites, and on Postgres the two statements can deadlock outright because they touch the same rows in opposite orders. Gap numbering only delays it. So a rank here is a string compared lexicographically, with fractional indexing to guarantee room between any two, and a move writes exactly one row. Verified on a running board: three cards appended as `a0`, `a1`, `a2`, and dragging the last to the top changed that one card to `Zz` and left the other two alone. Ten thousand appends leave the key four characters long.

The algorithm is embedded from a real Go file rather than held in a string, so the bytes a project receives are the bytes Grit's own tests run. A plugin that keeps its algorithm in a string literal has no tests for what it ships: the string compiles nowhere until somebody installs it.

**Two faults the build found.** `WIPLimit` became the column `w_ip_limit`, not `wip_limit`, because GORM looks for known initialisms anywhere in a field name and IP is on its list. The struct reads fine, AutoMigrate is happy, and the only thing that breaks is a write by column name, in a handler, in production. The column is pinned now, and a test checks every model every plugin emits, not just this one.

And the board landed three clicks deep under System, Extensions, because `SYSTEM_NAV` was the only anchor a plugin had and it has not rendered in the sidebar rail since v3.102.0. `grit:nav:content` is the anchor for a working surface: it renders beside the resources, where somebody would look for their board. Existing projects get it from `grit upgrade`, and the template and the repair splice the same constants so a repaired sidebar and a scaffolded one cannot drift apart.

**Four new documentation pages.** [Four ways to extend](https://gritframework.com/docs/extending) is the one that was missing: Grit has four mechanisms for adding to a project and nothing said which one a given job needs. Each has a unit. A resource is a noun, a plugin is a feature, a Grit UI block is a component, a blueprint is a whole application. It also names the trap: `grit ui add` gives presentation with nothing behind it, so adding a board that way leaves you with a board that displays nothing and saves nothing, which is worse than having no board because it looks finished.

The [marketplace](https://gritframework.com/docs/plugins/marketplace) lists official, Go module and community plugins; [blueprints](https://gritframework.com/docs/blueprints) does the same for the complete applications. Both hold a hand-maintained copy of a list the Go code owns, because a Next page cannot import a Go registry, so each has a test comparing them in both directions: a plugin that is registered but missing from the page fails, and a page advertising a plugin that does not exist fails too.

**Community plugins.** `grit plugin add github.com/someone/grit-calendar` now works, with the source named and confirmed before anything is cloned. Nothing from the repository is executed: Grit reads its `plugin.json` and writes the files that manifest names, which is the same trust surface as a local directory plugin. `grit plugin submit` prints the three-command checklist and the submission link, and the third command is the one people skip: the build *after* `grit plugin remove`, which is the only thing that proves the lockfile recorded everything the install did.

Also: `grit blueprint list` and `grit blueprint info`, next to `grit plugin list` and `grit ui list`.


## v3.413.0 - October 27, 2026

### A security dashboard you can act from, and a sweep that bans the addresses that keep attacking

The Security page used to show three numbers, an explainer for an escalation policy, and the ten most recent threats. Two of its panels could not show anything at all: `rate_limited_last_hour` was hard-coded to zero and `rate_limit_hits_5min` to an empty array, so the page always said there had been no rate limiting, whatever had happened. The threat log was unfiltered, unsearchable and ten rows long, which on a real deployment is a log of 18,000 rows read ten at a time.

It reads the whole of Sentinel now, through six new endpoints: the graded score with what the grades mean, threats and unique addresses and critical and blocked counts over 24 hours, the hourly shape of them, what is being tried and against which routes and by whom over seven days, the threat log filtered by severity and searched by address or path and paged, and who is banned with the way back out. The fake panels are gone rather than renamed.

**The sweep.** Sentinel's own auto-block answers a burst: ten high-severity threats from one address inside ten minutes. It cannot answer patience, and patience is what most scanning actually is. Four an hour for a week never trips that rule. So every six hours a scheduled job counts each address's high-severity threats over the last day and bans the ones over the line, which is more than three by default. Both numbers are settings (`SECURITY_AUTO_BAN_MIN_THREATS`, `AUTO_BAN_INTERVAL_HOURS`), and the same sweep is behind the dashboard's **Ban high-threat IPs** button, because a schedule only sees what arrives after it is switched on and the log it is switched on in front of is usually already full.

**High severity only**, deliberately. An actor's total threat count includes every low-severity heuristic it ever tripped, so banning on that number is how a dashboard starts refusing real users. Loopback and the private ranges are never banned, for the same reason auto-block exempts them: behind a proxy Sentinel has not been told to trust, every request carries the proxy's address.

**Two faults in Sentinel were found building this** and are filed rather than worked around quietly ( [sentinel#44](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/sentinel/issues/44)). `top_attack_types` is populated by the in-memory store and by none of the persistent ones, so on SQLite, Postgres or MySQL it is always empty; the attack-type panel sums the trend buckets instead. And `ListActors` ignores `sort_by` in every store, so asking for the busiest addresses returned the most recent ones; the ranking is done here. Both workarounds say which issue they are waiting on.

A third fault was ours and nearly shipped. Sentinel stores severities capitalised, and the first version of the sweep asked for `severity=high`. It matched nothing, scanned zero threats against a log holding eleven, and logged that no address was over the threshold, which is indistinguishable from a quiet week. A test now reads the severity words out of Sentinel's own source and fails if they stop agreeing.

`grit upgrade` carries all of it to an existing project: the configuration, the routes, the cron entry, the task type, the worker and both call sites of `cron.New`, which gained a parameter. The anchors match a gofmt-formatted file rather than the template, because gofmt aligns struct fields into columns and an anchor copied from the template matches the template and not one real project.

Two smaller things found on the way. A wrong name passed to the template loader panics half way through `grit new`, and nothing checked the call sites against the files, only the files against themselves; a test now checks all 96 of them, with a "did you mean" for the missing extension that causes it. And the inline-control budget test could panic instead of failing, on an apostrophe inside a JSX tag, which took the package down without saying what it had been measuring.


## v3.412.1 - October 27, 2026

### A new project passes its own lint, and the avatar cropper can be used without a mouse

A fresh `--triple` scaffold failed `pnpm lint` on an admin component nobody had touched, so the first push of a new project failed the CI that `grit new` had just written for it. Reported as [#116](https://github.com/MUKE-coder/grit/issues/116).

The crop area was a `div` carrying `tabIndex={0}` and `role="group"`, which says the element is not interactive, so Biome refused the tab stop. Its offered fix was to delete the tab stop, which would have left the cropper unusable without a pointer. The reporter said so, and was right.

The honest fix was to stop pretending a `div` is a control. **The keyboard path is three native range inputs**, Size, Horizontal and Vertical, below the picture. A range input announces its name, its value and its bounds without being told to, moves by its step on an arrow key, and is understood by every assistive technology. The old arrow-key handler moved the crop and said nothing about where it had got to; these report it. Dragging the circle is unchanged, and the Size control still grows from the middle, so the part you framed stays framed.

The same component had a second fault the report did not mention. Its four corner handles were real `<button>` elements with labels like "Resize from the top left" and **no keyboard handler at all**, so the keyboard tour of the dialog was four buttons that announced a job they could not do. They are pointer affordances now, out of the tab order, and the sliders are the way through.

**The reason this shipped is the part worth fixing.** Grit's CI scaffolds projects and builds every frontend, and a build says nothing about Biome's accessibility rules: Next compiles the broken markup happily. The nightly canary now runs each generated app's own `lint` script, the one a user runs, across the scaffold matrix. A unit test asserts the same property where it is cheap, so a regression fails `go test` rather than waiting for the night.


## v3.412.0 - October 27, 2026

### An address that keeps attacking is blocked, and a stored file is not mistaken for one

Sentinel v2.8.0, adopted. Two things in it, and a third that had to be fixed before either could ship safely.

**Every env-file probe is detected again.** Sentinel matched `/.env` but had stopped matching `/sendgrid.env` and `/laravel.env` in v2.4.0, and prefixed names are most of what a scanner actually asks for.

**Auto-block is on outside development.** Ten threats of High severity or worse from one address inside ten minutes bars that address for a day. It acts on what the address has done to your application rather than on a third party's opinion of it, which is the only thing that catches a scanner nobody has reported yet, and it counts through the same Redis counters as the rate limits, so threats spread over replicas add up to one total and a block made anywhere holds everywhere. The severity floor matters: High is what the scanner patterns score, so ordinary odd traffic does not accumulate towards a block.

**Loopback and the private ranges are never auto-blocked**, and this is the part that is Grit's rather than Sentinel's. Auto-block bars an address, and an address is only the attacker's when Sentinel is reading the real client. Behind a reverse proxy it has not been told to trust, every request carries the proxy's address instead, and `SENTINEL_TRUSTED_PROXIES` is empty by default because trusting a forwarded header you have not configured is worse. On a deployment where Caddy, Traefik, nginx or an ingress terminates TLS and that variable was never set, ten probes through the proxy would have barred the proxy: every user, for a day, from one scanner. Turning auto-block on without this would have been a worse bug than the one it fixes. Set `SENTINEL_TRUSTED_PROXIES` and the real client address is read, after which the exemption stops applying to anybody who matters; `SENTINEL_AUTOBLOCK_EXEMPT_IPS` adds your own monitoring and any partner that probes you, and follows the sign-in lockout's exempt list when it is not set, because both answer the same question.

**The local storage route is stepped aside.** Detecting env probes anywhere in a path is correct for a scanner and wrong for a file somebody stored: the local driver serves an object under the key it was uploaded with, and a field that accepts anything keeps the original extension, so a stored `config.env` is a real path the app has to answer. In production the WAF blocks, so that object would have started answering 403 on an upgrade that changed nothing anyone could see. The route is excluded from WAF inspection and nothing is given up by it: the storage layer refuses a key with a `.` or `..` segment, a backslash, a Windows drive letter or any key resolving outside the disk's root, whether or not the WAF is looking.

The exclusion is listed separately from the API-prefixed paths, because the file route is mounted on the engine rather than under `/api/<version>`. The first attempt put it in the prefixed literal, where it became `/api/v1/files` and matched nothing: dead config, silently, which this file had already produced twice before. A test now reads the route constant out of the storage template and the exclusion out of the routes template and fails if they disagree.

`grit upgrade` carries all of it: the exclusion, the auto-block config, the exempt ranges and the new variable, with the upgraded `wafExcludedRoutes` byte-identical to a freshly generated one. A project whose Sentinel config was hand-edited is left alone and told what to add.


## v3.411.27 - October 27, 2026

### A conditional rule could point at a field that was no longer there

`server_set`, added one release earlier, takes a column out of the create schema. When another field's condition read that column, the refinement generated for it went on saying `v.status === "lost"` for a status that was no longer in the object. That is a TypeScript error, so `@repo/shared` stopped compiling and the build of every app importing it failed.

A refinement is the one validator in a schema that reads a sibling. Every other one sees only its own value, which is why removing a field is harmless to them and fatal to this. Both writers now emit a refinement only for a field the schema actually has.

Dropped rather than kept, because a client that is never sent the field cannot evaluate the condition anyway. The rule itself is not lost: it is on the model as a `requiredif` tag, and `internal/fieldtypes` enforces it on every write that has a model, which is the API, a PATCH, a CSV import and a job. What goes is the inline message on the form, so the generator says so rather than dropping it in silence.

An existing test had been asserting exactly this output, for a condition on a field its own definition did not contain. It was demanding a file that never compiled, so it is fixed too.

Reported from a project built with Grit: grit#115.


## v3.411.26 - October 27, 2026

### A partial update had to send every optional date

`UpdateDealSchema.parse({ title: "New title" })` failed, asking for `expected_close` and `closed_at`. The update schema exists so a PATCH can send only what changed, and it was demanding every optional date on the model.

The rule said to add `.optional()` to every field unless it already had `.optional()` or `.nullable()`, and the documentation stated it that way too. The rule was the bug. `.nullable()` allows the value null, not an absent key, so skipping those fields defeated the partial update the same sentence promised. The docs now say what is true.

The same mistake made an optional date a required key on create: a form that left "expected close" empty had to send `expected_close: null` explicitly or fail. Dates, datetimes, files and rich text were all excluded from the optional suffix on the same reasoning, and all four are fixed.

#### A default now means optional

A field with `default: open` was mandatory on create, although the point of a default is that the server fills it in when the client says nothing. The generator read the default and sync did not, so the two also disagreed, which the parity test did not catch because its fixture had no defaulted field. It has one now.

#### server_set, for the columns a client never sends

A `closed_at` derived by a hook, a `last_activity_at` a service maintains: these were offered as input, so a form asked somebody to type a value the next write would overwrite. Mark the field `server_set: true` and it comes out of create, update and the admin form, the way id and the timestamps already do, while staying in the response and the entity schema.

Reported from a project built with Grit: grit#114.


## v3.411.25 - October 27, 2026

### Six commands the reference did not have

The command explorer presents itself as the complete reference and was missing six: `grit index`, `grit skills`, `grit doctor`, `grit scale`, `grit logs` and `grit docs`. An incomplete reference is a quiet lie, because the reader concludes the command does not exist rather than that it is undocumented.

All six are in now, read from what each one actually does rather than written from memory, and `grit port`, `grit index` and `grit skills` have sections in the cheatsheet with the reasoning, not just the flags.

#### And a warning that had stopped being true

The expert skills said `apps/web` and `apps/admin` have different palettes, and that copying a component between them produces an element that renders nothing. That stopped being true in v3.411.21, when both stylesheets came to be written from one function: the vocabularies are now identical, sixteen token names in each, the same sixteen, checked on a generated project.

Left alone it would have discouraged `grit port`, which is the move it now describes. The old failure is kept as the first thing to check when a ported component does come out invisible, since an older project can still be in that state.


## v3.411.24 - October 27, 2026

### grit index: the indexes the lists actually need

The second half of grit#112. Every generated list is `WHERE <scope> ORDER BY <column>, id`, and nothing created an index in that shape, so the database sorted the whole table on disk for every page. Invisible on a seeded table, and the slowest thing in the product on a real one: 2.3 seconds for one page of 500,000 rows, 16.6 seconds at page 20,000.

`grit index` works out what each list needs and writes the SQL. The three parts are already in the project. The scope first, because it is an equality the planner can seek to: `org_id` for a tenant-owned model, the owner column for an `--owned-by` one, nothing otherwise. Then the sort column. Then `id`, because the tiebreaker shipped in v3.411.21 means an index without that trailing column cannot serve the whole ORDER BY.

Only the default sort by default, which is the one every list request uses when nobody has clicked a column. An index per sortable column is write amplification on tables that are mostly written, and nothing at generation time knows which columns people really sort by, so `--all-sortable` and `--only deal=title,status` are there for when you have a measurement.

It writes SQL and creates nothing. The statements are CONCURRENTLY, which does not lock the table and therefore cannot run inside a transaction, so the file says to apply it with psql rather than through a runner that wraps everything in BEGIN. That is the reason this is not something AutoMigrate does while somebody is using the product.


## v3.411.23 - October 27, 2026

### grit port: the admin's components, in any app

The admin is where the interface work has gone: a table with sorting, filters, bulk actions, export and import, a form builder, the dashboard widgets. A customer portal usually wants some of that, and there was no way to have it. `grit expose table` writes a page with its own eighty line table rather than the admin's, so anybody who wanted the real one built it again, and the project ended up with two tables that behave differently.

`grit port table --to apps/web` copies the real one, and everything it imports, into any app in the project. On a generated triple that is thirteen files: the table, its column header, the cell renderers, the empty and loading states, and the five lib files they reach. The web app type-checks with no edits.

Copied rather than shared, deliberately. A package would mean decoupling every component from next/link, the icon map and the translation hook, adding transpilePackages, and rewriting the imports of every project that already exists. The components are also edited per project, which is the premise of the admin being yours rather than a dependency. What makes the copy cheap is that every Grit frontend uses the same `@/*` alias and the same design tokens, so a file at the same path compiles and is painted correctly with nothing rewritten.

It will not write to your package.json. A package the copied files import that the target does not declare is listed with the command to add it, because a workspace hoists those: the app type-checks today and fails when it is built on its own. A file already in the target is kept rather than replaced, since by then somebody has edited it.

`grit port list` shows the bundles: table, table-full, form, widgets, ui. A path inside the admin works too.


## v3.411.22 - October 27, 2026

### grit-critic

A twenty-second expert skill, and the only one that reviews work it did not write. It takes a feature somebody has marked done, uses it with real-shaped data, reads the backend for the bottleneck, checks that the tests would fail if the code were wrong, looks at the screens at phone width, and reports findings ordered by what each one will cost. It does not tick the box; the person who owns the phase does.

`grit skills` knows about it, which is the part of this release that is code.


## v3.411.21 - October 27, 2026

### A paged list could repeat a row and skip another, and two more experts

A page-numbered list sorted by the requested column and stopped there. Rows that share a value in that column then have no defined order at all, and the database is entitled to return them differently for every query. Postgres does exactly that as soon as the table is big enough to plan a parallel external sort: the order of tied rows depends on which worker finished first.

What that looks like from outside is not an error. It is the same row appearing on page 2 and page 3 while another one is never shown. Measured on 500,000 contacts with repeating names, reported with the query plan attached.

Both list paths now sort by the column and then by id, which is unique, so the ordering is total and identical for every query. The cursor path already did this; the page path did not, and nothing compared them, so they share one function now. `grit upgrade` carries it to an existing project.

The regression test asserts the SQL rather than the rows, which is the interesting part: SQLite returns ties in insertion order, so a test that walks the pages passes whether or not the tiebreaker is there and would have gone on passing through the whole of this bug.

### Two more experts, and the CLI knows about them

`grit skills` carries its own list of the pack, so that `status` works with no network. The list had not moved since the pack was nineteen skills, so two of them were installed and then reported as missing, and the summary line counted wrong.

**grit-tokens** reads Claude Code's own transcripts and says what a project has spent: billable tokens against cache reads, cost at rates you can edit, and a per-tool table separating what a tool put back into the context from what the model wrote to call it. It reads the subagents' transcripts too, which were a quarter of the billable total on the project it was written against. It writes a self-contained HTML page, and can report on a threshold and on every increment.

**grit-advocate** watches a build and files what is worth telling people about as an issue, with the evidence, the channel it suits and a draft. It has a bar that most of a build does not clear, and two rules that keep it honest: every number traces to the run log, the git history or the token report, and no client name or customer data ever reaches a draft.

A new project also ignores `.grit/token-usage.json`, the cache the first of those writes. It holds one machine's usage history and does not belong in a repository.

The pagination bug was reported from a project built with Grit: grit#112.


## v3.411.20 - October 27, 2026

### An upgrade put back a resource you had removed, and on a single project removal barely happened

On a project whose blog had been taken out with `grit remove resource Blog`, `grit upgrade` wrote three of its files back: the seeder, the web hook and the blog API helper. The seeder refers to `models.Blog`, which was gone, so a project that built before the upgrade did not build after it. The files had never been touched by the developer and had been deliberately deleted, and without git nothing said which command had done it.

Those three are written from the scaffold's own file maps rather than by the generator, so removal knew about them and the upgrade did not. The upgrade now drops the blog example's files when the project has no `blog.go`, decided in one place and applied by every writer that can emit one, in each architecture. Keyed on the model rather than on a record of the removal, because a model deleted by hand leaves exactly the same hole.

#### And the other side of it

Checking that fix turned up the same fault facing the other way. `grit remove resource` spelled two of its roots as `apps/api` and `apps/web`. A single keeps its Go code in `api/` and is itself the frontend, so on one of those the command deleted two files out of ten, left the model, the handler, the service, the seeder and the hook where they were, and printed &ldquo;removed successfully&rdquo;. It reads the architecture from `grit.json` now, like everything else does.

#### --plan is not a dry run

Its help read like one, and somebody ran it on a project with no git expecting to be shown what would happen. It has always upgraded as well as writing the runbook. The help says so now, and the command prints a line before it writes anything pointing at `--diff`, which is the flag that looks without touching.

Reported from a project built with Grit: grit#111.


## v3.411.19 - October 27, 2026

### A rebuild could leave the old server answering, and say so in one line

On Windows, a hot reload sometimes left the previous server running and still serving. The new one printed `bind: Only one usage of each socket address`, exited, and the old code kept answering every request as though nothing had happened. The edit was simply not live, and the only symptom was that it did not work. One developer lost an afternoon to a route that resolved to an older one.

#### Why air cannot fix this

air starts the binary through PowerShell, so the process it tracks is PowerShell rather than the server, and it stops the old one with `TASKKILL /F /T` on that pid. When PowerShell has already gone, the server underneath it is an orphan with no parent to be found through, and the kill misses it. air then rebuilds happily, because Windows lets the linker replace the image of a running process, and the new server binds a port the orphan still holds.

The obvious settings do not help. `kill_delay` is read only in air's Unix kill path and only when `send_interrupt` is on, and on Windows air logs that send_interrupt is unsupported and runs TASKKILL. That code is identical in the pinned version and the latest, so upgrading air changes nothing either. The fix had to be in the server.

#### Two changes

The port is bound before the database connects and before a single route is registered, so a port already in use is the first thing printed rather than the last. The message says what is actually happening, that your API is still answering with the code from before your edit, and gives the two commands to find and stop whatever holds the port.

And in development the new build asks whoever holds the port to step aside, over HTTP, on `POST /api/dev/step-aside`. A Grit server recognises the request and shuts down gracefully, draining its workers on the way out; anything else answers 404 and is left alone. Nothing is killed and no process id is guessed, which is the point: working out which pid owns a port and killing it means being wrong occasionally, and being wrong means killing something somebody else was using. The endpoint is mounted only when `APP_ENV` is a development value, and answers only on loopback.

`grit upgrade` applies both to an existing project, and updates `.air.toml` to interrupt rather than kill the old server, which is worth having on macOS and Linux where air does honour it. A main.go that has been edited away from what Grit wrote is left alone and says why.

Reported from a project built with Grit: grit#110.


## v3.411.18 - October 27, 2026

### grit sync wrote a weaker schema over the one the generator wrote

Two writers produced the Zod schema for a resource and nothing compared them. `grit generate resource` wrote it from the definition, which knows every rule. `grit sync` then rewrote the same file from the Go model, and sync is the documented step after generating, so sync's file is the one projects kept.

It was the weaker of the two in nine ways at once. Money became `z.unknown()`. A select became `z.string()` with its values gone. A foreign key lost `.uuid()`, a required string lost `.min(1)`, and the formatted types lost the shared schemas that trim, lowercase and bound them. A field required only while another field holds a value became required always. The slug and the owner column, both filled by the server, were asked for. And `version` was required on create although it travels as an ETag and the service drops it from the body. A create form validated with that schema could not be submitted at all.

#### Sync no longer decides

The fix is not a second set of rules in sync. The Go model already carries what it needs, so sync now reconstructs the field each column was generated from and hands it to `Field.ZodType()`, the emitter the generator uses. The create and update schemas it writes are byte-for-byte the ones the generator wrote.

Two columns the model could not describe now describe themselves. A slug carries `slug:"title"`, naming the column it is derived from, and the owner of an `--owned-by` resource carries `owner:"true"`. A third was missing entirely: a required number or money column carries `required:"true"`, because gin's `binding:"required"` rejects 0 and false and has never been safe to put on one.

There is a test that generates a resource with all thirty field types and fails on any field where the two writers disagree. The nine bugs are not the point; the tenth not being addable to one writer alone is.

#### Found while fixing it

The public form-share reader had the same fault from the same cause. It skipped a slug column only when it was literally called `slug`, read required from `binding` alone so every required number said optional, and offered `archived_at` to the person filling in the form, which is the fault grit#101 fixed in the admin and nobody looked for here.

Reported from a project built with Grit: grit#108.


## v3.411.17 - October 26, 2026

### A header the browser was never allowed to send, and a theme that stopped at the page

Two bugs that look unrelated and share a shape: a value resolved once, at the top, for a thing that happens further down.

#### The CORS allow list is a list

The multitenant plugin tells clients to send the active organization as `X-Organization-ID`, and did not add that header to the allow list in `internal/middleware/cors.go`. The preflight succeeded and the browser then declined to send the real request: no status, no log line, an axios network error with nothing behind it, and the same call working perfectly under curl. It waited for a second organization to appear, because until then the API picks the only one without being told.

The allow list was a string literal written straight into the response, which made every new request header a thing somebody had to remember. It is a list now, with `middleware.AllowRequestHeader` to add to it from an `init()`. The plugin registers its header from `internal/middleware/tenant.go`, the file that reads it, so `grit plugin remove multitenant` takes the header out by deleting that file. Nothing has to find a line in cors.go again.

`grit upgrade` reshapes an existing project's list and keeps every header already in it, including ones added by hand. Installing the plugin on a project that has not been upgraded stops before writing anything and says which command to run, rather than leaving behind a `tenant.go` that does not compile.

#### A theme scoped to a surface now repaints

The `midnight` palette says you can opt a single surface into it by putting `data-theme` on that element. You could not. Tailwind declares the `@theme` mappings on `:root`, and a custom property that references another one is resolved where it is declared, so a section that redefined `--bg-primary` inherited a `--color-background` that had already been resolved at the root: the tokens changed and `bg-background` did not.

The mappings are re-declared for a nested `data-theme`, `.dark` or `data-theme-mode="dark"`, so they resolve against that element's own tokens and its children inherit the result. Both stylesheets, from one writer: they were already the same nineteen lines in the admin's sheet and the web app's, and this is the second thing in a row that had to be written twice to be right once.

Reported from a project built with Grit: grit#107 and grit#98.


## v3.411.16 - October 26, 2026

### Web sign-in could not finish for a 2FA account, and social sign-in landed on a 404

For an account with two-factor authentication on, the API answers a correct password with a pending token and no user. The web login page did not look, so it set the cached user to `undefined`, stamped the session marker and sent the person to the home page. The password was accepted, nothing was signed in, and nothing said so.

The admin had handled this for a while, with a comment on the guard saying the unguarded read "is what used to break". The fix never reached the web template, which is the recurring shape of these: one of the two apps learns something and the other does not.

The web login page now has the code step, for an authenticator code or a backup code, with the trust-this-device option, and the session marker is stamped in one place, once there really is a session. `useLogin` guards the challenge and there is a `useVerifyTOTP` beside it.

#### And the OAuth callback disagreed with the API in three ways

It lived at `app/(auth)/callback/`, and `(auth)` is a route group, so it served `/callback` while the API redirects to `/auth/callback`. Every web social sign-in landed on a 404.

It also read `access_token` and `refresh_token` from the query string. The API stopped sending those and sets the HttpOnly cookies itself, so a successful sign-in fell through to the failure branch and reported "Authentication failed". The branch that would have handled them stored them with `Cookies.set`, in the URL and readable by JavaScript, which is the opposite of the policy the rest of the app follows. It was unreachable, and it is deleted rather than left unreachable: dead code that leaks is a leak waiting for somebody to make it reachable again. And it never stamped the session marker, so even a working redirect was bounced by the middleware on the next page.

A project that ran `grit add web-auth` before has the old page at the old path. The command removes it, but only when it is byte-for-byte one it wrote, so a hand-built page there is left alone.

Also from the same report: `grit add web-auth --help` described two files and writes about thirty. It now lists what it writes and says that running it on a project with its own navbar or account pages is a bigger decision than adding two helpers. It also names `OAUTH_FRONTEND_URL`, which decides whether a social sign-in returns to the web app or the admin, and defaults to the admin.


## v3.411.15 - October 26, 2026

### The generator and grit sync wrote the same schema file two different ways

`packages/shared/schemas/<resource>.ts` has two writers. `grit generate` keyed it by the JSON tag; `grit sync` rewrote the same file in camelCase. Whichever ran last decided whether the app worked, because the API decodes with `ShouldBindJSON` against `json:"contact_id"` and simply ignores a payload keyed `contactId`: the field arrives empty and the error names something the form did fill in.

In the project that reported it, six schemas were camelCase and one was snake_case, and the only difference was which command had touched it last.

Sync keys by the JSON tag now, in the entity schema as well as the create and update pair. That was the one doing the most damage, because it is the schema you validate a response against, so it rejected responses the API had just produced. It also skips association structs, which it was emitting as `contact: z.unknown()` beside `contact_id`, and knows the API's own date wrappers rather than falling through to `z.unknown()` for every date column. The same gap was in the generated TypeScript types, so that is fixed too.

#### Two gaps in the generated schema, from the same report

An optional relationship was still a required uuid. After the v3.411.11 fix the Go model and the admin form both knew it was optional and the schema did not, so a form built from it refused to save a deal with no contact.

And a conditionally required field was required unconditionally. `required: true` with `show_when` produced `requiredif` on the model and `requiredWhen` in the admin form, both correct, and a plain required string in Zod, which rejected every row the condition did not hold for. "Required while it is shown" is a predicate, not a flag, so it is optional in the object now with a `superRefine` enforcing the condition, which is the same rule the other two already expressed.

Verified by generating a resource with both shapes, running `grit sync` over it, and type-checking the shared package, the admin and the web app, all clean. One existing test had to change: it asserted the camelCase keys, so it had been holding the bug in place.


## v3.411.14 - October 26, 2026

### grit routes --write, for when the only thing that changed is a guard you wrote

Gating a single action is a hand edit, because `--roles` is per resource rather than per action:

```go
m.Staff.GET("/pipelines/export", middleware.RequireRole("ADMIN", "perm:pipelines.export"), h.Export)
```

That makes `internal/access/registry.go` stale, which `grit doctor` correctly reported. What it then suggested did not fit. `grit upgrade` moves the whole project onto the CLI's templates, which is a much larger decision than refreshing one table. The alternative it offered, `grit generate resource`, rewrites the route file and drops the guard that made the table stale in the first place, so following the advice loses the work that prompted it.

`grit routes` already parsed the route files correctly and showed the right permission. It just never wrote the table. It can now:

```bash
grit routes --write
```

It prints the table as before, then rewrites `internal/access/registry.go` from the same parse, and says whether anything changed rather than claiming work it did not do. `grit generate` and `grit remove` already refresh the table, and `grit upgrade` still refreshes it along with everything else. This is the narrow one. The doctor hint names it.

Verified end to end on a generated project: edit a guard by hand, run `grit doctor`, run exactly what it suggests, and confirm the hand-written permission reaches the table, the edit survives, and the warning clears.


## v3.411.13 - October 26, 2026

### A kept tenant.Unscoped handle leaked conditions and errors into the next statement

`tenant.Unscoped` in the multitenant plugin returned `db.Set(skipKey, true)`, and `Set` hands back GORM's chainable instance rather than a new session. One instance means one `Statement` shared across every call made on it, so a handle kept in a variable carried the previous call's WHERE clause and its error into the next one.

```go
tx = tenant.Unscoped(tx)

var existing models.Organization
tx.Where("slug = ?", slug).Take(&existing)   // ErrRecordNotFound, as expected

return tx.Create(&org).Error                  // also returns "record not found"
```

The `Create` inherits both. Two reads through one handle combine their conditions and match nothing. The one-shot form the doc comment shows, `tenant.Unscoped(db).Find(&all)`, was always fine, and keeping the handle is the natural next step, so this found people who had done nothing wrong and the failure pointed nowhere near scoping. The doc comment also said it returned a session, which it did not.

It returns a real one now, `.Session(&gorm.Session{})`, which is safe to keep and to reuse and leaves the one-shot form unchanged.

Every project with the plugin now ships the reproduction as a test, and that test was written before the fix and watched to fail with the reported symptom, *the create inherited the previous call's error: record not found*, then watched to pass. A second guard in the framework's own tests checks the line is still there, because the failure mode here is somebody tidying away a `Session` call that looks redundant.


## v3.411.12 - October 26, 2026

### The owner of an owned resource is never optional

v3.411.11 made an unmarked `belongs_to` optional, which is right, and swept up the one relationship that must never be: the owner of an `--owned-by` resource. It is stamped from the signed-in caller rather than accepted from the body, every query is scoped by it, and the generated `GetOwnerID()` returns it as a string. Making it a `*string` produced a model that did not compile:

```text
internal/models/note.go:49:9: cannot use m.UserID (variable of type *string) as string value in return statement
```

A nullable owner would also be a row nobody can see, so refusing it is right on its own terms rather than only to keep the compiler quiet. Every other relationship on an owned resource is still optional.

Worth saying where this was caught. The repository's own tests passed, because the thing that breaks is a generated project rather than the generator, and the suite that builds generated projects runs in CI. It is the gate that exists for exactly this, and it did its job within three minutes of the tag.


## v3.411.11 - October 26, 2026

### A relationship can be optional, which it could not be before

A `belongs_to` ignored its own `required` flag. Every foreign key came out `binding:"required"`, so a deal with no contact yet could not be saved, and the obvious workaround is worse than the bug: storing `""` in a key column is refused by Postgres with SQLSTATE 23503 the moment the constraint exists.

Optional relationships are ordinary. A task not tied to a deal, a contact with no company, a deal nobody has assigned yet. Each one had to be hand-written: change the model to a `*string`, add the empty-string-to-NULL conversion in the handler, edit the Zod schema and the admin form to drop `required`.

A non-required `belongs_to` now generates a `*string` with `default:null` and no binding tag, the `optional<X>ID` helper in the handler, `string | null` in the TypeScript type, `.nullable().optional()` in Zod, no `required` in the admin form, and a pointer assignment in the CSV importer. A relationship marked `required: true` is unchanged.

Six surfaces decide this and they each used to decide it separately, which is how it stayed broken: the model said required, the tree code said nullable, and nothing compared them. They now read one predicate. Two of those six were only found by compiling a generated project rather than reading the diff: the service layer compared a pointer to `""`, and the importer assigned a string to it. Neither is visible in the generator.

#### And sync stopped adding a text box for every relationship

`grit sync` read GORM association structs as missing fields. A resource with five `belongs_to` got five duplicate free-text inputs beside the relationship-selects the generator had already written correctly, five duplicate columns, and an editable "Archived at" date. The generated form was wrong the moment it was generated, because generate and sync disagreed about what a field is. Sync now skips anything carrying a `foreignKey` or `many2many` tag, anything that is a slice of a model, and any struct standing beside its own key column, which is how GORM infers an association in a model somebody wrote by hand. `archived_at` joins the bookkeeping columns it already skipped.

Filed as #100 and #101.


## v3.411.10 - October 26, 2026

### The field-types reference had no field types in it

`grit docs show docs/concepts/field-types` printed the page's prose and its section headings and none of its tables. The page calls itself the single source of truth for field mapping, and the four sections that hold that mapping came out empty. `--json` had the same hole.

Which made the one instruction every agent is given before generating a resource, look the type up in the binary rather than recalling it, impossible to follow. The person who reported it had to go and read `internal/generate/field.go` at the matching tag instead, which is exactly the failure the embedded docs exist to prevent.

The cause is worth knowing, because it will happen again. The reference pages render their tables from a `const` array at the top of the file and a `.map()` in the body, so every `<td>` holds `{row.type}` and the content lives in the array. The indexer read `<p>`, `<li>` and `<blockquote>`, and stripped expressions. Nothing failed: the page indexed, it just indexed the commentary and not the content.

The indexer now reads the const arrays a page actually renders and emits each object as a row. Prose and tables get separate budgets, because on a reference page the tables are the content and the prose is the commentary, and sharing one cap let the prose push the flags table off the end, which is the same failure for anybody looking up a flag. The field-types page went from no rows to all six of its tables.

Guarded by a test that asserts the content rather than the mechanism: the page has to carry `money | price:money`, `--owned-by` and the rest, however the index comes to be built. Filed as #99.


## v3.411.9 - October 26, 2026

### Removing the blog leaves a project that compiles and a test suite that does too

`grit remove resource Blog --force` already deleted fourteen files and reversed fourteen injections, and the project built afterwards. Four things were left behind, and the first one is the sort of failure worth describing carefully.

#### The sync engine's tests used the blog model as their fixture

`sync_version_test.go` and `sync_pull_test.go` reached for `models.Blog` because it was there and it had a `Version` field. Nothing in them is about blogs: they exist to prove that a sync update advances a row's version, which is the whole of conflict detection. But it meant deleting the blog resource broke the test package, and it broke it in the worst available way: `go build ./...` still passed and `go test ./internal/handlers/` did not, so a project looked healthy right up until CI ran.

Those tests own their fixture now, a `syncFixture` local to the handlers package. It carries the real `BeforeUpdate` hook rather than a simplified one, because that hook is the thing under test: a full-struct `Save` silently overwrites what `SetColumn` put in the statement, which is the bug those tests were written to catch, and a fixture without it would have passed while proving nothing.

#### And three smaller leftovers

A stale `blogs` entry in the authz catalog, so the role editor offered permissions for a resource that was gone, and then the empty `Publishing` group it left behind. The first pass at that missed the group, because the scaffold explains its built-in features with a comment above them and the comment outlives the feature: a group holding only comments is still empty. An orphaned `// Blog management.` comment above the stats routes. And the WAF body-inspection exclusion still naming `/blogs`, which stays harmless and reads as evidence the resource exists. The `/posts` and `/articles` entries beside it stay, since they are the scaffold's allowance for resources somebody may still add.

Verified the way it was reported: scaffold a triple project, remove the blog, then build, vet and run the handler tests. All three pass, and the only remaining match for "blog" in a generated API is a sample URL path in the field-type examples, which has nothing to do with the resource. Filed as #74.


## v3.411.8 - October 26, 2026

### Development used local disk while MinIO was running, and said MinIO was down

The storage probe asked MinIO on `localhost:9000`. Every project publishes it on `MINIO_PORT`, which defaults to 9002 so that several projects can run at once, so the probe asked a port nothing was listening on, concluded MinIO was down, and fell back to the local disk. The log line even said so: *MinIO at http://localhost:9000 is not answering, so files are being kept on the local disk*. Uploads worked, which is why nobody chased it, and every new project quietly stored files somewhere nobody had chosen.

`resolveMinioEndpoint()` was already in the same file, already doing the right thing: `MINIO_ENDPOINT` wins, otherwise the port follows `MINIO_PORT`. The probe simply did not call it. It does now.

The repair matters as much as the template here, because the project that has this is an existing one. `grit upgrade` was returning early on any project that already had the disk fallback, which is exactly the set of projects carrying the wrong port, so the fix would never have reached them. It now rewrites the probe in place and stays silent on a project that already has the right one.

Reported from a real project with a reproduction and the one-line fix, which is the whole of the diagnosis above. Filed as #97.


## v3.411.7 - October 26, 2026

### grit skills install, because an agent cannot type a slash command

There is a set of Claude skills that build with Grit: a router that reads your project and assigns the work, one expert per architecture, and specialists for resources, the admin panel, design, data, security, performance, deployment and review. They read the docs out of your installed binary rather than from memory, which is the point of them.

Installing them was the problem. They ship as a Claude Code plugin, and `/plugin` is a slash command a person types: it is not reachable from a tool call, and in the VS Code extension it does not exist at all, where it answers `/plugin isn't available in this environment`. So an assistant told to install them had to stop and ask, every time, in the one environment a lot of people work in.

An ordinary command is reachable. `grit skills install` puts them in at user level so every project sees them, and `grit skills install --all` adds the five skills from other projects that the experts use for design research and browser testing and work around when they are missing. `grit skills status` says what is there.

It checks afterwards rather than trusting the exit code. The installer writes to every agent it can find and will report a failure for one of them while succeeding overall, so a green tick based on the exit status would have been a lie roughly as often as it was true. It counts what actually landed, says so when only some arrived, and refuses to claim success when nothing did. It also says up front that a red mark naming an agent you do not use is not your problem, because the output is alarming the first time.


## v3.411.6 - October 26, 2026

### grit docs show works in the shell its own help was written for

`grit docs show /docs/concepts/field-types` is the example the command prints in its help, and in Git Bash on Windows it failed. MSYS rewrites any argument that looks like an absolute POSIX path before the process sees it, so the CLI received `C:/Program Files/Git/docs/concepts/field-types` and answered `no page at ...`, which reads as a missing page rather than a mangled argument.

That matters more than a path bug usually would. Git Bash is the shell most Windows Go developers work in and the one Claude Code uses there, so the one command that exists to stop an agent guessing a field type was the command that did not work. A rewritten path still ends with the page's own URL, so the resolver now recovers it by matching the tail on a segment boundary, and only when exactly one page matches: an ambiguous argument still gets the suggestion list rather than a confident guess. Not anchored on a `docs` segment, because twenty indexed pages are under `/blog`.

#### The Scout dashboard runs the code checks now, in development

Scout v0.4.10 added `WithRepo`, so `grit add scout` hands it the project root and the source findings land in the same scan series as the live ones instead of being reachable only from the CLI. The root is found by walking up for `grit.json` rather than configured, because the answer differs by architecture and by where the binary was started: in production it finds nothing, which is the right outcome.

Scout honours the path only when the environment is dev and logs a line otherwise. That gate was the condition of asking for the feature: a finding quotes the source line it found, so a dashboard reachable in staging or production has no business reading the tree.

The same release skips secrets in test fixtures, which takes a generated project from 73 findings to 66. The seven that went were signing keys in test files, which is not a finding anyone can act on: a test that signs a token has to contain a key, so there is no version of that file without one. The Scout page's breakdown has been re-measured rather than adjusted by arithmetic.


## v3.411.5 - October 26, 2026

### The Scout page explained the checks and never said how to run one

It covered `grit add scout`, the four settings, what each of the fifty-four checks looks for and how the access table makes the route checks possible. It did not say what to do next. There is now a **Running a scan** section, and it leads with the thing that was actually confusing: there are two scans, they look at different things, and neither does the other one's job.

The mounted dashboard at `/scout/ui/` scans your app as it is running, over HTTP: headers, cookies, TLS, DNS, files that should not be served, default credentials, and the route-table checks. It scans when you press the button, because Grit mounts Scout with no schedule, and every run is kept so the next one can be diffed against it. The CLI with `--repo` scans your source tree instead, which is where the `code.*` checks live: hard-coded secrets, dangerous sinks, unpinned and vulnerable dependencies. That one needs nothing running, which is why it is the one for CI.

The section gives the commands for both, for the CI gate (`--fail-on` with `--new-only`, which is the pair that works on a project that already has findings), for the diff, and for SARIF if GitHub code scanning is reading the output. It also explains what unlocks the aggressive modes, which was previously stated only as a rule: an active scan against a public host needs the target marked `allow_active` and proof you own it, via a `_scout-verify` DNS TXT record or a file at `/.well-known/scout-verify.txt`. A local address needs none of it.

One honest limitation is now written down rather than left to be discovered: the dashboard cannot run the `code.*` checks. Scout's targets have a repo field and no option sets it, so the mount passes a URL and nothing else. Filed upstream as scout#8, with a suggestion that it honour a repo path only in development, since a finding quotes the source line it found.

## v3.410.1 - October 23, 2026

### The saga page answers the question people arrive with

Anyone reading about sagas has usually just read about Temporal, and the first thing they want to know is whether this is that. The page did not say.

It does now, with the honest answer: the same pattern, the same flavour of it (orchestrated, one coordinator calling each step, compensations in reverse), and a different thing to operate. Temporal keeps progress as an event history in a cluster and rebuilds workflow state by replaying your code, which is why that code may not call `time.Now()` or `rand`. Grit keeps progress in two rows and replays nothing: it reads which step is next and calls it, so a step is ordinary Go and the only rule is that running it twice is safe. Durable timers, signals and child workflows are Temporal's, and a cluster is a lot of infrastructure for one application whose checkout touches four APIs.

Also added: a whole four-step saga written out with its compensations, and the three design points underneath it that the short example could not carry. Why the receipt goes last (a step with no undo makes every step after it a trap), why every `Undo` checks before it acts (compensation runs precisely when you do not know whether the thing happened), and why state goes through `r.Set` rather than a closure (the process that charged the card is usually gone by the time the refund runs).

Plus what the runner actually does, the retry defaults, every command, and the four admin endpoints for watching a run and pushing a stuck one on.

## v3.409.1 - October 23, 2026

### The money field groups as you type, not when you leave

v3.409.0 added the separators on blur, which misses the point: the moment you need to read the number is while you are entering it. Nobody can tell `50000000` from `5000000` by looking, and finding out after you tab away is finding out too late.

Now every keystroke regroups. The reason it was not done that way is real, though: reformatting a controlled input sends the caret to the end, so typing into the middle of a number becomes impossible. The fix is to put the caret back, counting the characters that are *not* separators rather than counting characters. Type `7` after the `50` of `50,000,000` and you get `507,000,000` with the caret still sitting after your 7.

Only the integer part is grouped while typing. Grouping the whole number means deciding how many decimals it has, and mid-typing there is no answer: `19.` is on its way to `19.99`, and settling it to `19.00` takes the decimal point out from under the caret. So `1234.5` reads `1,234.5` as you type it and becomes `1,234.50` when you leave, which is the one thing blur is still good for.


## v3.409.0 - October 23, 2026

### What each field becomes, what each flag does, and one syntax everywhere

The field types page listed what every type maps to in Go, TypeScript and Zod, and stopped there. It now also says what each one becomes in the database and the thing about it that the Go type does not tell you: that a `string` named something with "url" in it gets `size:500` because a tracking link does not fit in 255, that `one_to_one` gets `uniqueIndex` rather than `index` and that this is the entire difference between it and `belongs_to`, that `money` is two columns because one column holding "19.99 USD" is not something you can SUM. Modifiers have the same treatment, including which struct tag each one adds.

**The flags are documented.** `--faker`, `--seed`, `--public`, `--items`, `--owned-by`, `--append-only`, `--audit-reads`, `--roles`, `--tree` and `--tenant-owned`, each with what it actually changes. Most of them change the generated code in more than one place, which is why knowing one exists is not the same as knowing what it does.

#### One syntax

The talk showed the readable form in a slide's preview and the positional form in the terminal beneath it, which reads as two ways of saying the same thing rather than as one replacing the other. Every slide is on the readable form now, and so are the four blog tutorials, which are the worst place for the older spelling because they are followed line by line.

Every argument is written out, too: `client:belongs_to[Client]` rather than `client:belongs_to`, `photo:file[image]` rather than `photo:file`. Both work. The explicit one keeps working when somebody renames the field, and says what the upload accepts.

The conversion was mechanical and it damaged three passages, which is the normal outcome: a label containing a space was cut in half twice, and a deliberate "these two are equivalent" comparison became the same line printed twice. Repaired by hand, and then every converted spec was fed through the real parser rather than read: 27 of them, all parsing, with the derived labels checked (`past_due` becomes "Past Due").

#### The money field groups its digits

A money column in a table has always read `$1,234,567.89`, because it renders through `Intl.NumberFormat`, which groups. The input beside it read `1234567.89`. Telling six figures from seven by counting digits is the mistake that field exists to prevent.

Grouping happens when you leave the box and when a value arrives from elsewhere, never on a keystroke: reformatting while someone types is what moves the caret, and the field already held its draft separately for that reason. Commas are stripped on the way in, so a pasted `1,234.56` works, and the guard that decides whether to rewrite the box now reads the draft through a parser that understands them, because `Number.parseFloat("1,234.56")` is 1.

## v3.407.0 - October 23, 2026

### grit add scout: a scanner that knows which of your routes are protected

Scout is a security scanner that mounts inside your API, the way GORM Studio and Pulse do. It checks response headers, the TLS handshake, DNS records, whether a `.git` or `.env` is reachable, secrets committed to the repository, Dockerfile practice, reachable CVEs in your Go modules, and configuration such as Gin left in debug mode.

`grit add scout` Opt-in, unlike Sentinel and Pulse, which every project gets. A scanner that appears because you ran `grit new` is one nobody decided to run, and an undecided scanner is either ignored or trusted without being read. It also installs disabled, and refuses to mount without a password: its dashboard is a list of where your application is weakest.

#### The route table is the part worth having

A scanner looking at an application from outside sees URLs, so when it wants to report "this endpoint has no authentication" it has to infer that from the shape of the path. The path does not say. `/api/v1/auth/login` and `/api/v1/auth/me` sit in the same place and want opposite things.

Nor can it ask the router. Gin's route table carries a route's method, path and last handler, and nothing about the middleware in front of it; the running process genuinely does not know. That is why the admin's Routes screen has never had an access column.

Grit already solved this elsewhere. `grit` parses the route files, resolves each group's middleware chain and writes `internal/access`, which `grit doctor` fails on when it goes stale. `grit add scout` hands that table over, so Scout reads what each route requires rather than guessing:

`POST /api/v1/auth/login [] GET /api/v1/auth/me [AuthRequired] GET /api/v1/admin/blogs [AuthRequired, RequireRole(ADMIN), RequirePermission(blogs.view)]` Verified against a real project: 233 routes, each with its true chain. A route that should sit behind a role and does not is then something Scout can state rather than suspect, and it finds it without sending a request.

#### Two notes

The dashboard is signed with a key derived from your JWT secret rather than with the secret itself. One signing key shared between two auth systems means a token minted by either is valid to the other, and the two disagree about who may hold one. Derived rather than random, because a random key signs everybody out on every deploy, which is how a warning becomes something people route around.
