Adding Scout raises a project to gin v1.12.0 and GORM v1.31.2, which Go would have done silently on the first build. Doing it in the command puts it in the diff instead. The one genuinely new dependency is `coder/websocket`; eight of Scout's eleven were already there.


## v3.406.0 - October 22, 2026

### A field syntax you can read out loud

The positional spelling asked a lot of four characters. The colon meant the type, the type's argument and every modifier; the pipe separating options is a shell pipe, so an unquoted example silently lost half of them; and `=` was both "this label" and "this value", which is how a condition ended up with two of them in a row.

`# before cycle:select:monthly=Monthly|annually=Annually:when=kind=recurring # now cycle:select[monthly, annually] if kind == recurring` An argument goes in brackets, which is where a reader already looks for one: `belongs_to[User]`, `slug[title]`, `files[pdf, doc]`, `tel[UG]`, `rating[10]`. Labels are derived from the values, so `monthly` renders as "Monthly" and you write one only when it differs: `[monthly, annually="Every year"]`. A condition reads as a sentence.

The same syntax now works in a YAML definition, one field per line, so the file and the command stopped being two notations for one idea:

`fields: - kind:select[one_off, recurring] - cycle:select[monthly, annually] if kind == recurring` A field with more to say than a line holds is still written as keys, and that form now understands `if:` too. The two can be mixed in one file.

Both spellings parse, and produce identical fields: there is one parser, and the readable form is rewritten into the positional one before anything else sees it. Existing commands, tutorials and YAML files keep working.

Writing the grammar down found the rest of a bug fixed two releases ago. Five branches read their type's argument and returned, so every modifier after it was dropped in silence: a `belongs_to` could not be made optional, a `file` could not be made required, and a condition on a relationship, which is where one is most often wanted, did nothing at all.

Then building a billing application with these commands, start to finish, found two more.

**A conditional field could not be left out.** The model dropped `binding:"required"` for a conditional field, and the generated request struct did not, so a one-off project was refused at the binding stage for having no billing cycle: the exact failure the feature exists to prevent, one layer above where it was fixed. Binding runs before anything has looked at the row, so it cannot evaluate a condition, and the requirement now belongs entirely to the model's `requiredif` tag.

**A choice column kept its choices to itself.** Generating a seeder for a resource that already exists rebuilds the field list from the Go struct, where a select is just a string, so the options were lost and the seeder fell through to `gofakeit.Word()`. A freshly seeded demo opened on projects whose kind was "Thatcherite" and whose billing cycle was "sail", values the form's own dropdown cannot offer. A choice column now records its values in an `enum` tag, the way a formatted column records its format. Resources generated before this release keep seeding words into those columns until they are regenerated.


## v3.405.1 - October 22, 2026

### The docs checker could not read a condition that points at an existing column

Every field spec printed in the documentation is parsed by a test, because "the docs said to do X and X did not work" is the most repeated line in this changelog. The `when=` modifier broke it in a way worth recording.

A spec for `grit generate field` describes the one field being added, and its condition names a column the model already has. The checker parsed it standalone and refused it for naming a field that was not in the snippet, which is correct for a whole resource and wrong for a single field. It now checks a `--fields` spec whole, conditions included, and checks only the syntax of a single added field.

The release that carried the modifier therefore never published: its own test caught it. The documentation example was also written across continuation lines, which the extractor reads as separate fragments, so it is one line now.


## v3.405.0 - October 22, 2026

### when=: a conditional field, declared once, enforced in both places

The last release made a field conditional in the admin panel. Declaring one still meant editing two files by hand, and the half people would skip is the server half, because the form already looks right without it.

A field now takes a `when=` modifier, and the generator writes both:

`grit generate field Project \ "cycle:select:monthly=Monthly|annually=Annually:when=kind=recurring"` In the resource definition that becomes `visibleWhen` and `requiredWhen`, so the input is hidden on a one-off project and a cycle left behind by a project that used to be recurring is cleared. On the model it becomes `requiredif:"kind=recurring"`, which `internal/fieldtypes` enforces on every write that has a model: create, update, PATCH, bulk edit, CSV import and sync push. A recurring project with no cycle comes back as a 422 naming the field.

A conditional field deliberately never carries `binding:"required"`. Binding runs before anything has looked at the row, so it would refuse every record the condition does not hold for, which is the trap that makes people give up and leave the column optional everywhere.

Two things this found. Modifiers after a select's options were being dropped, so `status:select:a=A|b=B:optional` had silently stayed required since selects were added. And a condition naming a field that does not exist is now refused when you type the command rather than producing a predicate that reads an undefined property, which shows up as an input that never appears and nothing anywhere saying why.

The limit, stated in the [forms documentation](https://gritframework.com/docs/admin/forms#conditional-fields): a PATCH naming only the field a condition depends on is left alone, because the dependent column's stored value is not in the request and reading the row there would make every PATCH two queries.


## v3.404.1 - October 22, 2026

### The Go floor moves to 1.26.10 for a crypto/x509 advisory

GO-2026-6809 is a standard library vulnerability in `crypto/x509`, fixed in Go 1.26.10. It is not theoretical for this code: govulncheck reaches it through ordinary formatting, and the same standard library is compiled into every generated API.

The floor, the templates a new project is built from, this repository's workflows and the three checked-in example applications all move together. An existing project is raised by `grit upgrade`, which rewrites the `go` directive in the API's `go.mod` along with the Go pinned in its Dockerfiles and CI workflows.

One thing this release fixed on the way past: the test covering that repair restated the floor as a literal instead of reading the constant, so it had to be edited by hand on every security bump. It now follows the constant. The version comparison itself is per segment and numeric, which this bump is the first to actually exercise: 1.26.9 sorts after 1.26.10 as text, and a lexical comparison would have left every project on the vulnerable patch.


## v3.404.0 - October 22, 2026

### A form field that only applies when another field says so

A billing cycle belongs to a recurring project and means nothing on a one-off one. There was no way to say that. A field was shown always or never, so the choice was to ask a question that does not apply, or to leave the field out of the resource and lose it for the rows that need it.

Fields now take `visibleWhen` and `requiredWhen`, each a predicate over the current form values. A hidden field drops its required rule, because a question nobody can see must never be the reason a form will not submit, and `requiredWhen` takes precedence over `required` while the field is shown.

A hidden field is cleared rather than left alone. Omitting it would be a PATCH that keeps what was there, so a project moved from recurring to one-off would go on billing monthly on a column nobody can see. It is submitted as the empty value its type uses on a fresh form, which is a shape the API already accepts.

All three layouts honour it: the plain form, the stepped wizard and the grouped per-card editor, which each have their own field loop. In the wizard the predicate reads the whole form, so a field on step three can depend on an answer given on step one. Forms with no conditional field do not subscribe to the watcher at all, so nothing pays for this that does not use it.

The form is one half of the rule. The predicate is the admin panel's behaviour and nothing else: the API, a CSV import and a background job never see it, so the same rule still belongs in the service. The [forms documentation](https://gritframework.com/docs/admin/forms#conditional-fields) shows both halves.


## v3.403.0 - October 18, 2026

### The blog list and its stat cards held two copies of the same search

The admin blog list narrowed by a search, and the four stat cards above it counted rows over the same search. Each built its own `WHERE`: the service in `blog_service.go`, and the handler again in `blog_handler.go`, where it skipped the service and queried the database directly. Two definitions of the same thing, in two files, so nobody editing one would see the other.

Nothing was visibly broken, which is why it survived. It breaks the first time someone adds a searchable column: the table filters by it and the counts above it do not, and the numbers are quietly wrong rather than missing.

`BlogService` now states the search once in `searchScope`, used by `List` and by a new `CountQuery(ctx, search)`. The handler asks the service for that query instead of rebuilding it, and no longer touches the database at all, which is what the layering said all along.

Existing projects get both halves on `grit upgrade`. That ordering matters: the blog files are written for a new project and do not travel on upgrade, so the handler repair is skipped, with a warning naming the method to add, whenever the service repair could not run. A handler calling a method that is not there would not compile.

Four tests hold the property: the clause appears exactly once, the handler never queries the database directly, the repair is idempotent, and it warns rather than guessing when the file has been edited.


## v3.402.1 - October 16, 2026

### The desktop sync engine has tests, and now they run

The offline client had five tests covering the conflict path, and no CI job had ever executed them, because nothing in CI scaffolded a `--desktop` project. They pass, which was lucky rather than known.

There is now an **offline-sync** job that scaffolds an app with the desktop client and runs both halves: push and pull on the server, outbox and conflicts on the client. It builds only `./sync` on the desktop side, because `main.go` imports Wails and that needs webkit2gtk on Linux, while the engine itself is plain Go and SQLite.

### Eight more client tests, for the rules that squash the outbox

The outbox holds at most one entry per row, so nine offline edits to the same record become one change to push. Six rules decide what the surviving entry looks like and none of them were tested. Each is a different bug if it is wrong: an update on top of an unsent create must stay a `create`, or the server gets an update for a row it has never seen and the entry sticks in the queue forever; a delete on top of an unsent create must remove the entry entirely, rather than making two round trips to arrive at having done nothing.

Also covered: squashing is per row and keyed on `(model, id)`, so the same id in two tables stays two changes, and the outbox survives the app being reopened, which is the whole reason it is on disk.

All eight were verified the same way as yesterday's server fixes: by reverting a rule and watching the test fail.


## v3.402.0 - October 16, 2026

### Offline sync never detected a conflict

Every update pushed through `/api/sync/push` left the row's version unchanged. Two devices editing the same record offline both pushed, both were accepted, and the second silently overwrote the first. The version is the entire mechanism of conflict detection in the offline protocol, and it had never once fired.

The handler set the struct's `Version` to the server's value and relied on the model's `BeforeUpdate` hook to add one. The hook does fire, and calls `SetColumn`, but `Save` builds its SET clause from the struct's own fields and the struct's value overwrites the expression. So the row was written back at the version it already had, and the response reported that same version, which is why nothing looked wrong: the number the API returned always matched the number in the database.

It is now set explicitly to `serverVersion + 1`. The online update path was never affected, because it goes through `Updates(map)`, where `SetColumn` does win.

### Found by running it, not by reading it

The sync engine had three tests, all on soft deletes. The 556-line push/pull handler had none. A probe driving the real endpoints against a live API returned 26 checks with 9 failures, and the version bug was the first of them.

There are now ten tests through the real handler, covering what the probe did: that an update advances the stored version and reports what it stored, that a second push at a stale version is refused with the server's row attached for a merge, that the version advances on every update, and that a version in the client's payload is ignored. On the pull side: tombstones travel and carry `_deleted`, live rows do not, an oversized batch is refused, an unknown model is refused, and the keyset cursor does not drop rows that share a timestamp.

That last one is the test worth having. With a cursor of the timestamp alone, the second page asks for `updated_at > T` and every remaining row at exactly `T` is skipped, forever, with no error anywhere. Both fixes were verified by reverting them and watching the tests fail.

### And the handler is upgrade-delivered now

`internal/services/sync.go` was framework-owned; `internal/handlers/sync.go` was not. A correctness fix in the sync protocol would have reached new projects only, leaving every existing project with conflict detection that never fires. Both files and their tests now arrive with `grit upgrade`.


## v3.401.1 - October 16, 2026

### No link to a profile that was never taken

The k6 bridge added yesterday printed three links when a run finished, including the flame graph. With `PULSE_PROFILING` off there is no profile, so that third link was a 404, and a tool that prints dead links stops being read. It is now printed only when Pulse reports that it took one; the run is still recorded and still compared either way, and the script already said which you got.

Pulse v1.5.1 landed the same two fixes in its own bundled bridge, from the report filed off this work: its own cookie jar, and a login that returns `null` instead of throwing. Both arrived at the same shape Grit generates, which is a good sign for the shape. The floor moves to `pulse v1.5.1`, though the library itself is byte-identical apart from its version constant: the change is in `examples/k6/` and the embedded dashboard build.


## v3.401.0 - October 16, 2026

### Your load test now tells you which function fell over

k6 can tell you p95 went from 40ms to 310ms at 500 virtual users. It cannot tell you which function, and neither can an external APM at the resolution that matters. Pulse can, because it runs inside the API process.

`grit generate perf` now writes `perf/pulse.js` beside the k6 script, and the script registers its run with Pulse before the load starts and closes it after. Pulse takes a CPU profile over exactly that window and keeps it against the run, so the Test Runs page gives you, on one screen: before / during / after traffic **per route**, queries per request and N+1 findings in each window, and the flame graph of the seconds the load was running.

On a generated project with a deliberate N+1, one 20-VU run reported 16.23 queries per request, 606 N+1 detections, and **zero slow queries**. An N+1 that is invisible at one request a second is exactly what falls over under load, and no slow-query threshold will ever catch it.

Pulse had the `POST /pulse/api/test-runs` endpoint since v1.0 and nothing in a generated project ever called it, so the Test Runs page was empty in every Grit app ever created. That is the actual change here: the best feature in the area was gated behind a curl nobody knew to write.

### Three defects the first real run exposed

Writing the integration was easy. Running it was where the bugs were, and all three would have hit anyone who wired this up themselves.

**The run recorded nothing, and said so.** `pulse: login failed (403)`, body `CSRF_INVALID`. `setup()` logs into the API first, which sets a session cookie, and k6 keeps one cookie jar per virtual user. So the Pulse login carried the app session cookie, and Grit's double-submit CSRF middleware correctly refused a cookie-bearing POST with no `X-CSRF-Token`. The bridge now uses its own empty `http.CookieJar`, which is also semantically right: the Pulse dashboard is bearer-token auth and wants no cookies at all.

**The generated script pointed at the wrong port.** `--target` defaulted to a hardcoded `localhost:8080`, so any project on another port got a load test that could not connect to it. It now reads the project's own `APP_URL` from `.env`.

**The resource scenario could never pass.** The script registers a throwaway USER, and a resource generated by `grit generate resource` requires ADMIN or its own permission, so every call 403'd and the error-rate threshold went red on a perfectly healthy API. Pass `PERF_EMAIL`/`PERF_PASSWORD` to load-test role-guarded routes; without them those scenarios are skipped rather than counted as failures.

The whole bridge is fail-soft by design. Unset `PULSE_PASSWORD`, disable Pulse, or point it at an unreachable host, and every call returns null with a warning. A load test must never fail because its observability sidecar had a bad day.

### Pulse v1.5.0, and two things that are no longer true

The floor moves to `pulse v1.5.0`, which closes the three issues raised from here while writing the profiling post.

The **N+1 table now names the file and line** that issued the query, in an *Issued from* column, along with the route and the suggested fix. It recorded the caller of every query all along and surfaced it only in a 7MB CSV export. And the **flame graph defaults to real CPU time** instead of goroutine stacks, where a connection parked in a read counted on every tick and the hot code was a sliver you had to hunt for.

The blog post that found those two has been updated rather than left standing, because it told readers to avoid a page that is now the right one to use.


## v3.400.2 - October 15, 2026

### An allocation budget is a figure about a toolchain, not about your code alone

The allocation budgets added in v3.399.0 failed in CI, and the reason is worth more than the fix. That release argued that an allocation count is a fair thing to fail a build on because, unlike a timing, "the same code allocates the same number of times on every machine, every run". The first half of that is true: the count does not move with the machine or the load. The second half is not, because it moves with the Go release.

Verifying an access token allocates **56** times under go1.26.9 and **41** under go1.27.2. The newer runtime does the same work with fifteen fewer allocations. The budget was set at 50 from a local run on 1.27, and CI pins 1.26.9, so it passed on the machine that wrote it and failed on the machine that enforces it. Which is the oldest mistake in performance work: a number measured somewhere other than where it is judged.

Budgets are now set from the oldest toolchain the project supports, because that is the one that allocates most, and each budget carries both figures in its comment. The budget for token verification is 70. The test reports the Go version and platform alongside every count, since a count without its toolchain cannot be compared with anything, and when one fails it now says to re-run under the Go version CI uses before concluding the code got worse.

The v3.399.0 entry above has been corrected rather than quietly edited, because the claim was the argument for the feature.

### Why it took two releases to read the failure

Both the CI and Live workflows reported this as the word `FAIL` and nothing else, because they piped sixty packages of `go test` output through `tail -30`. v3.400.1 fixed those steps, and the next run named the test, the path, both numbers and the budget on the first line. The fix for the budget itself then took one command.


## v3.400.1 - October 15, 2026

### Three things CI caught that the local test run did not

v3.400.0 was tagged and did not publish, because the release workflow runs the whole test suite and three tests in `internal/doctor` failed. They failed on a fixture: a `go.mod` written out with the library versions that were current the day it was written, so raising the Pulse floor made a project that *is* up to date report two findings. The fixture now builds its require block from the floors themselves, which means a floor bump cannot break it again, and the one test that wants a library behind its floor says which library and which version.

The lesson is that the floors have one declaration and had two readers, and only one of them was derived.

### An unchecked sign conversion in the JWKS code

gosec flagged `uint64(pub.E)` in `internal/services/jwtkeys.go`, twice: once where the JWK is built and once where the RFC 7638 thumbprint is computed. An RSA public exponent is an `int`, and a negative one would convert into an enormous positive number, so the published `e` would not be the exponent the key signs with and nothing would say so.

No key `x509` will parse has a non-positive exponent, so this was unreachable rather than exploitable. It is now one guarded function used by both call sites, which is the shape that was worth having anyway: an exponent is encoded in one place, and an invalid one produces a zero byte that every client rejects rather than a silently wrong key.

### A CI step that hid the failure it was reporting

The generated-app jobs ran `go test ./... 2>&1 | tail -30`. Over sixty packages that prints thirty `ok` lines and the word `FAIL`, and nothing about which test failed or why, which is exactly what it did the one time it mattered. Those steps now keep the whole log, print the tail when everything passes, and print the failing tests with their context when something does not.

A truncation that discards the only interesting part of the output is worse than no truncation, because it looks like it is reporting.


## v3.400.0 - October 15, 2026

### Pulse v1.3.0, and 38MB of the heap back

Two issues were raised against Pulse from here while profiling a generated project. Both are fixed and released, and Grit now floors at `v1.3.0`.

The first was that the profiler was the largest thing in the heap. The in-memory backend reserved its whole ring-buffer capacity at startup, so a process serving almost nothing carried about 38MB of empty buffers in a 45MB heap, and anyone looking at their own memory graph was mostly looking at the tool. It now grows with what it actually holds. Profiling a freshly generated API after the upgrade, `inuse_space` totals 6.7MB and no Pulse allocation appears in the top nodes at all.

The second was that Pulse could tell you a route is slow but not that it got slower. A route that went from 40ms to 90ms three deploys ago looks healthy, because 90ms is not slow in absolute terms and nothing in a point-in-time view remembers the 40. v1.3.0 keeps a rolling per-route baseline and reports the current figure as a ratio against it, with a lifecycle record so a step change can be attributed to the deploy it followed. That is the difference between an investigation and a fix.

### Profiles you can fetch from a running process

`PULSE_PROFILING=true` serves heap, allocation, goroutine, mutex, block and CPU profiles as standard pprof protobuf, so `go tool pprof http://host/pulse/api/profile/heap` works and `-diff_base` compares two captures. The dashboard says which route; these say which line.

It is off by default and it takes two switches to turn on, the setting above and `PULSE_PROFILE_ENABLED` in the environment the server runs in. A profile is an unauthenticated description of your program, and a thirty second CPU profile anyone can ask for repeatedly is a denial of service, so one forgotten setting should not be enough to expose it. Mutex and block profiling cost the runtime something merely to collect, so they stay off until `PULSE_MUTEX_PROFILE_FRACTION` or `PULSE_BLOCK_PROFILE_RATE` is given a number. Asking for a block profile without one answers 409 and names the option to add, rather than returning an empty profile that reads as "nothing is blocking".

`PULSE_EXPLAIN_SLOW_QUERIES=true` puts the database's own plan for a slow SELECT on the Database page. Off by default because it issues extra queries against your database, and EXPLAIN only, never EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so the slow query is not run a second time.

### Existing projects get the switches too

The mount lives in `internal/routes/routes.go` and the settings in `internal/config/config.go`, and neither file is framework-owned on upgrade, because both are files a project edits. Left there, a new project would have profiling and every existing project would not. So `grit upgrade` now adds the four settings, the options on the mount and the documentation in `.env.example`, and refuses to touch a file somebody has rewritten, naming what to add by hand instead. An upgraded project and a freshly scaffolded one produce byte-identical `config.go` and `routes.go`.

### A repair that had stopped working, and the test that now notices

Running that upgrade turned up something else. `repairQueuedAuthMail`, which moves auth emails off bare goroutines and onto the queue, recognised a project by matching the full signature of `deliverVerificationEmail` up to its opening brace. The function later grew a `string` return, so the anchor stopped matching, and the repair printed "not the file Grit wrote" and returned early on every single project, including one Grit had just written.

The anchors now stop where the parameter list does, which is the part a return type cannot move. More usefully, there is now a test asserting that every anchor a repair uses to decide it has nothing to do is still present in the template that is supposed to contain it. A repair whose anchor has drifted is worse than no repair, because it fails as a warning people learn to scroll past.


## v3.399.0 - October 15, 2026

### Allocation budgets, so a performance regression fails a build

Generated projects shipped three benchmarks and nothing that ran them. A benchmark tells you how long something took on the machine that ran it, which on a shared CI runner is a number that moves on its own, so it cannot fail a build honestly. An allocation count can: it does not move with the machine or with the load.

**Corrected in v3.400.2.** This entry originally said an allocation count is "the same on every machine, every run". It is not the same across Go releases: token verification allocates 56 times under go1.26.9 and 41 under go1.27.2. The budgets below were set from a local run on the newer toolchain and failed in CI on the older one.

`internal/handlers/perf_test.go` now asserts a budget on three paths that run on every request or every list request: verifying an access token, binding list parameters, and writing a list response. They measure 41, 40 and 36 allocations today, with budgets set above that so an ordinary refactor passes and a change in kind does not. CI runs them without `-race`, because the race detector allocates on its own account and the resulting counts are not the ones your users get.

When one fails it names the path, both numbers, and why that path is worth watching, and says that raising the budget in the same commit is a legitimate answer. The point is to make the new number a decision somebody recorded rather than a drift nobody saw.

### What the profiler actually found

The budgets are not a guess. Profiling a freshly generated API with `-cpuprofile` and `-memprofile` put `runtime.mallocgc` at 15% cumulative and `scanObject` at 11%, with JSON rendering at 14.75% and `reflect.unsafe_New` the largest single source of allocated objects. Excluding bcrypt, which is deliberately slow, allocation pressure and the garbage collection it causes are the dominant cost. That is the thing worth a budget, so that is what got one.

### A benchmark that had been failing quietly

The profiling run also showed `BenchmarkAuthRegister` logging `no such table: email_verification_tokens` on every iteration. The test helper migrated three tables and registering issues a verification token, so every register in the suite did the work and threw it away. The tests still passed, because a verification token that cannot be stored is logged rather than fatal, which is why the noise sat in the output looking like somebody else's problem. The table is now migrated with the others.


## v3.398.0 - October 12, 2026

### Sign-in limits that do not punish an office for sharing an address

Sentinel v2.7.0 fixes the two issues raised from here: a lockout now bars the (address, account) pair rather than the address, and the CAPTCHA tier is no longer configured when no provider exists. Both are adopted.

Adopting them exposed that Grit's own limits had become the binding constraint. The per-route limits are counted per client address and count every request rather than every failure, so a successful sign-in consumes one. At five sign-ins per quarter hour, behind an office, university or mobile carrier NAT, the sixth person to arrive in the morning was refused: the limit meant to stop password guessing was stopping people logging in.

Those limits are now flood control and nothing more: 30 sign-ins per 5 minutes, and the other credential routes loosened to match. That is safe because guessing is caught precisely elsewhere, and by counting failures rather than attempts. The pair lockout bars one account under attack without touching anybody else sharing the address, an address accumulating roughly four times as many failures is refused outright, and the account lockout still catches the attack spread across a botnet. `SENTINEL_LOCKOUT_EXEMPT_IPS` names egress ranges that are never barred by address, and are still counted.

Also fixed: a MySQL project was handing Sentinel a MySQL DSN under the Postgres driver, because every branch that was not SQLite went to Postgres. It could not connect, so the API ran with no security storage at all. v2.7.0 added a MySQL adapter and it is now selected, with `parseTime` set, without which the audit log's hash chain cannot verify what it stored.

### Stable, and how to tell

Nothing in the docs said whether the version you were looking at was a finished release. The machinery was already right and invisible: the release workflow marks a tag containing `-rc`, `-beta` or `-alpha` as a GitHub prerelease, and `grit update` asks for the latest release, which excludes prereleases, so an update never moves you onto one.

That is now written down, on [the stability page](https://gritframework.com/docs/stability#release-channels), and shown: a prerelease is labelled next to the version wherever the site displays it. No label means stable, which is why there is no badge saying so on every page.

### Every system design page now starts with what the thing is

The 29 system design pages opened with a trade-off question, which assumes you already know the topic. Each now opens with a plain definition: what caching is, what multitenancy is, what an audit log is. The check that runs over these pages enforces it, so a new page cannot skip it.


## v3.397.0 - October 12, 2026

### Tokens another service can verify but not forge

Tokens were signed HS256 with a shared secret, which is right for one service and stops being right as soon as a second one has to verify them. HMAC verification needs the same key that signs, so every service that can check a token can also mint one: in an estate of a dozen services, each holds something that forges an administrator token, and the blast radius of the least important one being compromised is all of them.

Set `JWT_PRIVATE_KEY` and the API signs RS256 and publishes only the public half at `/.well-known/jwks.json`. A verifier holding that can check every token and provably cannot sign one. The shared secret remains the default, because for a single service it is one environment variable with nothing to distribute.

### Rotation that does not sign everybody out

Each key gets an id derived from the key itself, per RFC 7638, so the id in a token and the id in the published set cannot disagree and a new key gets a new id without anybody remembering to change one. Tokens carry it in the header, and a verifier that meets an id it has not seen refetches the set.

`JWT_PREVIOUS_PUBLIC_KEY` keeps the key you are retiring in the published set and accepted, so tokens it signed stay valid until they expire rather than everybody being signed out at the moment of the switch. Drop it once one refresh lifetime has passed.

### Issuer and audience

`JWT_ISSUER` and `JWT_AUDIENCE` are written into every token and checked on every token that carries them. That is what stops a token minted for staging being accepted by production when a secret has been copied between them. Checked only when present, so turning them on does not invalidate tokens already in circulation: those carry neither and age out within one refresh lifetime.

### What the live check proved

A generated project was stood up with an RSA key, a user registered, and the access token it issued verified using nothing but what the JWKS endpoint publishes. Then the algorithm confusion attack: a token signed HS256 using the published modulus as the shared secret, which a verifier that trusts the header's `alg` would accept. It is refused with a 401, because the accepted algorithm is pinned to what the deployment actually signs with rather than read out of the token.

Using it also found a bad error message. A key path that does not resolve was reported as &ldquo;invalid key: must be PEM encoded&rdquo;, which says nothing about the real mistake, and the real mistake is nearly always a relative path resolved against the wrong directory: the server runs from the API directory, so a path that works for a CLI command from the project root does not. It now names the variable, the value and where it looked.


## v3.396.0 - October 12, 2026

### A lockout you can get out of

The account lockout bars an address after ten wrong passwords. It is keyed on an email address, which anybody can guess, so anybody could lock anybody else out. The victim's obvious move, resetting their password, left the lock in place: they were refused with the same &ldquo;invalid email or password&rdquo; as before, having just set the password themselves. The only ways out were waiting or an administrator.

A completed reset now clears the lock. Proving you can read the mailbox is strictly stronger evidence than waiting fifteen minutes.

The owner is also told. Over HTTP there is nothing to say, because &ldquo;this account is locked&rdquo; confirms the address exists and the sign-in route answers every failure identically on purpose. The mailbox is the one channel where saying it leaks nothing, so that is where it is said: somebody has been trying, here is a link that lets you back in now. It is sent off the request path, and keyed on the lock rather than the attempt, so a run of failures does not send a run of emails.

### Passwords checked against the breach corpus

The password rules measured shape: long enough, mixed enough, not one of a few hundred obvious ones. `Summer2024!` passes all of them and is in every credential-stuffing list in the world. Shape is a weak proxy for whether a password is actually compromised, because credential stuffing is not guessing, it is replaying known passwords.

`PASSWORD_BREACH_CHECK=true` checks the chosen password against the public corpus when registering, changing and resetting. It uses k-anonymity: the password is hashed locally and only the first five characters of that hash are sent, so the service never learns which password was asked about and never sees the password.

Off by default, and it fails open. It calls a third party, and failing closed would mean somebody else's outage stops every registration here, which is a self-inflicted incident caused by an advisory check. Five tests cover that behaviour, including the endpoint being unreachable.

### The challenge tier can now fire

Sentinel's sign-in shield has a middle tier that asks for a challenge before it starts barring addresses, and it sets that tier's threshold of its own accord whether or not a provider exists. No provider was ever wired in, and Sentinel validates only for more than one provider configured, never for none. So the tier was configured, unreachable, and silent about it.

`SENTINEL_TURNSTILE_SECRET` and its hCaptcha and reCAPTCHA siblings are now passed through. Set one and the tier works; leave them empty and it stays dormant rather than looking like a defence.

### Retry-After, where it is safe to send it

The second-factor route refuses a locked account with a 429 and now says when to come back. The sign-in route deliberately does not: there, naming the wait would confirm the address exists, so a locked account still answers exactly like a wrong password. Once the password has been checked the caller already knows the account exists, and the header leaks nothing.


## v3.395.0 - October 9, 2026

### Every architecture, generated and used

Grit offers eight shapes. Until this week, no single pass had generated all of them, stood them up and used them. Six releases later, each one has been scaffolded fresh, built, type-checked, migrated, started and driven through a browser as the same contact app, with an owner-scoped resource and every field type the generator emits.

It found thirty faults. Every one of them is now a test that fails without its fix, and every fix was re-verified on a project generated by the fixed binary.

### What that pass was actually worth

The honest summary is that compiling and a green suite told us almost nothing about these. Four of the eight shapes had something that stopped them working and none of it showed in a build:

- A **single Next** project's admin panel could not reach its API in development at all. The browser calls its own origin, which is right once the binary serves the built frontend, and nothing bridged the two processes in dev.
- A **Wails desktop** project did not build: one route rendered a component it never imported. It stayed hidden because `type-check` was failing first on an unrelated missing file, on three frontends at once.
- A **single Vite** project did not type-check, and was the one shape with no `type-check` script to find out with.
- An **API-only** project's README told you to run four commands, all of which failed.

And one fault appeared five times, once per tier, with a different misleading symptom each time: a console violation naming a port nobody configured, a blocked sign-in, a phone calling a dead port, a 500 from a different project's server, a 404 from Next. The API's address was written down in several places and only some of them moved. There are tests for that family across every shape now.

### What else came out of it

A generated mobile app shipped the framework's logo as its own icon, splash and favicon, and painted itself the framework's purple whatever theme was asked for. An `--owned-by` resource put a required owner picker on the admin form and the server discarded the answer. A `belongs_to` column read `<relation>.name` whatever the related model was called, so a column pointing at anything labelled by a title or a number rendered a dash. A picker at the bottom of a form opened its list off the window. A boolean column said "Active" whatever it was called.

Three security items the pass surfaced through CI rather than through use: Go 1.26.9 for an HTTP/2 crash, `golang.org/x/net` v0.60.0 for four more, and a Wails pin three minor versions behind in four places.

### Why this is a minor and not a patch

Nothing here changes an API you call. What changed is the evidence: the claim that Grit generates eight working shapes is now something somebody has checked one at a time rather than something the build implied. The [stability page](https://gritframework.com/docs/stability) says so, and says plainly what that exercise still does not cover: it is a person opening a browser, not a job in CI, and five of the thirty faults were in work that had shipped hours earlier the same day.


## v3.394.5 - October 9, 2026

### Every command in an API project's Quick Start failed

The README was one fixed triple-tier page whatever shape was generated. So an `--api` project was told to run `pnpm install` and `pnpm dev` with no `package.json`; a SQLite project was told to start PostgreSQL, Redis, MinIO and Mailhog in Docker; the project structure named `apps/web`, `apps/admin` and `turbo.json` whether or not they were there; and the Services table listed a web app and an admin panel on a project with neither.

It is the first file anybody opens, and for one shape every line of its Quick Start was wrong. `grit new` has printed the right steps per shape for a long time, so the knowledge was there and only the README did not ask for it. It describes the project that was generated now: its Quick Start, its structure, its services, its stack, and the one of the two no Docker sections that applies.

### A single Vite project did not type-check, and had no way to find out

`nextToTanStack` rewrites `next/link` and its siblings to `@/lib/next-compat`, which is where the shim lives in a standalone TanStack app. A single project kept its only copy under the admin panel and converted one site component, which then imported a module that was not there.

Nobody had noticed because that shape was also the one with no `type-check` script at all: running it reported a missing script rather than a missing module. It has both now, and a test covers the single project alongside the monorepo apps it had been written for.

### A single Next project's frontend could not reach its API

In that shape the Go binary embeds the built frontend and serves it, so the browser is right to call its own origin, and `api-core.ts` does. In development they are two processes, Next on 3000 and the API on `APP_PORT`, and nothing joined them: every page that loaded data got a 404 from Next. The whole admin panel was dead in dev.

The Vite sibling of the same architecture has had the answer since it was written, as a dev proxy for `/api`, `/studio`, `/docs`, `/pulse` and `/sentinel`. This is that, as a Next rewrite, and it follows `APP_PORT` like the proxy does. In production the paths resolve on the binary's own origin and the block is inert.

The same file hoisted the project's `.env` from `../../`, which is the project root from `apps/web` and two directories above the project in a single one. So `THEME`, `SOCIAL_AUTH_ENABLED` and `API_URL` were all invisible to that shape.

### Two more places the API's address was written down

The server-rendered blog client read `API_INTERNAL_URL || NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL || "http://localhost:8080"`, missing the `API_URL` that the rest of the app and the generated `.env` both use. In the same app, one file followed the setting and one fell back to 8080.

And the desktop client still carried a port of its own as a fallback, which is dead now that its config defines the address at build time, but a literal nobody reaches is still a literal waiting to be reached.

This went wrong five times in one sweep, once per tier, each time with a symptom pointing somewhere else: a console violation, a blocked sign-in, a phone calling a dead port, a 500 from another project's server. There are tests for it now, across every shape, so the sixth one fails in CI rather than in a browser.


## v3.394.4 - October 9, 2026

### The Wails desktop app did not build

`apps/desktop/frontend/src/routes/app/profile.tsx` rendered `<PasswordStrength>` and never imported it. The component was there, and the two other routes that use it import it properly. One missing line, and `tsc` failed, and `wails build` failed with it.

Why it had not been caught is the more interesting half, and it is fixed below.

### type-check failed on every TanStack frontend for the wrong reason

`routeTree.gen.ts` is written by the router's Vite plugin during dev or build, and it is gitignored. So on a project nobody has run yet, `tsc` cannot find it and reports an error in every route file: the web app, the admin panel and the desktop client, roughly twenty errors that are all one missing file.

That is worse than having no check, because it buries a real one. The missing import above was sitting in the middle of that noise, and the only reason it ever surfaced is that `wails build` runs Vite first and `tsc` second. The check now generates what it reads: `tsr generate && tsc`, with `@tanstack/router-cli` to provide it. A check that needs somebody to have run a build first is not a check.

### The desktop app had no icon, and its Go module did not build

`build/appicon` was created as an empty directory. Wails reads `build/appicon.png`, a file, which is also what the project's own README describes. It is drawn now from the project's accent colour, the same placeholder the mobile app gets, with a note beside it saying what it is.

And `//go:embed all:frontend/dist` had nothing to match on a fresh scaffold, so `go build ./...` and `go vet ./...` both failed in that module. `wails build` worked, because it builds the frontend first; every other Go tool, and every editor, reported a broken package on a project nobody had touched. There is a page there now explaining itself, and a committed `.gitkeep` beside it, because a real build overwrites the page and a fresh clone has to satisfy the embed too.

### Wails was pinned three minor versions behind, in four places

`go.mod` asked for v2.9.2, the release workflow installed the CLI at v2.9.2, and two READMEs told people to install `@latest`. Wails prints a warning on every build when the module and the CLI disagree, and the `@latest` instruction guaranteed they would. All four say v2.16.0 now, and a test fails if the module and the workflow ever diverge again.

The desktop module is its own module, so the API's dependency floors do not reach it, and `go mod tidy` took the `golang.org/x/net` Wails asks for, which is below the one carrying the fix for GO-2026-6617 and three others. It pins v0.60.0 now, like the API.

### And the fifth place the API's address was written down

The desktop client's `api-client.ts` read `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` and fell back to the literal `localhost:8080`, and nothing set that variable for it. The dev proxy named the same literal.

So on a project that had moved `APP_PORT`, a desktop app called a port nothing was listening on, and when something else happened to be there it answered: sign-in came back 500 from a server belonging to a different project entirely. The config resolves the address once, from `VITE_API_URL` or `APP_PORT`, and hands it to both the proxy and the browser bundle.

That is the third frontend to have had this, after the Next apps and the Vite ones, and the pattern is the same every time: the API's address is written down in several places, some of them literals, and only some of them move.


## v3.394.3 - October 9, 2026

### A generated mobile app shipped Grit's brand as its own

`icon.png`, `adaptive-icon.png`, `splash.png` and `favicon.png` were four copies of the Grit logo. So an app called `cm2` had the framework's mark on the home screen, on the splash, in the browser tab and in whatever a store listing would have shown. The sign-in and sign-up screens rendered the same file at 76px, and the sign-up screen told the user to "Get started with Grit in seconds".

The rule has applied to the web app and the admin panel for a long time: a generated app shows its own name, copy and theme. The mobile app is the surface where breaking it costs the most, because an app icon is what somebody sees before they open anything.

The icons are drawn at scaffold time from the project's accent colour, with a README beside them saying they are placeholders and what each one is for. The auth screens draw the project's own initial, taken from `lib/brand.ts`, which reads the name out of `app.json` so renaming the project renames it on screen. The splash and adaptive-icon backgrounds follow the theme too: they were Grit's near-black on every project, including the default theme, whose background is white.

### And painted itself purple whatever theme it chose

`grit new shop --theme emerald` produced an app whose sign-in button, focus states, tab bar, stat cards and switches were all `#6c5ce7`: Grit's default accent, belonging to no theme anybody picked. There were 29 hardcoded copies of it.

The machinery was already there and unused. `tailwind.config.js` defines an `accent` from the theme, so every class only had to say `accent`, and the handful of colours a class cannot reach come from the palette, which is where the gradients and the tab bar already got theirs.

### The seeder wrote one set of variable names for three bundlers

Every frontend got `NEXT_PUBLIC_` names. A Next app reads those. A Vite app reads `VITE_`, so its `.env.local` named a publishable key the app could not see and an API address it ignored. An Expo app reads `EXPO_PUBLIC_` and was not in the list at all, so it got no file: no key, no address.

Each symptom points somewhere else. A public endpoint answering `INVALID_API_KEY` looks like a key problem. A phone calling a port nothing answers looks like the phone. Each app is now asked what it is, by the config file it has, and gets the names it reads.

Expo gets a port rather than a URL, because a phone cannot reach `localhost`: that address is the phone. The app derives the dev machine's LAN address from the host Metro is served on and needed only the port to go with it, and that port was the literal `8080` in `lib/api.ts`, so moving `APP_PORT` broke all three resolution paths at once.

### Two gaps in checks that already existed

The Expo app had no `type-check` script, so `turbo type-check` skipped it in silence: the same fault found on the Next tier two releases ago, in the one app the test for it did not cover. It is covered now.

And `grit start server` wrote no dev log, nor did any `grit start <app>`. The log existed only when `grit start` ran everything at once, which is the thing an `--api` project cannot do and a `--mobile` project does not do by design. Those two shapes had nothing for an agent to read. Every start path writes it now, in the same shape, so `grit logs` cannot tell them apart.

### Five accepted Trivy findings, each with an expiry

excelize v2.11.0 is its newest tagged release and five denial-of-service fixes are on its master branch, unreleased. govulncheck reports none of them as called, and adopting an untagged upstream commit into every generated project is the worse risk, so they are accepted in `.github/trivyignore.yaml` with the reason and a date the acceptance runs out. A bet nobody re-examines is how a known hole becomes a permanent one.


## v3.394.2 - October 9, 2026

### A TanStack frontend could not reach its own API

The mirror image of the fault the Next frontends had, found on the next tier in the sweep. There the policy was stale and the client was right; here the policy is right and the client is stale.

`vite.config.ts` resolves where the API is, from `VITE_API_URL` or `APP_PORT`, points the dev proxy at it and authorises exactly that origin in the Content-Security-Policy. The browser bundle never saw that answer: `api-core.ts` reads `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`, Vite only exposes a variable to client code when it is set with the `VITE_` prefix, and a project configures its API with `APP_PORT`, which is not one. So every request went to the `localhost:8080` fallback and the policy the config had just written blocked it, as a console violation with no HTTP status.

The config now hands the client the value it already resolved, so the proxy, the policy and the bundle cannot disagree. That is what the comment above `apiTarget` always claimed.

### The realtime client shipped process.env into a bundle with no process

Vite does not polyfill `process`, so a module reading `process.env` throws the moment anything imports it. The converter that rewrites those reads for the rest of a Vite admin never saw `lib/realtime.ts`, because that file is written straight to disk, and `vite build` uses esbuild and does no type checking, so nothing caught it before a blank screen would have.

There are three clients and there were two spellings. Each now says which bundler it is for, in one place, so a fourth cannot quietly inherit the wrong one.

### golang.org/x/net v0.60.0, for four called vulnerabilities

[GO-2026-6617](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6617), GO-2026-6612, GO-2026-6611 and GO-2026-6603, all reached from a generated API. The first is the same HPACK encoder race go1.26.9 fixed in the standard library a release ago; the module carries its own copy, so raising the toolchain did not raise it.

Caught by the scan that generates an app and scans that, rather than the one that scans the CLI, which is the reason that job exists: the CLI does not depend on `x/net`.


## v3.394.1 - October 9, 2026

### Go 1.26.9, for an HTTP/2 crash reachable from every API

[GO-2026-6617](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6617) is a race in the HPACK encoder that crashes an HTTP/2 server, fixed in go1.26.9. It is reachable from any generated API's own server and from the CLI's update client, and `govulncheck` said so on the release that had just gone out, which is what that job is for.

The floor moves in one place and reaches everywhere: the `go` directive a generated `go.mod` carries is what setup-go and the release workflow install, and an older toolchain downloads it rather than refusing. Every workflow, every Dockerfile and all three checked-in examples move with it. `grit upgrade` raises an existing project.


## v3.394.0 - October 9, 2026

### Documentation an agent can read, pinned to the version it is true of

Grit ships several releases a week, so an agent reading today's website inside a project scaffolded three weeks ago is confidently wrong, and nothing told it so. `grit docs search`, `grit docs show` and `grit docs list` read an index of 194 pages compiled into the binary, so they work offline and they answer for the version that built them. Agents get the same thing as `grit_search_docs` and `grit_read_doc` over MCP.

Every answer carries its version, and a project scaffolded at a different one gets a warning saying which is which. That is the whole point of embedding the index rather than fetching a website.

The ranking took four attempts, and each one is a test. The changelog has 807 headings, so a naive heading count made it the best answer to every question ever asked. Headings are now weighted down as a page accumulates them, a page with more than sixty of them is scored as an aggregate rather than a topic, and coverage only counts when the terms land in a title or a heading rather than anywhere in the prose.

### The dev server writes down what it printed

A Grit application logs to stderr, which left an agent helping with it nothing to read: it could see that a command exited non-zero and not what went wrong. `grit start` now tees everything into `.grit/logs/dev.log`, keeping the previous run beside it. `grit logs` reads it with `-n`, `--errors`, `--grep` and `--json`, and `grit_dev_log` and `grit_last_errors` do the same over MCP.

`--errors` was wrong when it was first written, and using it is how that was found: during an outage where nothing started at all, it reported "nothing failed". Its patterns now cover a missing toolchain, an `ELIFECYCLE`, a non-zero exit status and a Node `ERR_` code, and the lines of context around a failure come only from the process that failed, because an API panic surrounded by Vite's output is not context.

### The conventions that cost an afternoon ship with the project

Fourteen rules that existed only as accumulated experience are now in the `AGENTS.md` every project is generated with, which went from 96 lines to 198. They are the ones whose symptom points somewhere else: an icon in the admin's icon map is not automatically a named export, a change to the login screen is six edits across six files, auto-numbering has to call `sequence.Next` directly or models and services form an import cycle.

Three of them are mechanical, so they are `grit doctor` checks rather than paragraphs: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` without `nodeLinker: hoisted`, an `APP_URL` whose port has drifted from `APP_PORT`, and a caret range on Next. All three leave a project that builds cleanly and is quietly broken.

### A generated app survives Grit being deleted, and CI proves it

The first question anyone asks about a framework with one maintainer is what happens if it stops, and it had only ever been answered with a paragraph. A CI job now scaffolds an app, generates the shapes people actually use, deletes the binary, checks that nothing named grit is on `PATH`, and then builds, vets, tests and type-checks the project. It also fails if the generated `go.mod` requires the Grit module, because an application that carries the framework with it is a different claim from the one being made.

### Six things found by building a contact app and looking at it

Every one of these was in a shared component or a generator, so every generated project had it, and every unit test passed throughout.

**The Content-Security-Policy and the app disagreed about where the API is.** The policy read `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` alone while the client fell back to `API_URL`, which is the name the generated `.env` actually sets. Move `APP_PORT` the way the comment above it invites you to, and the browser blocked every request from the web app and the admin panel, reporting it as a console violation naming a port nobody configured rather than as an HTTP status. Both read the same names now, and `grit upgrade` repairs an existing project.

**The API's address is written down four times.** `APP_PORT`, `APP_URL`, `API_URL` and the `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` that `grit seed` writes into `apps/*/.env.local` once and never overwrites. `grit doctor` checked one pair of them. It checks all four now, and says which file holds the stale copy, because a frontend calling the wrong port reports a network error or a CORS failure and never the setting that is wrong.

**`--owned-by user` put a required owner picker on the form and threw the answer away.** The service is explicit that the owner is whoever is signed in and never the body, and it is right. The admin panel did not know: it refused to submit a new contact until an operator chose a user, and then stored a row owned by the operator. Picking Jane Cooper and reading back a row owned by `admin@example.com` is how it was found. The owner is off the create and edit forms and out of the Zod schemas; it stays a column, because a table is a read.

**A `belongs_to` column showed `<relation>.name` whatever the related model was called.** The form next to it already resolved the label properly, so a contact's Group column read "Family" and its User column read a dash: a User has a first name and no name at all. Every relationship to a model labelled by a title, a number or a code had an empty column. The column uses the same rule the dropdown does now, and an email address counts as a label, so a picker of people can tell two Janes apart.

**A picker at the bottom of a form opened its list off the bottom of the window.** The panel is portalled and `position: fixed`, so nothing could scroll it back: only typing into its search box reached the options. The date picker in the same file has flipped above since it was written. Both relationship pickers do now, and the panel is never taller than the space it has, so the search box and the create action survive a tight fit.

**Two labels that were right for one column and wrong for the rest.** A boolean column said "Active" or "Inactive" whatever it was called, so a contact's `starred` column read "Inactive". It says Yes and No. The not-archived tab was labelled "Published" on every resource; a Contact is not published, and it is labelled Active. And a table with no rows in it told you to adjust a search you had never made, which is the one piece of advice that is useless to somebody who has just generated a resource: an empty resource now says so and an empty search still suggests widening it.

### pnpm run type-check type-checked nothing and exited 0

The root script runs `turbo type-check`, turbo matches tasks by name, and four app templates declared `typecheck` without the hyphen while the web and admin apps declared no such script at all. Turbo found nothing to run, printed "No tasks were executed" and exited 0.

That is the worst shape a check can take. A missing script is noticed; a command that looks like it ran, says nothing and is green is relied upon. A project generated this way could ship a type error through the CI step whose whole purpose was to catch it. One name now, three tests that every app declares it, that nothing declares the other spelling, and that the root script names a task that exists.

### examples/saas shipped without internal/storage

A `--exclude=storage` meant to skip the uploads directory also ate `internal/storage`, and the example would not build from a clean checkout. Copying a project into `examples/` now diffs the two file lists before the commit.


## v3.393.0 - October 8, 2026

### A customer portal, checked in and tested

The question people ask before starting a SaaS with Grit is whether their customers have to log into the admin panel. They do not, and `examples/saas` is the answer with the code attached: a subscription product whose customer portal lives in `apps/web` beside the operator console in `apps/admin`.

One users table, one login, one API, two front doors. The portal is not a second API: `/account/billing` reads `GET /api/subscriptions` and `GET /api/invoices`, the same endpoints the admin reads, with the same JWT. What makes it the customer's data is one flag on three resources, `--owned-by user`, which puts `authz.ScopeOwned(ctx, query, "user_id")` on every list and `authz.Owns(ctx, &item)` on every read, inside the service where a job and a command get it too.

Two mechanisms, not one, and the example needs both. A permission gets a customer through the door: they are a plain `USER` holding `subscriptions.view`, `invoices.view` and `usage_records.view`. The owner scope decides which rows are behind it.

It is checked in rather than described because data isolation in a README is a claim. `portal_isolation_test.go` makes the requests: a customer sees their own subscriptions and invoices and not the other customer's; a guessed id answers 404 rather than 403, because 403 confirms the row exists; the operator sees both, so the test cannot pass on an API returning nothing to anybody; and a signed-in stranger without the grants gets 403. They are verified to fail when the protection is removed. Deleting the `ScopeOwned` line turns the first one red with *Ada can see Basil's subscription*.

CI builds it, vets it, runs its tests, runs the isolation tests again on their own so a failure names the breach, and type-checks the portal. It is the third checked-in application and each earns its place differently: `library` proves an app generated at an earlier version still builds against today's libraries, `commerce` that hand-written code calling into generated code keeps compiling, and `saas` that the owner scope is still on the query. It is the only one of the three whose failure would be a breach rather than a build error.

Seed it and you get two customers, `ada@example.com` and `basil@example.com`, both with the password `customer123`, on different plans with different invoices. Sign in as each and compare, then sign in to the admin and see both.

### A date column could be filtered but not sorted

Found while building the example, which is what examples are for.

A generated resource's `Sortable` whitelist was built by testing each field's Go type against `string`, `int` and `uint`. A date's Go type is `*jsontime.Date` and a timestamp's is `*jsontime.DateTime`, so neither matched. Every date column in every generated project was filterable and not sortable.

It failed quietly, which is the part that made it worth a test. `paginate` drops a sort column that is not on the whitelist rather than refusing the request, so `?sort=issued_on` returned 200 with the rows in whatever order the database chose. The portal's invoice table showed October, August, September and looked like it had a sorting bug rather than a missing permission. An invoice list that cannot be ordered by its issue date is the obvious case of this, and bookings, events and anything else with a date on it had the same hole.

Dates and timestamps are sortable now, and so are floats, which covers `float`, `percent` and `rating`. Booleans are deliberately still out: ordering by true before false is a sort nobody asks for, and every name on that list widens the surface that reaches SQL. Existing projects get it by regenerating the resource, or by adding the column to `Sortable` in its service by hand.


## v3.392.0 - October 8, 2026

### A form with edits in it stops being easy to throw away

The admin had no `beforeunload` anywhere in it. A resource form with twenty fields, a rich text body and three uploads could be lost to one click on the sidebar, and nothing said so: no prompt, no warning on tab close, nothing on screen suggesting there was anything to lose. The row went back to how it was and the typing was gone.

Every generated form now tracks whether it is dirty. While it is, a quiet "Unsaved changes" sits beside the save button, and leaving asks first.

Two listeners, because they catch different accidents. `beforeunload` covers closing the tab, reloading, and leaving the site. It does **not** fire on a Next ``, which is a client-side navigation the browser never hears about, and in an admin panel that is the common one: you click Users in the sidebar with a half-filled form behind you. So the second listener sits on the capture phase of every click, finds the anchor the click is heading for, and asks before the router gets it.

It asks with `window.confirm`, which is ugly, and the prettier option was considered and rejected. The admin's own confirm modal is asynchronous, and by the time it resolves, the navigation it was meant to stop has already happened. A native confirm is the only thing that can block a click synchronously. Looking right is worth less than working.

A modified click still opens a new tab without being asked, an external link falls through to `beforeunload`, and both listeners come off the moment the form goes clean, so a saved form stops asking. The guard is off while a save is in flight: asking "leave and lose them?" about the save itself is how a prompt teaches people to click through it without reading.

### A counted card narrows the table to what it counted

Since v3.373.0 a list page has carried a card per value of each counted column: Lead 18, Customer 25, Churned 17. Every one of them was a `div` carrying `hover:border-border/80`, so the whole row lit up under the pointer and none of it did anything.

That is a worse fault on a counted card than anywhere else, because "Lead 18" is exactly the number somebody wants to click. Those cards are buttons now. Click one and the table narrows to those rows; click it again and the filter comes off, because a filter you cannot remove from where you applied it is one people reload the page to escape.

The generic cards are untouched and stay `div`s. Total and This Week have no subset to narrow to, and they lose the hover state with it: a border that lights up is a promise, and theirs had nothing behind it.

One behaviour worth knowing before it surprises you. Every count on the page describes **the rows the table is currently matching**, which is the contract since v3.373.0 and the reason the numbers agree with the Insights panel below them. So filtering to Lead leaves Customer reading 0. Clicking it still works and still shows all 25, but the number beside it is the count within the view, not the count you would get. Proper faceted counts, where a value's own filter is excluded from its own tally, mean rebuilding the query once per counted column in `internal/paginate`, and that is the hottest path in every generated project. It is a change of its own and not one to make at the end of another.

Both of these came from reading [jubayer910/Admin-panel](https://github.com/jubayer910/Admin-panel) (MIT), a portfolio admin whose settings form keeps a sticky save bar reading "Unsaved changes" or "All changes saved", and whose project list puts counted tabs above the table. Grit's forms are modals and pages rather than one long settings screen, and it already had the counted cards, so neither is a copy. The ideas are the borrowed part.


## v3.391.0 - October 8, 2026

### A password meter that measures the password

Every screen where somebody chooses a password now shows how strong it is, on a named ladder from **Very weak** to **Very strong**, with the five rules listed underneath and a check against each one that is satisfied. Sign up, reset, both profile pages, the account page, the desktop client: fifteen screens in all.

Before this there was one bar, on the admin account page, and it filled one segment per rule met. That looks exactly like a strength meter and is close to the opposite of one. The password `a` fails two of the five rules, so it lit three of five segments: a single character shown as more than half way there. Every other screen in the product showed nothing at all beyond a placeholder reading "At least 8 characters".

The ladder is an estimate of how hard the password is to guess, which means it discounts the parts an attacker gets for free. Twenty `a`s and `abcdefghijklmnopqrst` are both twenty characters and both **Very weak**, because every character after the first repeats or continues a run. `Passw0rd` passes four rules and is **Very weak**, because it is on the list attackers try first. `correct horse battery staple` is **Very strong**. And nothing the form will refuse for being too short or too samey can read above **Weak**, so the bar never contradicts the cross beside it.

The strength and the rules stay separate on purpose, because they disagree in both directions and that is the useful part. A 90-character passphrase is **Very strong** and still cannot be saved, since bcrypt will not hash it; the checklist is where that gets explained, rather than the meter calling the strongest kind of password weak.

### Four things found by building it

**The admin account page checked four of the five rules it listed.** "At most 72 characters" was in its array and in none of its code, so a password bcrypt cannot hash got a green check there and a 422 from the API. It had its own private copy of the rules, which is how: the test compared ids and labels between the server and the page, and a rule with no code behind it matches on both. There is one module now, read by every screen, and the test also checks that each listed rule is one the code can actually report.

** Five of the admin's six auth styles never set `autoComplete` on a password field. ** Nor did the web app's sign-in and sign-up, the desktop client's profile, or the standalone desktop app. Without `current-password` a password manager does not fill the sign-in form; without `new-password` it neither offers to generate a password nor offers to save the one that was typed, which pushes people towards something they can retype from memory. That is the opposite of what the meter beside it is asking for. All thirty-one password fields now say which kind they hold, including the two that hold neither: an OAuth client secret and the password on a shared form link are not the operator's credential, and a manager that saves either has stored the wrong secret under the wrong account.

** `grit add web-auth` wrote a web app that could not type-check. ** `AuthShell.tsx` is a dispatcher that imports all eight shells by name and picks one by theme. The admin registered all eight; the web app registered three. So the command wrote a dispatcher importing five modules it had not written. Nothing failed at install time and the dev server compiles only the page that is open, so the first sign of it was a build. Both now read the same list.

**The standalone desktop app promised six characters.** Its sign-up placeholder read "At least 6 characters" while the API has enforced eight for as long as the rules have existed, so it was inviting a password the server would refuse.

### Terminology, API design, and AGENTS.md per directory

Three documents for anyone working on Grit itself, human or agent. **TERMINOLOGY.md** settles the words that have two meanings in the repository: architecture against tier, scaffold against generate, and which of the admin-panel predicates answers which question, since asking the wrong one is how a double shipped a user menu linking to a page that was never written. **API_DESIGN.md** writes the HTTP contract down as a contract: the envelope, the status codes, 400 against 422, why a record the caller may not see answers 404, and the helpers that write all of it. And six scoped **AGENTS.md** files, one each for `internal/scaffold`, `internal/generate`, `cmd/grit`, `internal/ui`, `docs` and `examples`, each saying what the source of truth in that directory is, the rules that are easy to break there, and how to verify a change.


## v3.390.0 - October 7, 2026

### A long passphrase returned a 500

`golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt` refuses anything over 72 bytes outright. The password rules had a minimum and no maximum, so this passphrase

`correct horse battery staple correct horse battery staple correct horse 9!`

which is 74 bytes and passes every other rule, reached the model's `BeforeCreate`, failed to hash, and came back as `500 INTERNAL_ERROR: Failed to create user`. A long passphrase is the strongest kind, so the people turned away were the ones doing the right thing, and the error told them nothing.

There is a ceiling now, counted in bytes rather than characters because an accented letter is two and an emoji is four. It sits with the other four rules, so registering, changing and resetting all get it, the admin's checklist shows it, and the Zod schema says it before the round trip. The answer is a 422 naming the limit.

The password package was written at scaffold time only, so the fix would have reached new projects and left every existing one answering 500. It is framework-owned now, which means `grit upgrade` delivers it.

Found reading [zitadel](https://github.com/zitadel/zitadel), whose hasher validates that an encoded hash's cost parameters are within bounds before trusting it. Grit had no bound at all at the other end.


## v3.389.0 - October 7, 2026

### Every `--single --next` project failed to boot

Not intermittently. Every page threw `TypeError: _interop_require_wildcard._ is not a function` and `react.createContext is not a function`, the app showed the error overlay and reloaded, and the errors name React and webpack internals, so they read like a React problem. They are a resolution problem.

Next under webpack requires `@swc/helpers` from its own compiled client chunks, and pnpm's default isolated layout does not put that anywhere Next can reach: `node_modules/@swc` did not exist. `.npmrc` has asked for `node-linker=hoisted` for exactly this reason for a long time, and pnpm 10 ignores it when a workspace file is present, reading `nodeLinker` from `pnpm-workspace.yaml` instead.

A `--single --next` gained a workspace file when its frontend moved to the project root, and lost the setting with it. The workspace carries `nodeLinker: hoisted` now, and the `.npmrc` stays for projects without one.

The same file also listed `frontend` as a workspace member. A single's frontend has been the project root since v3.380.0, so that named a directory which is not there.

**If you have a project in this state:** run `grit upgrade`, then delete `node_modules` and `pnpm install`. The lockfile and the module layout both have to be rebuilt; the upgrade alone will not do it.


## v3.388.0 - October 7, 2026

### The CLI, redesigned

Built to the style guide in `cli-design/`. The rule it turns on is that colour has to say something: green worked, yellow read this, red stopped, blue is a thing you can type or pick. Body text has no colour at all, because the terminal's own foreground is the only value readable on every theme anybody runs.

Every role is a pair, a dark-terminal value and a light one, so the output reads on both without configuring anything. The brand is cobalt: `#6AA7FF` on dark, `#0B57C9` on light, each with an ANSI-16 fallback for terminals without 24-bit colour. `GRIT_THEME=light` overrides the detection when a terminal will not answer.

Colour never carries meaning alone: every status has a glyph as well, so the output still reads with `NO_COLOR` set, piped to a file, or on a console that cannot draw `✓` and gets `ok` instead.

### Results, not activity

Thirty-four lines of `→ Scaffolding Go API...` are now a checklist of finished nouns with their timings. The difference shows at the end, which is when anybody reads the whole block: a list of nouns is a summary of what you got, a list of participles is a transcript of a process that is over.

The stage that is running is rewritten in place when it finishes. In a pipe, in CI, or with `NO_COLOR` set there is no cursor control at all, just one plain line per stage, so a build log stays readable.

`grit new` ends with a result line carrying the facts ( `Created my-app Single · Atlas · 14.2s`) rather than &ldquo;Project created successfully!&rdquo;, and the next steps are commands in brand colour with their comments aligned beside them, no `#`, because they were never shell comments.


## v3.387.0 - October 7, 2026

### The database is a question now

`grit new` asks for it, after the architecture, the frontend and the theme. It was `--db` or nothing, so everybody who ran the command without flags got Postgres and a docker-compose they had to start before the project would do anything. SQLite is the shortest path to a running app and it was reachable only by reading the flag's help text.

The options are built from the same table the flag validates against, so the picker and the flag cannot drift. That has gone wrong before: five themes shipped that only `--theme` knew about, and a missing option is invisible in a way a rejected flag is not.

### The CLI is not purple any more
